On the 29th Jyly, 1847, I left Moscow by diligence, for Nijhni, Novgorod, &ccémpanied by Mr. Marshal, with whom I had seen a portion of the two Russian capitals. Ourimmediate purpose, was to fisit the grand fair so famous in the cqnmercial history of northern Europe, which is annually held there.

After passing through,several paved Streets, we entered the-most agreeable of the suburbs of the town, where we crossed, one of the bridges of the river Jaousa, which enters. the city from the north-ea8t, and falls into the Maskva at a short distance beyond the upper walls of thé Kremlin.

The whole of <the wicinity of this stream in these suburbs exhibits the rarest objects of interest that are, perhaps, any wkere to ba,seen withfn the walls of acity. In passing the bridge, on the left hand appear many Villas, which, wth the buildings of several public

institutions, adorn the outskirts of the town; and on the opposite hand, upon the banks of the river on both sides, may be seen neat one and two story houses, painted ‘generally white, with green roofs, and with gardens and shrubberies inclosed within railings, pree senting altogether one of the most pleasing! as well as novel views jmaginable.g

But if.we Were gratified with the “ieee prospect from this site, it bore no comparison with that which presented itself from the rise of a little hill-which forms the Ieft bank of the Jaousa. The whole city, trowned by its venerabla Kremlin, and displaying its hundreds of gilded and gaily paintededomes and cupolas, was here beheld at one view, and, with_a foreground of beautiful villas and gardens, presented to us a spectacle unlike in character, and not inferfor in interest, (0 any scene, not indebted to.Nature for its grandeur or beauty, that it had been my fortune at any timeeto behold.

After, passing the gate of the outer wall of the city, we came upon sn open plain counjry. Here and there, at different distances, aj%peared groves of firs and birch-trees, and at intervals, fields sown chiefly with rye, whtch was in some instances already under the operation ‘of the sickle. Buf the land seemed everywhere to beebut indifferently cultivated. °

Our first*change of horsgs was at the small town of Bogorodsk, where we observed nothing differing from what had seemed to characterise all the towns of the inferiof class that we had before seen. Soon after this, we passed a princely edifice, situated aboyt half a verst from the réad, upon our righthand. It consisted of a low,long regular building, with wings united to the centre by handsome colonnades, and was painted with the usual lively colours of bright yellow wad light green ; and we afterwards learned, that it was the property of a boyar of large estates in this part pf theecountry. The’ woods

‘about this building were tastfully planted; but the effect was in some degree spoiled, as is not unfrequently the case with similar edifices in our own country, by a pool of stagnant water in the foreground.

+ At eight o'clock, we stopped to take tea at an inn at the government post-station in a emgll viflage, where we had the pleasure of makjng the acquaintance of several of our fellow-passengers, who ‘were seated in another department of the diligence, and among whom was Herr Kroff, a German commercial gentleman, from whom We afterwards received many civilities at N ijhni Novgcrod.

Our road, upon the second day, was through a fine country, well wooded, and apparently better cultivated than any we had hitherto seen in Russia. At the distance of every eight or ten® versts, the soil is here watered by a rivulet, from the hanks of whieh the land ever y where rises gradually to the height of one or two hundred feet on both sides, and fotms a coptinuous plain, sometimes sufficiently undulated for the travelley, to obtain a tolerable fiew of tlte immediate country around. At one o'clock in the afternoon, we arrived at the city of Vladimir, which is situated i in the ‘midst of this productive plain. Bat wg remained here only long enough to take a hasty repast. °

This ancient city, since jt ceased to be the capital of a grand duchy or principality of Russia, in the early part of the fourteenth century, has gradually declined in wealth and population. It is still, however, the capital of the government of the same name, and remains surrounded by a fitch and earth ramparts, though the number of its inhabisants does not now exceed 7000 souls.

We had no opportunity @f observing more of the town, than that its principal street through which we passed, was spacious, and formed chiefly of houses of brick and stone, but a very few of which were equal in appearance to those of the meaner sort in Moscow.

In the country that we passed through towards the same evening, we observed that the crops of every ‘kind, were more fprward than those in the western part of the distriet; and theerye and barley were generally under the sickle.

Our way, during the early part of ‘the third morning of our journey, lay through a still finer and betters cultjvated country than we had yet seen, exhibiting a rich varicty of edark groves, green meadows, and ex- ‘tensively cultivated plains. About two hours before noon, we passed the river Oka,by a floating bridge ; and about noon, we entered a dense fir-forest.
At the moment, of *reaching this forest, a little scene, slighgly illustratjve of the primitive condition of the Russian peasantry, afforded us a minute’s.

amusement. Thére w&s here a clear and flowing stream; and it Ifappened that the hgat of the day, which was excessive, had atflacted a party of fair bathers from a neighbouring village, who were sporting in the water and upon the yiver’s banks, just as if this portion of the’ earth were still a paradise, and the daughters of the land quite unconscious ofthe necessity or convenience of clothing..

The road through the forest was gloomy, and relieved only occasionally by the presgnce of a party of wood-cutters. “The forest had been the resort of robbers, gnd was now infested with bears and wolves, from which the roads however were kept tolerably free, by a systematic arrangement for watclring, which was quite novel tous, 'At intervals are placed especial guards of the forest, who repose at the Weight of fifteen or sixtecn feet above the ground, upon beds of fir-boughs laid on frames which rest upon four posts, and afe protected from the o

sun and the rain, by straw roofs or canopies, raised above them. - In these frail watch towers, these guards are secure, at least from the attacks of any wild beasts during their hours of repose at night, and they can see the further by day, and judge better of the enemy’s strength, before exposing themselves to too unequal a combat. Beneath their beds,or upon stands close at hand, vest spears, resembling boardiug-pikes, ready to serve them to combat with the wild beasts when required. ;

In the centre of the forest, we found a post-ifin, at which we stopped to change horses. As soon as we had alighted hére, Mr. Marshal and myself approached the door, in search of some refreshments, while the rest of the party dispersed, we fnew not whither. But such appeared to be the filthy state 8f the sole room of which the house seemed to consist, that after -peeping in at the door, we could net make up our minds to enter; nor could we get anything to satiefy our appetites, which happened to be most inconveniently good. The inn seemed to be in the po€session of three women, whose appearance and demeanour we thought presented the nearest approach to: those of the most Savage races of our diversified species, qhat we had ever Seen in any country where a post-road was known.

When we found that we could get nothing to “eat, and neither tea, nor wine, nor anything to make a refreshing drink pf, we asked for some water. This, indeed, they gave us, but neither willingly ndéy abundantly ; and it was so bad, that although we were very thirety, we could ‘not drink it; so we sat down upoh some stumps of trees nearat hand, and amused ourselves, by endeavouring to scold our postilion for not having told us on the way, that we weredo-day to pass through such a destitute country. But this was not just; for it was our part to. have maffe inquiry concerning the accommo-
dation upon the road, and not his, to have cared for anything but his own necessities and those of his horses. j
We were not however to starve, and good was in store for us, of which we had not dreamed, and which our impatience scarcely deserved :
.“ Mahy, dream not%o find, neither deserve, And yet are steep'd in favours.”

At a moment, while we were trying to soften the hard heart of the bad specimen of the beau sexe at whose mercy we seemgd to be, and who we were convinced had some milk, from haviag seen a cow in thé wood, our travelling companion already pentioned, who was well acquainted with the country, and who had removed with all the other travellers, ffom the dirt about the house, to the wood upon the opposite side of the road, and made a fire, suddenly summoned us to come and partake of cold fish-pie and hot téa; and we had now a famous feast. _ As soon as all eur appetites were satisfied, we continued our journey; and, at'fiv@ o’clock in the evening of the same,day, we came in sight of the place of our destination. °: -. : The towh of Nijhni Novgoyd, as we approached it, * appeared befgre us, situated upon elevated ground, upon the ‘south paint at the conflyence of the rivers Oka and ‘Volga. But the fair is held upon the left bank of the Oka, at about a verst (or three-quarters of a mile) from the poirft at which its stream unites with the great river of Russia, and immediately opposite to the busier portion of the town, to which its site is connected, at this season of the year, by a floating bridge. « + ° We had to pass through a part of the fair on our way to the town. And what we now thus accidentally and prematurely saw, did not give us a very favourable impression of the character -of this @urious place of ex~

change. We saw nothing indeed but lines of rough sheds, enveloped in a thick cloud of dust, raised by the men and beasts of burden which were moving from place to place, and which was not a little augmented by our heavy vehicle and the six horses that tramped before it.

, My companion expressed quis disappointment very strongly, at our having made Ssuch a journey to see, ‘as it appeared, a parcel of half wild sheep-skirr clad fellows, engaged in exchanging inferior objects of commerce, in a cloud of dust almost too dense to leave the mew and their beasts visible at the distance of half a dozen yards.

After crossing the bridge, the diligénce stopped, and our German friend left us, and we entered our hotel, where we were fortunat€ enough to obtain two rooms which were cénnected by a door between them. We found the windows of both closed’; afid we were told that we should by‘ng means -open them, as*the rooms, if we did so, would be instantly filled with dust, of which a dense cloud was even here floating gt all heights in the air. Finding, therefowe, the heat oppressive, we threw off our coats, and seated ourselves upon our beds to enjoy a little repose.

We had not, however, been many minutes at our ease, before*we had a strangé visit Of congratulation ab our safe arrival. While we were calmly, talkinge over the incidents of the journey, with the door between our two rooms standing open, Mr. Marshal’s door was violently struck and suddenly burst open, and a gentleman in shirt and trousers rushed in, and with an English hyrah ! and’ the phrase, not less especially English, “D—° nit, haw are you, my fine fellow? ” accompanied by the maddest gestures, greeted my friend and congratulated our arrival. =

Our welcome visitor, proved to be Mr. Wilkinson, a youhg commercialegentleman of Hull, who had been bd acquainted with Mr. Marshal at Moscow. He had left that city some time before us, with a Russian-servant and interpreter, and had been waiting in the expectation of receiving letters that were to be addressed to him here. And for the want of some occupation, or ofa previous training to enjoy or endure solitude in a crowd, he had fallen into a statg of ennui that he found almost insupportable. -But while he was in this condition, as he described it fo us, and reposing upon his bed, his servant had seen us alight from the diligence, and perceiving that we were Englishmen, had inquired of the conductor wha? were our names, which, as soon as he heard, he carried to his master, who at the name of Marshal, started from his bed, and hastgned to pay his friend this: congratulatory visit.

Tue celebrated fair which,is now héld at Nijhni Novgorod, dates its proper institation from the year 1648, at which epoch it was established at Makarief, about fifty miles lower down the Volga than the site upon which it is at present held. ° In the year 1816 however, upon the accasion of the destruction of its buildings by fire, it was remove to its present site, where it is less exposgd to the annual inundations of the great river, which had contifually threatened its destruction while it yas held at Makarief. Since this time, the encouragement of the government, an@ its admirable position in the very centge of the vast inlané navigation of the empiré, have raised it to be, probably, ‘the greatest * place of exchange of meychandise actualby pehbited upon the face of “the globe.
But before we mingle with the busy throngs at this great gathering of the commercial world, it will be as well to make a faw concise remarks toncerning the ‘races which compose the Russian people.

The Russians empire is inhabited by a humber of nations and tribes of different origin and language, and of various degrees of Gajlisation: ffom that of the refineMent attained by a portion of the Sclavonic race, differing in nothing? from, that of. the most advanced people in Europe, down to the condition of the half wild man still roaming over the Siberian - deserts, and subsisting by the use of the bow and arrow. Neverthe- ‘less, all the seemingly distinct races, which we find settled, or following still their pastoral or nomadic lives, between the, Ural mquntains and the western districts of the empire, appear togderive their origin from two séurces—from. the great Caucasian family, and from the Mongoltan tribes. From causes however, the details of which belong to the history of barbarian conquests, to that of constrained and voluntary emigration, and to tte effects of manners morals and customs, upon the increase. and “decrease of numbers among particular races, the proportion of the population of Mongol origin, which was once considerable, is not now supposed to exceed a hundredth part of th&t of the entire empire.

The portion of the population delonging to the Caucasian family, inhabiting Russia Proper, has been divided, and proBably very, justly, into‘three brayches, the Sclavonic, the Thule or Fian, and tle Tatar.. And it is with tolerable exactness ascertained, that the first of these, the Sclavonia, contpose about nine-tenths of the whole of the populationeof Caucasian sorsin in the empire. The

‘people of this race are, however, subdivided into Russians properly so called, Lithuanians, Poles, Lettes, Wallachians, and Servians, “the Russians of all these being so greatly predominant as to compose about twothirds ef the population of. the empire, or, amounting to about forty millions of souls. Those, indeed, of this bfanch of the grand Caucasian famtily, may be gon sidered to*compose the more solidsportion of the éntire population.
In a word, the true Ryssian nationality is formed, like our own, from the amalgamation of a variety of races, of which one chiefly stamps the character and shadows

the destiny. Just in the same manner that all the races that successively settled in Britain, have mingled the elements of their character, only to modify that of the Saxon, it is evident, that all the blood of all the races that have settled in this empire, will finally be confounded with, and only modify that of the epredominant branch of the Sclavonic race of theggrand “Caucasian family which has given its name to the country and its inhabitants.

- We found, on the acenas after our arrival at Nijhni Novgorod, that we were just in time to witness a religious ceremony, which is in usage, of consecrating the W&ters of the river before the proper opening ofthe fair. The ceremony cannot fail to interest the stranger, from the importance which is attached to it by the Russians. Indeed, until this service is performed, although there is a great deal of business previodsly transacted, the fair is not, in a religieus, or truly Russian sense, deemed lawfully open; and, all prior transactions are considered by the Proper Russian, merchants, asesuch only as Jews and pagans might be yardoned fer being concerned in, and as haydly entitled’ to success.

We breakfasted early ;. and under thé charge of our young friend, whose ecstasies at our arrivat were now calmed down to more sober joy, we recrosged the bridge * over which we had passed, on the preceding day ;°and turning upon our left, weemade our way across an open space strewed with iron in every form in which it is made arrarticle of commerce, and with such other coarse goods as pottery, and ropes and hides, to about half a verst above the bridge, where the crowd was gathering to witness the ceremeny above mentioned.

Upon arriving near the place where the consecration takes place, we found gread,preparatiofis made for the occasion, and some thousands of people assembled. About fifteen or ttenty, yards from the bank of the river had been erected a pavilion set on piles, and connected with the shore by a railed gangway, and probably large enough to hold about a hundred persons. The bishop of the diocese, who was to perform the ceremony, was not long before he made his appearance with a, namerous retinue. The procession advanced from what segmed the centre of the fair, through a dense multitude, formed of the votaries of commerce from many nations, and of every grade, which divided and left an alley open, by which the priests with all the gorgeous symbols of their religion, approdthed the iver. The bishop carried in his right hand a cross, and was preceded by about half a dozen other priests, one of whom hore a large crucifix, |and followed by several more, and after these by a train composcd of the civil an@ military officers, including his excellency the governor of the department, to which was added a host of the inferior orders of the officials from the » churches*; andethere were also two ladies in the procession,

Arrived at the river's bank, the whole party in regular order, crossed the gangway to the isolated pavilion over the stream. We would have followed them ;- but even among sucl®a wild-looking set pf fellows in sheep-skins, of which the,crowd for the greater part consisted, our most respectable appearance, was not sufficient to gain us admittance. However, we contrived by clambering up a pile of bales of merchandise that was near the water, t® obtain a tolerably good view of the little holy place, and of the ceremony of the cousecration which now took place.

In the centre of the platform of the-pavilion was ‘eft an opening resembling the well of a fishing-vessel, with a low railing afound it; ags between this andean outer railing, the parties that had composed the procession now stood, the priests generally og the tnner side.

The bishop held a book of prayer open in his hand; and from time to time, water was drawn from the stream, and received certain especial benedictions, ‘by prayers accompanied with the sprinkling of incense.

This was all we were able to observe of the act of consecration, by which the Volga qnd all its tributaries were sanctified, and every thing that Noated, or was to float upon their thousand streams, on it§ way to tlfe fair, or on its passage hence, whether thes property of Jew, Turk, pagan, or Christian, was equally blessed and made lawful for the most pious Russian to purchase and deal in. But a scene followed, which was more open to the observation of a stranger, SeTnd was well calculated to impress us with the truth of opinions which we previously entertainfa concerning the lively and sincere piety of the people, hewever different may be the form in which it is shown, ftom that in which we are accustomed tg regard dets of faitlf and religious exercises, among ourselveg We had, before the ceremony comjnenced, observed a pgrty of the police set to work, to drive some of theamultitude out of the river, in which they had been standing immersed almost up to the middle; but we did not know the reasons, either for this, or for the fove of these good people for the water, by standing in whith they ¢ could see no better than from the shore, until the mystery ‘yas noweex~ plained. At the moment,the procession wholly gained the shore upon its return from the pavilion, there was a rush from all sides into the river, every one. being eager to dip himself as quickly as possible in the waters of the freshly consecrated stream. Nothing could more reserible the bathing of a party of pilgrims at the Jordan. The haste, however, of the pilgrims of the Oka, was much greater than that of these of the holier river. Some, in their eagerness to get holy water enough, and perhaps afraid dhat the virtue of what was now sanctified might too quickly depart, yet fearful of getting beyond their depth, after dashing in, stopped as suddenly, and stood up to their kaees in the stream, and bending forwards, threw: water upon their heads with their hands, and splashed and paddled about, more like ducks ig a pond, newly awakened from sleep, than like wholly terrestrial bipgds; while the more courageous, or more piobs, proceeded and stood immersed up to their chins m the water. Others, less eager, or perhaps less regarding the quantity than the quality of the purifying element, formed themselves on each side of the Walk of the _Procession, where several of the priests, who carried MitZe vases of the water: more immediately blessed, and such little. brooms as are used in the churches for a like purpose, dashed the holy fluid about with a prodigalityethat nothing bift its plentifulness might excuse? We ourselves, too, were at this time among"the crowd ;°and we egjoyed as much of the
_sacerdotal bounty. as might have been less agreeable

Similar ceremonies, for the canctification of every~ thing, were performed upon a comprehensive scale throughout the fair. But the merchant that occupied the dwelling which was nearest to the place at which the waters were consecrated, was entitletl, upon the occasion, to.a double privilege, on account of the position which he enjoyed. His apartments, into which the priests entered, received the greatest quantity of the sacred water which all, in larger or smaller proportions, shared, and, he was favoured, to the full capacity of his rooms, with the company of his friends, whom, he entertained at a Champagne dinner, The whole day was, in fact, devoted to these consecrations. From the palace of the governor of the department, which stands in the midst of the fair, to “the meanest shed, all were sprinkled with the consecrated water. Every artiele of e

merchandise aid of food*was blessed, until nothing remained unholy. Thus the coffee and sugar which we afterwards took for‘our breakfast, and the meat, but the fish especially which swim in+the consecrated stream, upon which we dined, and the tea that we took in the evening, as well as our bowl of punch, if we thought proper to finish with this, were,all holf.

. It should be remarked here, however, that this disposition towards making everything sficred, is a sentiment peculiarly interwoven with the Russian character, and, that the ceremony which we have just seen, is but such as takes place ever ywhere, sith sdinething or other for its objegt, upon & great scale, periodically, but also upon a smaller scale, continually, The rivers are blessed every where, as they begin to swell in the spfing, that the s@cred water may render the land more productive. The fruits of the land also receive the same blessing when in the bléssom, that their growth may be accelerated, and again at maturity, that they may nourish those who partake of thefh. The great consecration of te-day -was to render holy the fruits of industry and the produce of art, as well as to sanctify the bargains and dealing of those wha came to transact business at the fair’ And just as the cultivator of the soil léoks for the blessing of Heayen, through the sanctification of the Church upon the druits wltich are raised by the sweat of his brow, so the merchant hopes, by the same favour, to see his dealings thrive and his purse replenished.
We did not follow the religious party any further, during the performance of their pions offices, but proceedell to take a first general survey of the fair.

We walked directly from the water side, towards what appeared to us to be the centre of the great place of exchange, After passing ‘by héaps of the coarser descrtption of good» before mentioned, between the river and the first line of the sheds, and crossing the ends of several passages and alleys, formed by temporary stalls, and shaded from the sun by awnings across from the roofs of the sheds, we entered a great square, which forms the most open, but not the busiest quarter of the fair.

The entire side of thjs open space, is formed by one of two fronts of a handsome stone building, the centre part of whtch is occupied by thé military governor of the department or government of Novgorod, ‘at this time the Prince Urasoff, and the wings of which contain — the Tiffereadgp pic offices, with the residences of several of the especiaPofficials fay the time of theeduration of the fair. The remaining three sides of the square are occupied chiefly by shops for the sale- of goods by retail, and are ornamtnted’ by colonhades. In the centre of the grand” public edifice, a btoad double archway, supported in the middle by buttresses, conducts from the open sqeare ta the inner and more important “lines and alleys of the fair. Within thig archway, also, there are a numberof stalle appropriated, for the greater part, to the sale of valuable and fine goods, chiefly by retatl; such as Persian shawls and gowns, and
Chinese silks Pak the East, and trinkets and jewellery’

from the Wgst. The grand staircase, Iéading to the governor’s apartments in the, palace, is also here, as well as the entrance to several of she public offices, and that to the grand restaurant of the fair.

Afte? passing the archway, we came into the very centre of this grand deposit of the exchangeable produce of half the nations of the world. Great order and regularity, in the plan of the buildings for the a&commodation both of the merchants and of their stores may be here remarked. Immedjately opposite the.centre of the governor’s palace, on this side, a double line of low stone buildings with colonnades,*form a grand ‘road

way which. is called the centre alley. This runs through the chief seat of all the great transactions of the fair, and terminates upon another square, which has its upper end formed by the national church, and one of its sides’ by a mosque, and the other by an Armenian church,

Upon each side of this maip thoroughfare run six other lines of buildings, equally substantially constructed ; and from the square proceed liries crossing at right- angles all the lines that run parallel to the grand _alley.

‘The grand alley, is appropriated chi to®the sale of goods- by retail ; whilg in the liffes which run parallel with it on both sides, are deposited the cloths, furs, cotton and other manufactured goods, which form the great staptes of the produce of the Christian nations. But the lines that cross*® these, form the*- depoSits of the Chinese, Persian, Buchara,°and Tatar merchandise, which is indicateg by their style of construction and dgcoration.

In these grand divistons of the fair, every line, or some portion of it, is appropriated to the deposit and sale of some particular description of goods, such as custom or convenienc@ fas classed under the same head. In the fair are found®all the more- important productions of the East and the West, and the North and the South. Here arg exchanged the produce of the industry of Western Europe, improved by the advance of the arts, for the furs of Siberia, Kamtsehatka, and even Russo-America, and for the works of pure human labour fsom Persia, Bochara, Tatary,° Asia Minor and the mountains of Turkestan, and for the silks and teas of China. Here may be met the merchants, and theiy assistanty in the vérious national costumes of all these distant countries, except China,
the merchants of which country are represented by the Tatars.

This substantially built part of the fair, does not include above half the edifices of all sorts, which compose the great commercial depository. The rest, however, consist almost whglly of large temporary sheds, which are necessarily *emoved after the season of business, to void the ifundations, from which even this site of the fair is not wholly secure, and by which they might otherwise find their way to the Caspian Sea. On some of the stone buildings we were shown the mark of the las inundation, at about seven feet from the ground.

The whoRef this great area, except the side by the river, for the better protection of the goods against fire, which may not be brought “in any’form into the fair, is surrounded by a wide canal in the form of a horseshoe, beyond whith, especially on the side below the fair, in reSpect.to th® course of the river, thefe are houses for refreshment and entertainment.

Among the gcenes exhibited at this great concourse of nations,, not the,least attractive to the stranger from Western Europe, is that which is presented by* the shipping on the river. The Russians, whether designedly or not, have a way ‘of relieving the formal moments that precede the announcement of *dinner, during «he assembling of the guests, by the introduction of a Kind of )semi-meal called zakooska, which some translate luncheon, but certainly improperly, on accoynt of*the different relative times at which these two mealseare take. Few of ethe Continentals, although they read of cabinet dinners, alderrgen’s feasts, and of the dining and feasting of the leading members of a thousand institutions of one kind or another in England, have any idea of the nature of the influence of these entertainments upon the affairs in which those who attend them are AssWiated,.or indeed of their effects generally upon our entire soci#l conditign. Certainly, the state that debeted their political affairs once when, sober and once when inebriated, were in the wrong in*supposing, at least if the effects of their intoxicattmg beverages were Ijke those of Port wine and Sherry upan ourselves, that their debafes were more erfergetic when. under the influence of them. Wnuar remains to be said concerning the fair in the true spirit in which i¢ should be refarded, may be perhaps appropriately preceded by a few remarks concerning the peculiar classificatien of the commercial orders generally throughout the country, arid upon the relation’ which ghey bear to the rest of the Russian . people.

It has often been supposed in Southern Europe, that Russia has degraded her trading population, and arbitrarily sujected this indispéngable class in every civilised state, to the, disrespect of their equals, or even of their inferiors, beth in worldly condition and in their natural position among the other arders of the people. But this impression is certainly erroneous. The.student of political economy might, on the céntrary, search the history of the commercial classes under every form of goverhment, from the time the Pheenicians came to purchase the useful metals in owr remote island, and through the age when the proud argosies of the royal merchant of tlte Queen a6 commercial states ~—,
“ Like seigniors and rich he See of the flood, Did over-peer the petty trafhckers,” ‘
down to the latg sovereigns of Egypt and Holland, and not find a system better adapted to the political age of the country in which it exists, than that Which obtains in Russia.

Here, the political and social position of the trading portion of the population, and the sanks of he classes into which they must necessarity be divided, are regulated by a just standard, and defined by law.”.Thus, alf those who are engaged in any way in commercial transactions, are formed into three grades, which have severally their place in society in proportion to their wealth, which must be regarded for the most part as the,represem®ttive

‘of merit, as Well as the legitimage standard by which the position they ought to ocgupy should be ascertained. But besides the conveniences arising from the order which this-arratigement introduees into the social relations among the people, it has the advantage of encouraging enterprise and ¢ndustry among the whole class, the superior grade being open te every one who is able to accumulate sufficient wealth to attaia that ratik.

The three grades int which the trading population are thus divided, are termed the first, the second, and the third guild; and the amount of the wealth which determines the grade to which ghey severally Bclong, is ascertained by a tax of 1} per cent per agnum, which is levied upon the capital, whether nominal or real, which they declare themselves to have engaged in their affairs. The amount necessary to entitle the merchant to the rank and privilege of the first guild, is 60,000 rubles; that which is. necessary to the second, is, only 500], rubles ; andthat which is required for the third, is but 4000 rubles., se

The merchants of the first guild, have exclusively the privilege of carrying on forgjgn commerc®; and besides their rank among the members of the commercial fraternity, they have Severgl of the privileges of the nobility ; while the merchants of the second and third guilds have no higher privileges than ordinary burghers.

As to the foreign merchants in Russia, they enjoy the same privileges as the merchants of the first guild, in everything essential that concerns foreign commerce; but they aye not permitted to engage in the internal trade of the country. * It certainly seems to me that nothing could be more judicious, or more worthy of imitation, than this Russian mode of classifying the commercial order of thepeople. For acquired wealth, under the system upon whieeEuropean society is based, must in general represent memt of one, kind or other; and industry and perseverance, which are clearly the means by which men of this order become rich, are at the same time the qualities in men by which the stdte is most benefited and civilisation the most advanced, and without which no“ability, no genius, ne enterprise, can in an equal degree contribuje to the interests and solid advantages of socigty.

Nevertheless, since the possgssion of these means to riches, is not incompatible with great depravity of character, it would appear at first to be wrong to deem wealth asquired by the pdssgssion of them, as a proper guide to distinguish merit of any kind, or determine’ the rank tp which men should be entitled in civilised society. To this objection, however, an answer must easily suggest itself. By the qualities through which richeseare acquired the state is benefited, and the state repays those who possess and use them for her advantége, by conferring rank and distinction. | But where the moral conduct seems.to fprm a contfast to those qualities by which the state has determined the formal rank ¢@f the citizen, public, opinion operates to counteract the disadvantages which might arise from the too great réspect paid to those ‘who possess attributes
which, however, they may benefit the state, politically considered, when unaccompanied by corresponding virtues, have not -a favourable effect upon the general interests of society.

affected, as it appeared to uS, either ienorance of, or indifference concerning, all matters of the kind, and always brought the subject back again to the affairs of trade.. Our conversations with the Tatars were more lively, partly owing, as it appeared to us, to their greater intelligence, and partly to their sbejng Mequainted with the Russian tongue. Among.other thifgs, he asked whether we had any, mosque in England, for any residant Mussulmans or Visiters that might be among us. And to this, my friend who acted as interpreter, added, as he informed me, and doubtless with intent to compliment my country, that as we were considered in Europe, to be, after the Russians, the Germaps, and the French, the most tolerant people in the world, there could be little doubt that, if any Tatars thowght proper to come and settle among us in sufficient number, that they would he admitted, if not to equal privileges with those who professed the proper religion of the country, at least to such as the Jews enjoyed, who, though not quite put on a level with the Christians, had many synagogues ift our cities.

Our conversation stigl proceeded a little further upon “the same subject. No one who is acquainted with the Koran, antl the opinions which the Mahomedans hold of the Author of Christianity, and also with the opinions entertained by the reformed Jews in England concerning the Author of our religion, can fail to recognise one remarkable smnilarity, -amid many wide differences, between the two opinions entertained by these people severally upon that particular head. The Moslems, it is clear, regard “ Jesus the son of Mary” as a prophet only second to the author of their religion ; 3; while the reformed Jews, who have rejected the old scafidal of imposture, still vetained by the rest, regard ‘ Jesus of Nazartth” as a,reformer of the corruptions which crept into their system duying the Babylonian captivity, and as a just as well as bold opponent of the hypocrisy of their priestsp whoepersecuted him even to death.* There is betwee these two religigns in relation to each other, also, a perfect agreement concerning the unity of the Beity, with entire exemption from the least approaches to idolatry.

These two circumstancés in particular formed the subject for the rest of our discourse with our Mussulman friends; but as details concerning conversations - that*were not always very clear to the parties by whom they were held, would necessarily be very tédious, I shall only further report the answer of the chief
