I must further add, that every one tg whom the account of this affair wag related thought it the luckiest thing in the world that I did not strike the anagistrate ; for, in case the fellow had uttered any thing that might have seemed a defmite command to take prompt vengeance, which it was believed he was very likely in that case to have done, the Yakoute peasants} that surrounded him would not have hesitated a mdnent to knock out my brains, Future travellers in Siberia, therefore, ought to beware of an encounter with any zasidytell that,they may chance to find upon the banks of the Léna.
CHAP. XV. vor4GE DOWN THE LENA—continued.

IMMEDIATELY opposite to Vintimskaia the River Vintim falls in a fine bold stream into the Léna; and as the great river does not here become broader, the force of the current is considerably augmented. : We had qp this day the first southerly wind that favoured us during our voyage, accompanied with rain. The land on either side of the river wasehere lower than any we bad seen for some days, and a greater quantity of snow appearéd upon the country, especially on our right hand; and there was but little diminution VOL. II. N
‘of the ‘cold. During the.night we passed the viflage of Chanfarinskaia.

The text day we crossed the line of the 60th degree of latitude; and although the sun at this season in this parallel is still near six hours below the horizon, it was hardly dusk at midnight. Our course was here easterly ; and the wind, which had changed to that direction, was now colder than we had before felt it at any time since we-embarked. The face of the country was here similar to that through which-we had passed upon the preceding day, shaded with the deeper green” foliage of the several varieties of the firs of more stunted. growth; and’ the snow and. ice were in the eusual quantities.

In the middle of the day, we passed by the village of Bagajarinskaia. In the afternoon, the wind was suffliciently strong to impede our progress considerably, until a contrivance of the mother of invention to counteract its effects was thus constructed aud employed. The boatmen rigged a large square frame, composed of poles of about ten feet in length, by which was held extended a closely wrought net. At two of the corners of this were tied large stones, and at all the corners were attached the ends of ropes; which led to a larger rope at about twenty feet from the frame, precisely after the manner of the logship and line. This frame was now thrown into the stream, and one side of it sinking by the weight of the stones at two of the corners, placed it exactly in the position of the logship when overboard, with its upper edge even with the surface of the water. And now, while this drifted with the current, wholly unaffected by the, wind, as the line was paid out, it discovered ‘to us that we were losing, by the counteraction of the, wind, about a verst and a half an hour, or, in other words, stemming the stream through this opposition of the elements, and drifting that distance

less ‘py the land during: the hour than ‘the’ current was runngg. But,: upon making the~rope fast, the frame instantly acted like a propelling force against the wind, and appeared. nearly to-negative its effects. A sail, or a few yards of canvass would doubtless have ‘Obtained, for.us all the advantage we received from the invention, even better than our net.

Towards evening we approached a more mountainous country; and during the period of the dim light, in the short absence of the sun, we passed through a strait, which the navigators of the Léna have rightly named ‘Tchookhea—the Magnificent. The natural objects here ‘present the most striking of all the scenes which this mighty river exhibits. I saw them, unfortunately, but imperfectly ; for I was not previously informed of our approach towards any thing remarkable, and I was sound asleep when we passed through the grandest portion of the strait. Happily, however, I rose by accident, while we had yet a distant yiew of the remarkable objects by which it is formed. At the distance of ten or fifteen versts, by full daylight, it appeared like a vast rent in the range of mountains, which are here composed of granite rock. But this distance was too great to observe it from, to admit of the spectator speaking confidently of the breadth of the passage, or of any thing further concerning it.

The whole country, indeed, at this part of the Léna is magnificent in the extreme. It resembles some of the grander passes of the Rhine, near the sources of that river, with the advantage to the spectator, who may be navigating the Léna, of flgating upon a far mightier®stream. In some places, indeed, appear the boldest and most picturesque scenery tha may, perhaps, be any where beheld, bordering any river in any land. The most striking that I saw to advantage was at the mouth of the River Ora, which falls by a

- narrow channel, between high and precipitous jocks upon the left bank, into the parent stream. I9 was such as we think we could gaze upon for ever. But there was a novelty which formed a portion of it, of a very rare kind among the natural objects that mountain lands exhibit. ‘The mother of the arts was here seen rather as a copyist of the works of men’g hands than as the model to guide them. Perhaps Nature has no where produced any thing more nearly resembling the works, of men “than the prodigious rotks with which she has here bordered and overhung this great river# I was for a minute or two deceived: and: believed we. were looking upon -the remains of the architectural works of some race of our species that might have inhabited the land, when the great mammoth trod the firm earth of the country, at this time watered by the mighty Léna. The appearance, indeed, which is here presented of architectural ruins has so hear a resemblance to many remains of the productions of the earlier ages of European history, that they will excite the wonder and interest of every traveller who beholds them. We seemed to look upon a vast fortress with several towers, one of which appeared gven circular. ‘The proper walls of the place, overhanging the water of the narrower stream, seemed to be supported by artificial stone work, resting upon jets or steps of the tock; and upon the side of the land, as far as the sceming walls were not hid from the view, was seen even the appearance of.a lofty gate. Nay, even loopholes appeared to be pierced in several parts of the walls, If a race of genii were dwelling up this romantic river, and had been occupying themselves in constructing works in imitation of our ancient - fortresses, they could not be said to have been unsuccessful. There is, indeed, a traditionary legend among all the native races in this part of Siberia, con-

cerning this partieular spot of the Léna, which relates that*the banks of the Ora are inhabited by certain spiritual beings, whose will has great influence upon’ the destinies of men. Thus, all the navigators of the great river, who thread this pass when the season vill permit, stay and bathe in the Ora, or at its mouth, which is thotight to be complimentary and highly pleasing to the spiritual inhabitants of the vicinity.

I cannot help here confessing a weakness, that possessed me at tis particular epoch of our voyage. This ‘vas a strong inclination to contemplate, and dwell on the thought, of some day returning to make a home of seme ravine among these rocks, here to dwell and pass the remainder of life alone, or with the Tungouse tribe of natives, far from all the ills that we know man, in civilised life at least, is heir to... And although this might be to. fly. to others we know not of, that may be greater, I am able to say that I have seen much of the way of life of the Indian, and I believe his condition, generally, to be less subject to the severer ills than that of the greater portion of civilised men.

The views,every where, near these grander passes of the Léna, were on all sides most magnificent. Rocks of all forms composed the summits of the mountains: deep green verdure covered their less elevated steps, and filled the valleys, which opened and closed to our sight as we swept rapidly down the current; and a line of sparkling ice bordered each shore, only broken at intervals by the passage of the waters of some tributary river jnto the parent stream. °

After passing through the reaches which presented the boldest and most picturesque scenery, te observed less snow upon the hills, and none upon the lower lands; and there was less ice in the river. There was also now some diminution in the force of the eurtent by the increase of the breadth of the stream,

We had during this day been making.a south-east course, until, after re-crossing the line of the GOth degree of latitude, towards evening, we attained a great elbow in the river at which the stream again’ turns to the north-east, to pursue its proper course’ towards the Aretic Ocean,

This point, at which the river turns; exhibited the most agreeable views, among those of tamer fnterest of any we saw upon the Léna. The right bank, which is, as@ usual, the highest, is here formed by a very gradually « rising piece of r ground, which was cleared of all trées or shrubs, and: seemed laid out in pasture. Two houses were to be seen, each of which appeared to be occupied by the possessors of one half of this portion of reclaimed land amid the wastes which the shores of the river generally present. |

The next day we entered the proper territory of the Yakoutes. The Yakoutes are the people the most remote from the seats of civilisation of all the semi-barbarous settled tribes, that have been in reality subjected to Russian dependence and received any of the benefits of regular government.

About mid-day, we were passing a lower country than usual, where there was less snow to be seen upon the hills than we had hitherto observed, and less ice on the shores of the river. Soon after this hour, we passed a scattered settlement of Yakoutes ‘apon.a tract of low pasture ground.

The first of the Yakoute race that we6 saw in their proper country were a few fishermen, who came alongside to offef us some sterlet. The men appeared to resemble the Bouriats in feature, and they are doubt~ less of Mongul origin. They’ have very little beard. But it was particularly remarkable, that all those we

saw on this occasion, though I did not afterwards observe the seme thing general among the tribe, had elongated and pointed chins. As to clothes, though it was cold, they had no more than some strips of hides partially: covering their bodics. Their canoes afforded myself, at least, much interest, from their resemblance to those of the AmericaneIndians. They were formed of birch bark, and, save a little variation at the extremities, were precisely similar to those of the Mohawks. They were the smallest, however, that I ever” saw, and they warried each but one man, who managed them with a kind of double paddle. When he impelled his frail bark,ehe held this, in the middle, and dipped the two ends, which were formed alike, alternately in the water. We saw afterwards, however, some canoes belonging to these people, which were formed of single logs, like those nearer ‘the sources of the river.

Late in the day, we encountered.so strong a wind, that, although it ‘blew across the river, deprived us of all the power we were accustomed to obtain by the oars over the boat’s drift. We now resorted to our frame.and net above described, by the aid of which we passed safely through several reaches. At length, however, the violence of the gale overcame all our efforts, and we were driven on shore for the first time by the wind, since we embarked, upon a low bank, which bordered a swampy tract of country, over which were scattered a number of the log huts of the Yakoutes.

None of the huts that formed this Yakoute settlement were near the shore, nor were any of them easy to approach. § The whole tract of land apon which they stood had been lately inundated, and was still wet and soggy; but, as I was anxious to see seme of the dwellings of these people, I set off, accompanied by one of our crew, who was a Yakoute, and who loaded himself withs empty bottles, which he hoped to bring back filled with milk. After passing over half a verst of wet ground, covered with the decayed grass of the last year, we came to the nearest of the houses, where we found a family, consisting of an aged couple, some young women and girls and boys. They were a very little better dressed than the fishermen we had seen, and in the same material, and were a'l seated upon the ground round a small fire in the centre of the hut. The old man, as we entered, saluted us, and appeared pleased at our appearance, and requested, by signs and speech, that we would seat ourselves upon a mud bencl that was by the wall on one side of the hut. This we_ declined doing, l.owever, as.we did not know how soon the boat might be able to proceed; and my Yakoute companion informed him, that we were only come to purchase some milk, if it was to be procuied, and to pay for which we had brought with us some tobacco.

He told us, however, that his cattle were all astray - in search of the young grass that was already springing upon the-drier lands in the rear of the settlement. And all he had to sell us was some sterlet, which had been caught the day before, and which, as we had plenty of the same fish on board, we did not purchase.

Nothing could be more wretched than this Ya, koute dwelling. It was a mere log hut, with a few poles laid across, over which sheets of birch bark were spread, forming a flat roof, in which an opening was left in the middle for the. smoke of the fire to escape. Many of the houses of this people are of mud, and some have picket walls, bedaubed with mud, and banked up,outside to four or five feet high with the same material,

There eould hardly be a better illustration than this hut and its occupants afforded, of the painful character of the earlier stages which usually conduct men from a state of absolute barbarism to the econ-

dition we call civilisation. The life of the wild man may be regarded as a dream, and the earliest stage of his social existence may be compared to the first moments of consciousness, when we awake from sound slumber and when the realities. of life have not yet blotted out of the memory the impressions engendered in sleep. Hig visions of free thought and independent action have passed away, and his understanding is confounded by his iinperfect conception of eyery thing around him, arfl his spirits are depressed by comparing ‘kis condition with that of men with whom he is asso~ ciated, but with whom he has little or no sympathy. More®ver, his arm has lost its power to provide for his subsistence, through his ignorance of ‘the arts with which his new mode of existence renders it necessary he should be acquainted. Noy would a similar comparison be wholly inapplicable to the condition of the mass of the peasant class of the Russo-Siberian people. The condition of the’simple peasant, whose repose has not yet been disturbed by the first stages of education, or by contact with the inhabitants of the towns, is abundantly tranquil; but no sooner is this broken by commerce of, any ‘kind with the other classes of the people, than he is found shorn of all his original virtue, ‘without having acquired any just impressions of the obligations which men owe to one another in society. There was nothing of sufficient interest to keep us ten minutes in this Yakoute hut; and we did’not visit a second. The distances between the dwellings were great, and ‘the passage from one to the other was rather too much to yndergo for the possible purchase only of a mere luxury such as that of which we were in search. We saw several cattle, however, grazing ata distance, among which wer® probably the old man’s cows. There were alsd several horses, that appeared to be searching for the young grass beneath the decayed remains of the last year’s growth. And all of these were perfectly white, which, indeed, is the universal colour of the horse in the Yakoute country.

Tt was near midnight when the wind sufficiently abated to admit of our proceeding on our voyage. But it was perfect daylight-as we launched again into the. stream at this hour. Not a star was visible ; but the sky, from the very ridges of the dark hills in the north-west, up to the zenith, was beautifully tinged with purple and red. And, as it now fell calm, we again rapidly advanced ; and before eight o’clock in ‘the morning, we had once more passed beyond the latitu-. dinal line of the 60th degree:

‘The next morning several canoes came alongside with soine fishermen of the native tribe of the Tungouse, none of whom we ‘had before seen. But, as a better opportunity will occur to speak of this tribe, it will be sufficient here to observe, that whatever may be their origin, the most remarkable circumstances connected with their mode of life and condition, are the vast extent of country through which they wae or in which they sojourn at different seasons of the year, and their docile character, which enables them to dwell where they will, unmolested by the Russians, or by the Yakoutes, or Bouriats, or any other tribes of more settled habits than themselves. They may be said to have not yet awakened, from the wild man’s healthful slumber, to the painful experience of the degradation incident to the first stages of society. Happy, however, is it for their future prospects, that the terms of.the Russian contact with the wild man are free from the ferocity of that of the Spaniards, and from the ancompromising character of that of the English, both of which, by different*means, have led to the extinction of whole ‘nations, even ‘in some instances so completely as to have established very
generally, though, let us hope, very falsely, an impression, that every nation must perish, when brought into contact with another in advance of it in its social institutions.

The canoes of these Tungouse were like those of the Yakoutes. The men we now saw were slighter made than the Yakoutes, and bore a far greater resemblance to the Indians of North America than to the Tatar races of men. Yet it is remarkable that they resemble more the Indtans of the eastern coast of America than those of the western coast, as far, at least, as my observation in that hemisphere has extended, which, indeed, hasebeen chiefly among those of the eastern coast.° Those we now saw wore deer skins, and were much better dressed than’any of the Yakoutes we had hitherto seen.

The next morning we reached a considerable village called Olekininsk. We had a few goods to deliver here; and as it happened to be the residence of a zasidytell and a gorodnichii, it was of sufficient dignity to oblige us to perform ceremonies enough to cause us two hours’ delay.

During qur detention here, I took a Salk through the place,’ tolerably secure, that there could not be another zastdytell like the one of Vintimskaia upon the banks of the same river. The inhabitants of this village are composed, about equally, of Russo-Siberians and Yakoutes; and they appeared to be the most ruffianly set of fellows that we had yet met with, A party of half-naked men were in one place quarrelling over the cajcase of a cow they were cuéting up, and others were lounging about in groups, as if they had no proper occupation. But the sight the most novel was that of fout or five beggars, who were the first that might be properly so called, and the Jast that I saw in Siberia. They-were petitioning the parties that were quarrelling for some of those parts of the carcase that we are wont to throw to the dogs, @ertainly, however, the condition of the pope of the place, whom we happened also to see, and who was the fattest of all the holy men I remember ‘having seen, in Siberia, the good Khomba Lama excepted, did not indicate this poverty to be universal Among the *women that appeared, and which may be mentioned as a novelty, there was one of considerable beauty.

Shortly before’we left this place, Lieutenant Rosinburg, of the Imperial navy, arrived in a similar vessel to that by which we were descending the river. I have not before mentioned that I had the pleasure of making this gentleman’s acquaintance at Irkoutsk. He was now proceeding with his wife to Ayan, a port upon the coast of the Ochotsk Séa, in which the Russo-American company have lately founded an establishment, in order to join a ship to arrive from Sitka, the seat of government of the Russians in their American possessions. He had heard in his passage down the river of the conduct of the zasédytell ‘of Vintimskaia, and had been so annoyed by the circumstance, as to write immediately an account of it to the governor-general at Irkoutsk. **It was the luckiest thing possible,” said ‘the gallant. sailor, “ that I did not happen to arrive at the time of. the occurrence}; for, had I been there, I should have forgotten the respect due to office, and have thrashed the fellow into a stock-fish.”

I could not help agreeing with the lieutenant, that it was certainly very fortunate that he did not arrive in time to makesuch a terrible example of the,unfortunate ' man.. But I will take this opportunity to remark that, wherever I efterwards went, I found the same feeling prevail, and the same disgust expressed, at the conduct of the drunken magistrate. In general, however, it was thought that it was better.that the affair had closed
as it did, than that the man should have been so severely threshed.

Early the next morning we passed Marchinskaya. Several of the people of this village came off in canoes, to offer for sale some huge teeth of the mammoth, which were the first remains we met with of that mighty habitant of the ancient world — of the animal that, should the skeleton at St. Petersburg perish, and all the ivory remains of his species be one day worked into ladies’ trinkets, will no doubt pass for a fabulous creation -of men’s imagination before the dawn of natural science, and the date of the first records of prgper natural histevy.

I must ‘mention that we heard here, though the circumstance may perhaps be known to the naturalists of Europe, that all the ivory teeth or tusks that are discovered, at least at this part of Siberia, are found standing directly upright in the ground. Whatever speculation this circumstance is calculated to suggest, it seemsrat least to indicate that the animals perished by some sudden change in the condition of the material substances amidst which their remains are found. Some of the natives informed us, that the imperishable portions of the remains of these animals exist in such abundance in the islands of the Arctic Sea, off the coast of Siberia, that the very land seemed as if they were composed of them.

Soon after passing this village, we met some more Yakoutes in their canoes, fishirg. The sterlets were here so plentiful, that we bought of one party, thirty of them of the.size of small cod-fish, for atout a pound of tobacco, and again, five more as large as moderatesized cod, for six or seven pounds of rye flour.

The snow and ice had gradually diminished since we passed by the higher lands, and we now observed very little of cither. The river and the face of the country had also much changed. The river had become broader and less rapid, and the hills were lower, and the valleys of greater extent. In several places promontories of picturesque form, and:partially covered with stunted firs, jutted out beyond the ordinary line of the shore; and by the winding of the stream, these appeared gradually to-close and open, which sometimes gave to the scene the appearance of a lake, and at: other times presented a perspective, resembling that ‘ which the succession of reflections from inirrots placed opposite to each other, presents to the eye in a larges apartment,.

It was calm during this day, and we had the+3ame scenery until the evening, when the weather, which had been, with the exception of a few short periods of strong winds, remarkably serené since we embarked, : changed over our heads to a tempest, but without causing any agitation of the air beneath. Dark clouds'now seemed to roll against one another by the force of the opposed currents of air, and forked lightning flew across the sky at an elevation that seemed scarcely higher than the hills, and loud peals of thunder burst over our heads, and resounded from hill to hill through the still air, with terrible evidence of the mighty power possessed by the material elements of our planet, which seem at such a moment as if they had broken loose from the restraint imposed upon matter by established laws, and were about to reduce the beautiful order of nature to original chaos. 1 ;

While this frightful state of the elements continued above our heads, not a drop of rain fell, and none of our men put themselves under shelter. Thus an opportunity was «forded to mark the effects of the storm upon the men of the several races, of which our crew were composed. The Russo-Siberians were seized with religious awe; and they fell upon their knees and remained

perfectly still, and said their prayers inaudibly, and continuaJly. crossed themselyes. ‘The Tatars seemed but little affected. The Yakoutes fell upon their knees in the same manner as the Russians; but instead of making the sign of the cross, they covered their faces with their hands and bent their heads upon some packages by which¢they knelt. And this little difference in the effect of the storm upon the Russians and the Yakoutes I was the more particular in remarking, because, as the latter crossed themselves after- the manner af the Russians before every church as we passed by it, ew did not suppose that any difference in their manner of expwegsing their feelings would upon this occasion have been observed. This, however, was not the sole evidence that fell under my observation, as will hereafter be seen, that although they may be very loyal subjects, and very obedient to the laws, they ‘are not yet thoroughly subjected to the spiritual influence of the religion they ‘outwardly profess. <

At length the rain came down in torrents, and the storm, without a breath of air having been perceived upon the water, now passed away, leaving a degree of warmth in the atmosphere such as we had not felt until now.

The day after this, we had the same scenery as upon the two preceding days; and the weather was so fine, and the temperature so much changed, that it seemed as if nothing were now wanting, but the full-blown leaves of the birch groves, to establish the summer.

This change in the weather so truly characteristic of the climate, recalls to the memory the seasons that have passed since the commencement of these travels in Siberia, and upon which a few remarks may be now made with more confidence than they might have been offered upon any previou8 occasion.

It is commonly said of those countries which axe situated in high latitudes, that they have but two seasons. If we there estimate the four periods, into which we divide the year by their several lengths, in proportion to the duration of the same season in the more temperate climates, it would scarcely be less erroneous to say, that the Siberians know but one season, than that they enjoy less than four. The four seasons, in fact, in all the inhabited portions of this country, are as distinct as those of any other, country within the samé zone. If,"however, we compare them with those we experience in this country for instance, we may say that the winter there embraces nine months out of the, twelve, and that two months only may be called mer, and we shall thus leave but one month for the seasons of spring and autumn. Butif we consider the spring to commence with the first signs of reanimation in the vegetable world, and autumn to end with the fall of the last perennial green leaf, then we must deduct a month from the long winter, which we ought} however, to add to the summer, without giving a day more to the seasons of autumn and spring.

It was some time previous to this, as has been mentioned, that the first indications of the spring were to be seen among the groves of birch trees in the sheltered valleys by which we were drifting. Nevertheless, the heat until this time had not exceeded 8 or 9 degrees, But the change in the temperature was now so great, that the thermometer stood at 14 or 15 degrees, and the rays of the sun at mid-day were absolutely hot. We had embarked with the very first breaking up of the ice, upon the ninth of this month ; and had Sidecd buta few days afterwards observed the first appearanee of the green leaves, and upon this the 28th day of May of the time we are keeping, and the 9th of June of our time, we experienced the first day of summer thus characteristically established. Yet some snow was
sti to be segn on the declivities of every hill, and some, ice along the shores of’ the river, though it was hourly diminishing in quantity.

Another characteristic of the climate of Siberia generally, is the prevalence of a serene state of the atmosphere. -Three especial exceptions only to this apparently general law have been mentioned up to this time during these travels, and two of these occurred where the places themselves are exceptions to the general characttr of the country. During almost the Whole of the rest of my sojourn and travels in this land, avhatever was the temperature of the air, or even the appearmee of the sky, still the calm state of the atmosphere commonly prevailed; and this often during some of the heaviest falls of snow.

About mid-day we passed the village of Oimouranskaya, and in the evening that of Sineskaya. Here the river became between six and seven versts in width, and was full of fow islands covered with small birch trees, while the shores were rocky and precipitous.

After this we floated between rugged hills, where needle-formed peaks of granite rock were observed shooting up hetween the dark firs, and presenting a most novel and picturesque scene. Larly the next day we passed the village Arinskaya. We observed more ice in the river here than we had seen for several preceding days; and we had a chilly wind until the afternoon; when, as the sun declined, the wind fell, and the atmosphere - resumed its wonted serenity and warmth.

At eight in ghe evening, we passed the government post of Bestiatskaya, at the distance of just eightyfour versts from the place of our destination. The river had here still increased in breadth, and there were many low marshy islands at intervals, covered with the remains of the grass and -reeds of the last summer,

On either side, the-land close to the yiver was now “lower than usual; but we observed a mountainous ‘country at some distance upon the left hand, and a few hills at a greater distance upon the right.,

Our rate of drift was now slower than at any time during the voyage, and.did not probably exceed five versts an hour. During the early pag of the night we passed some cliffs of sandstone, upon which were gathered myriads of swallows, that were the first of the birds of summer we saw duritg our voyage. But notwithstanding this tolerable assurance, that te change we experienced in the weather was not merely temporary, our advance towards the northggemegions did not seem to be moré rapid than that of the season, in respect to the effects of the temperature upon the vegetable world; for the green leaves of the smalier birches that flourish here, were not more forward than those we had seen in the valleys about a fortnight earlier.

The day after this, a dense mist hung upon the water all the early part, of the morning, and obscured the coasts upon both“sides from the view. During this state of thé atmosphere, we drove againgt a low island, but this accident caused us only a short detention. By eight o’clock, the weather began to clear; and as our view extended, we found ourselves drifting among islands, so numerous that the shores of the river which were here generally low, were’ still not definable, In the middle of the day, however, we drifted by a high cliff upon our left hand. After this, the scene resembled that whicle is. observed id some of the bypader channels, but oftener near the entrances of several of the larger rivers of ¢he world, such as the Rhine and the Nile. Many low islands of considerable extent appeared, with narrow channels between them. Later in the day, as the mists wholly dispersed,.upon our right hand, there
was no appearance of hills of any considerable elevation, whether far or near; but upon the left, a chain of mountains of irregular forms, was apparent at the distance of thirty or forty versts.

As the night approached, while the sun was gradually diminishing his distance from the horizon, in his oblique and rapid courge from the western point of the heavens towards the north, the spectacle was: most gratifying to behold. So gradual is his descent at this season in this latitude, afeer the first three hours past noon, that as lg now approached the misty peaks of the high land in ghe north-west, while we glided swiftly down the stream, he pr ed to us the appearance of a luminous globe that was rolling along the ridge of the mountains in the midst of voleanic vapours and terrestrial fires.

At length, we obtained the first sight of Yakoutsk. The town is seated within an inlet or little channel of the river, formed by a marshy island, and through which a very little current flows, and at the distance of about a verst from the mam stream. All possible efforts were now made to direct our unwieldy craft through the channels between the islands we had still to pass, to gain the prpper position required, in order to approach the shores before we might, by the force of the current, be swept beyond the town ; and, early in the evening, we were near the prime object of our long expectation.

As soon as we were clear of the main current of the great stream, we landed a part ef our crew, in order to track our vessel to the town. And now, late on the evening of theglst day of June, or the 13th ly our style, and the twenty-fourth day after leaving Irkoutsk, and the twenty-first from that of our embarkation, wf moored in safety by the bank in front of the town of Yakoutsk.

Yaxoursk is the capital of the department of the same name, which is the largest of the provinces of Eastern Siberia. It lies in the latitude of 62 degrees north, and beneath the meridian of 129° 40’ east of Greenwich. It is the most northern of the provincial capitals of Siberia, and is’ the place of residence of the civil governor of the department, and of an ispravnik and a gorodnichii. “.It possesses a population estimated at | 4000 souls, composed of the mingled race of Russe- Siberians and Yakoutes, with a few pure Russians, who are chiefly officials in the service of the government and of the Russian Fur Company, and one or two * merchants. : OF thos¢institutions, which are the most important of all that properly belong to civilised life, the establish- .ments for thé instruction of the rising generation; there are at Yakéuisk only two very meanly appointed schools. One of these ig, however, a general school, similar to the establishments in the larger towns, though it is without

the privileges with which the gymnasium of Irkoutsk isendowed. The,other is a schoo! intended for the instruction of boys designed for the church, and especially for the mission among the aboriginal inhabitants of this” part of the country. “But though the climate should for ever restrain the increase of ‘the inhabitants of these districts of Siberia within limits too narrow to afford scope for the attainment of any high degree of refinement, even this little step in the right direction is gratifying to behold.

eAt the general school, there,were at this time only éwenty boys, and four or five girls, and at that for the clergy,“@aby about eight or ten boys. At the former of these schools, nothing was yet taught but reading and writing in the Russian tongue, the, language of the Yakoutes not having yet been sufficiently reduced to rules, to admit of its being studied by other means than practice and the ear. The scholars, however, at this school are chiefly Yakoutes and children of the mixed race; but those at the clerical school, are for the most part i the purely Russian race.

The Yakoute language, nevertheless, in all the ordinary transactions of life, is here greatly predominant over the Russian, and it is said to be easily acquired. The Russians, indeed, even those who are in the service of the government, and not permanently established, are fond of the language, and acquire it with that wonderful facility with which their fellow-countrymen in Russia Proper acquire all tlre polite languages of Europe. A lady, whom I shall have again to mention, willing one dgy to compliment my natiof, as I am bound to suppose, after speaking of her progress in the predominant tongue at Yakoutsk, said, “ Tife Yakoute language, I assure you, sir, is esteemed here just in the same manner that the English is esteemed at St. Petersburg.” It might hardly have been polite, when the lady’s intention was taken into account, to seem to sce any thing incongruous in the comparison. But admirable as we must acknowledge to be every effort of men towards communicating the blessings they enjoy to those especially who remain*still in the condition, probably, almost as low as that.of the first of our . species, it is impossible to sojourn among’the inhabitants of this unfavoured region of our planet, and contemplate alone the fair side of the picture of their prospective condition. The country, which does nét produce food for its inhabitants, without the application of a degree of Jabour wholly disproportionate to the results of the same labour elsewhere, must rise and declins#With the increase and diminution of the accidental sources of its existence. We in England, indeed, though the comparison may not be much happier than that which has ‘just been mentioned, although we are not fed entirely by the produce of our own soil, make up for the deficiency by a means which we hope will be perpetual, or cndure to a period the most remote to which it may be the duty of finite beings to study the interests of posterity. The inhabitants of this*part.of Siberia are, indeed, in like manner, for the present, in-some mcasure compensated for the privations to which they are subjected on account of the rigour of their climate, by the possession of an article of commerce in the produce of their -forests. This source of their maintenance will, nevertheless, decrease in proportion to the inercase of their: numbers, and must finally fail them. By the fur trade, indeed, they mainly now exist; or at least by this trade, their condition has become -supevior to that in which the natives were found at the conquest of the | country; dnd with its extinction, which the increase of inhabitants in.northern Europe generally, and the conscquent increase of the demand for the furs in which they clothe themselves, will sooner or later accomplish,
this cold region will cease to produce the means of maintaining men in sufficiently dense communities to admit of. that state of society in any of its degrees, which we term civilisation..

Yakoutsk is at-present the centre of the fur trade of Siberia, and is annually the depository of furs to the amount of upwards of two- millions of rubles. Salt and talc are here also exchanged for merchandise consisting chiefly of such articles as those of which, it will be remembered, our cargo consisted. ° e Notwithstanding the somewhat heterogeneous madéerials which compose the population of this provincial town, @egjhe eye of a stranger, the inhabitants appear to be almost wholly Yakoutes, on account of the features of the face, in particular, of that race being more distinctly marked than those which distinguish the proper Russians. The proportion of Yakoutes, however, of unmingled blood, does not exceed a quarter of the population. The mixed race, in the light in which they are chiefly seen by strangers, seem quite conformists to all Russian usages, though this is not in all things in reality the case. At their homes, and in their domestig affairs, and in their language, they are Yakoutes; while in their religion, and in regard to the social rights which they have been admitted to enjoy, they are not now distinguished from their dollowssubices even of the pure Russian race.

Allusion has been. before incidentally made to the greater facility, in comparison avith othgr races, with which the Russians of the Sclavonic family mingle with the abggigines of the countries, whieh have been brought within the compass of their dominion, Isvidence of this is to be seen in all’ parts of ehe Russian empire, but no where more clearly than in Eastern Siberia, and in no part of Eastern Siberia so remarkably as in this ancient territory of the Yakoutes. By this

happy disposition in the character of this race, many nations of different origin, which the vast empire embraces, have been subjected to the discipline which has renderéd them capable of enjoying the advantages - of equal laws and equal rights. Thus the conquerors: have been saved from the stain on their nationalcharacter which rests upon that of the Spanish name, and from the inconveniences which our pride of blood has occasioned us, and the empire from the internal wars which under any other state of things would have arisen, and retarded the increase of population, and thg general diffusion of civilisation which, in the degrees, we have’ seen, or are to see, have marched band in hand from the Baltic Sea even to the Pacific Ocean. But at the same time, while at Yakoutsk we find the best example. of these happy consequences of this accommodating disposition of the Russians, it is here also, that in comparing the Russian: conquest of the aboriginal inhabitants.of the country with the conquests ‘of other nations of which history affords us ample examples, we discover the more essential moral causes of the different results that the: sequel of their several wars has produced. The Spaniards, whose conquests form the greatest contrast with those of the Russians, carried before them the cross, for which they opened a passage by the sword, and by worse means, carrying on exterminating war against all who submitted not blindly to their authority, and embraced not the faith which was to them a religion of blood with no other moral than that which recognised the right of the strong to commit every kind of violence against the, weak. The Russians, wiser, and better endowed with the true spirit of the religion they profess, have carried with them also the same emblem of peace and good-will from Heaven towards man. But the means by which they have opened the passage for the symbol of their faith, and

by which they have planted it in new soils, has been justice and equal rights, for the firm establishment of which their tolerant spirit has, been the pledge. Thus, while the Spaniards lighted the flames of war and hatred which are far from being extinguished even at this day, and afterwards converted to Christianity only in name, the feeble remains of the people ' whom they nearly destroyed, the Russians have by their humanity subdued and reclaimed whole nations of far more barbarous races than any whiclrthe Spaniards encountered, wand added them to.the number of which their empire «consists, and to whom their laws and their protection _ exten, Wheresoever, indeed, we find the Sclavonic in contact with any other race, we observe the mingling of the two people bear a due proportion to the advance of Christianity, and that advance also, to bear its proportion to the greater or less amount of the charity with which it has been promulgated, after making allowance for the dégree of firmness with which the ‘ancient religion of the people has been found established, and the proportion of good senst and absurdity with which it owginally abounded. Thus, for instance, where the ancient faith has-been found accompained with regular codes of scriptural law, and to have a regular clergy both studious and sincere, such as in the case of Islamism and also of Buddhism, of which the Tatars form the exanrple of the first, and the Bouriats of the second of these religions, the conversions and mixing of blood have been slow; whereas, among those nations whoge established religion has tot presented any such rampart against the assaults of a purer faith, but has been found full 6f such abominations as men in all stages of civilisation wonder at observing in their own species, the rapidity of the conversions and the mingling of races has been proportionally greater.

Tn the case, indeed, of the conversion and adoption of this particular people whom we are now among, the world has seen, or at least history will record, a novelty of a very rare kind, and to which the traveller, though he is not in possession of sufficient information to enable him, to speak with exactness concerning the formal proceedings by which it appears to have -been accomplished, can bear testimony is a reality. It may be said, almost without a figure, that a whole nation of idolaters have been converted to the religidn of civilised man by the decree of a Christian prince. The religion of the Yakoutes- was mere idolatry of the grossest description, and the superstitions by which it 3 accompanied, were, in general, such as were not difficult to eradicate. But when the way had been prepared for this decree by the Russian popes, suddenly like a meteor, and which brings to our minds the conversions of Constantine and the apostle of the Gentiles, a ukase proclaimed that the good and loyal nation of the Yakoutes were thought worthy to enter, and were: consequently admitted into the Russian Church, to be henceforth a part of the Czar’s Christian family, and entitled to all the privileges of the rest of his children. Now although we cannot look into the seeds of time, and ‘say which grain will grow, and which will not,” it is at least certain, that the Yakoutes have been ever since rapidly ad~ vancing towards that degree of civilisation which the country they inhabit may be supposed capable of admitting.

Not a doubt remains of the sincerity of “the converts generally among the Yakoutes. We sheJl see cause, however, upon another stage of our journey to think otherwise of"some that are removed from the example and influence necessary to attain the desired end. This, nevertheless, withdraws nothing from the principle which has been held to have governed the Russian
conquests, or of the fruits generally of which it has been productive.,

In fine, if we are able to draw no other moral from a review of the past and the present condition of the Yakoutes, than that which the -contemplation of the fruits of moderation and charity in religious affairs affords, we at least learn that no such law exists in nature as that which, when the Tungouse were mentioned a few pages back, was said tg be supposed: by some to govetn the contact between a people in advance in the degrees of civilisation, and a race only yet in the infant stages of society. But perhaps to no people can, such™™gsson as that which is taught in the general history of the contact between the Russians and the barbarous races, be more useful than the English, who, ‘however we do praise ourselves,” have stronger and more groundless scruples than any other people concerning the mixture of our blood with a race we deem ’ inferior to ourselves. :

As we landed at Yakoutsk, there were a dozen or two men and women gathered upon the shores of the little port. The costume of the men we obsefved differed very little from that of the Siberians generally, but that of the women was novel to us. The men wore skins, cut in imitation of the caftan, trousers, fur caps, and short boots of untanned leather; but the women were dressed in very short caftans, also of skins, with a border of the breadth of half the length of the skirt in scarlet cloth, and enormous bear-skin caps. They also had the short boots of untanned leather; but their legs were bare, like those of our Highland men.

The merchant and myself obtained apartments as soon as we landed, in one of the houses elose to the bank, at which our vessel, doomed to be in a very few days converted into a house to shelter some Yakoute family from the winter’s‘cold, was now moored. Our quarters thus secured, and it being too late for business, ‘we set out for a stroll round the town, full of.the same agreeable feelings that most people, after a long voyage experience during the fitst moments of freedom upon terra firma, of the enjoyment of which they have been so long deprived.

We found the streets of the town laid qut with the same regularity as those of the greater part of the towns both.in Russia and_ Siberia, and the town divided into two nearly equal parts by a ‘brook of not very limpid water, for which space enough, however, - has been. left for ‘a fine river to flow, with a public promenade on either side.

We counted during our walk, six churches, all of which had been painted in the usual yellow and green, but none of them had much remaining of this mark to distinguish them from the ordinary houses of the town. There is also a convent here, with a church belonging to it; and there are some remains of an old Cossack fortress, which is said to have -been erected by the conquerors of Siberia so long ago as 1647.

We found nearly ail the town, save the building above mentioned, to consist of a sorry sek of wooden houses formed of the materials of the craft which descend the Léna, which are broken up for that purpose as soon as their merchandise is landed; and, as none of them seemed to have ever been daubed with paint of any colour, they presented a sombre and miserable appearance. We only observed glass in the windows of one or two of the houses, which we afterwards found belonged to the merchants of the town, all the~ rest having merely small apertures where tale was used in the place uf the more transparent substance, Many of the houses are enclosed within very high palings formed of the same materials as the houses, but which we could not discover were of any other use than the convenience they afford for confining the dogs.

Our tour was not performed without such labour ang incouvenience as the novelty which the place presented was hardly sufficient to counterbalance, owing to the nature of.the ground upon which the town appears to have been somewhat injudiciously built. The houses. are nearly all, in fact, set upon a mere morass ; and the snow which had lain upon this during the winter, had only lately melted; and the heat of the sun for the last two or three days had so dried the surface, while the ground bene@th still retained its moisture, that an elastic ,erust had been formed upon it, that rendered walking most laborious and fatiguing.

limsegnsequence of this inconvenience, we occupied. more time in our walk than we were aware of, and when we returned to the shore, we found our men all asleep, though the sun was above the horizon. However, upon consulting our time-pieces, we discovered by the hour, that the ever-welcome source of light had just risen upon another day, instead of being, as we had supposed, just about to set upon that of our arrival. The sun in fact, at this season, in this latitude, disappears but for a brief time; and, as his lowest descent beneath the horizon, is not equal to that when we still enjoy twilight, there is no diminution of the full light of day at any time during the night; and as a bright and red sky had covered. the whole northern quarter of the heavens during his absence, we had not missed his rays, nor had we any idea that we had commenced another day, until our attention was cabled to the time, and our watches indicated the hour of half-past one in the morning. Upon,this discovery, we retired to tke our neces- Sary rest,

During the course of to-day, Lieutenafit Rosenburg arrived with his family; and I had the satisfaction of hearing from him, that the littleadventure at Vi intimskaya had caused great regret to every one of all classes of the people whom he had met since itsoccurrence. His own feelings upon the occasion have been already reported. Upon the following day, I accompanied the gallant lieutenant. in a visit to the government-house. We found the governor at home, ‘and we met with the accustomed polite reception. The next day we dincd by invitation with his excellency, and met the leading resident people of Yakoutsk, consisting chiefly of the chinovnik of the town. There was only one, however, of the company, besides the lieutenaz.t, with whom I was able to converse. This was a Swiss gentleman by bYrth, and, I believe, an Israelite, but some time a captain in the imperial army, and now, in reysed for his services in the wars in the Caucasus, promoted to serve the government in the capacity of post-master at Yakoutsk. I confess I thought this rather a strange reward for a soldier after a campaign, until I was informed, that when appointments of this kind are made, they are for five or three years only, and that they qualify those who creditably discharge their duties during that term, for higher employments in Russia. There was also, at this dinner, a Romish priest, who had come from Irkoutsk, where he usyally resided. He had been long accustomed to make this voyage every two or three years, to confess a small detachment of his widely scattered flock that resided here, and which only amounted to six souls. This was certainly to be deemed a meritorious example of devotion to that church, when it is considered how great must be the diffidulties of the ascent of this rapid river, the smooth descent of which ‘only has been described in the foregoing chapters. And when I conversed with the priest upon this subject, with the aid of a friend, I could. not help recommending him to insist with the members of his litt¥e flock, as an additional motive for them to live without sin, that the sufferings which they

entailed upon another, were greater than the pleasure which their sins would probably afford them; or, if this were not likely to succeed, that some means should be tried to accomplish the important business by correspondence. The church whose priests are proud, when pride will advance their objects, and the meekest of mankind, when meekness will better effect their purposes; whose emissaries terrify the prince by their threatened anathemas, and flatter the beggar by their humility, andewhich boasts of its capability to adapt its jnstitutions to every condition of man, might surely better accommodate itself to the circumstances ‘of a countsy, of which it perhaps possessed no map at the time of fe great councils and convocations.

The next morning, I called upon the captain above mentioned. He had) while at the Caucasus, married a.lady of German descent, from whom I now met a polite reception. The lady. was looking forward with much anxiety towards the moment when they might ascend the Léna, and return to Russia to enjoy once more the comparatively temperate air of their native climate, and meet again their long-parted friends.

The captain’s house was a sample of the better sort of houses of the town. The dwellings at Yakoutsk of every description are warmed precisely in the same manner as those of the comparatively inmilder districts of Siberia. The chief variation’in them consists in adapting the windows to meet the greater degree of cold which is here experienced above that jn the towns where, we have already seen so many precautions taken, «The windows of the captain’s house which looked upon the miniature port, and faged the south, were at this season of the ordinary size; but. they were socontrived that, during ihe winter, they might be contracted to a round aperture of not above a foot in diameter, in which treble glass panes resisted tlie approach of the enemy. The houses of an inferior class, however, have no other windows than similar apertures, in which talc supplies the place of glass in summer, and ice in winter.. At the commence-. ment of the severer season, pieces of ice from one to two feet in thickness, or, more properly, in length, cut into the right form, are placed in the apertures, and fixed quite firmly, by pouring water into the interstices, just as molten lead might be poured upon less dissolvable substances for the purpose of cementing them, and with the same effect.

In the houses of the inhabitants of the Russian racey this means of forming the windows is sometimes attended, with a little inconvenience, on account of the heat kept up in the rooms causing the ice to drip. Such, nevertheless, is the intensity ‘of the cold, that even when a room is heated to 16 or 17 degrees, the ice may remain, dry. This, indeed, is no more than we see in much less cold: climates, where the ice, as every one who has been ir. Canada in the winter time will remember, remains sometimes an inch thick on the windows in an atmosphere of equal temperature to that above mentioned. In the houses of the natives, the ordinary heat kept up, is not sufficient to take any ‘effect upon ice of which a portion is necessarily exposed to the external air. About 8 degrees has been before mentioned as that in which the Bouriats delight in the winter time; but I was informed that the heat most agreeable to the Yakoutes at the same seasonf was about 5 or 6 degrees; and, moreover, that when the thermometer was at the freezing point, they did not always take che trouble to procure artificial heat. It must be remembered, however, that the dresses of both these races cre formed of the skins of beasts, and not of the produce of the loom.
No very brilliant light can cf course be obtained at any time of day through such a medium; but, as

lamps are necessarily kept burning for twenty-one hours out of the twenty-four during the severer season in this latitude, the houses might almost as well be without windows as witli them at that tinie. I next made a visit to my naval friend. On arriving at his domicile, IJ found his wife and a child and two women servants preparing for- their journey across the country to the ocean. Gospojah Rozuelung and her maidens were in dreadful spirits at the prospect before ‘them. The lary herself, indeed, had been accustomed to long voyages and painful journeys; but the report of the character of the journey before them had quite subdued her wonted courage, The distance from Yakoutsk to*Ayan, the new settlement of the company before mentioned, is about the same as that which we had to perform. But they did not calculate upon accomplishing their journey, on accouit of the character of ‘their party, in less than ‘sixty days, which would be more than doublé the time allowed for ours; and during the whole of this period they would necessarily be encamped in a desert and dangerous country. A wellarmed man, itideed, on either side of each of the women and the child was indispensable, on account of the close character of the woods in many places, and the number and the fierceness of the bears, which rendered necessary the constant watch and guard of men whose quickness as well as coolness might be depended upon. It may be easily supposed, that this new life for two months required some previous,training ; and for this purpose, the lieutenant had turned a spacious enclosure which was attached to the house én which he was lodged, into a kind of military riding-school, in which the party were now about to perform their first exercises. The lady had once been accustomed to horse exercise; but she had not mounted for nine years, and she was now very timid in sitting her horse. VOL. II. P

The child was snugly stowed in a basket, which was lashed upon the horse’s back. But the maidens of the party were. the great difficulty. One of them -had never been on horseback beforé, and she was now only placed upon her saddle to be taken off again weeping ‘with terror, as well for the present as for the thought, no doubt, of the future ; so that it was doubtful whether : she would be able to attempt the journey.

At length, after very much ado, the rest sat firmly enough on their’ horses for a first trial; and, as soon as they had made a few turns round the court, the men of the party mounted also, and fell into the regular order of the future march..The lieutenant and a Yakoute, both armed, the lieutenant with a tomahawk and pistols, and the Yakoute with dagger alone, preceded the rest. After thése came the lady and her child and the more courageous of the two maidens, guarded by Yakoutes on either side. And in this manner they moved on with slow and solemn march round the court, so sad and sorrowful, that theylooked more like a cavalcade of the tired soldiers of some barbarian chief conducting a ‘captive beauty with her maidens to a place of security, than a party training for defensive war with the wild beasts during a voluntary journey. The whole of the party, however, with the exception of the most timid of the maidens, who could not be persuaded to sit upon her horse that day, after an hour or two's practice, went very well through their exercise for a first essay.:

Tuer weather had been ‘extremely variable during the first days of our detention at Yakoutsk. Sometimes a scorching sunshine during the greater part of the day, was succeeded by a cold wind and rain in the evening; and the thermometer did not, after our arrival, indicate more’ than 11 degrees of heat, until the seventh of the month, when it rose to 13. On the ninth, it stood at 15 at eight oxlock in the morning, and at 16 at noon, and on the tenth at 16 in the morning and.17 at noon, with every appearance of settled weather.

From the time that I had heard at Krasnoyarsk of the perpetual duration of the frost in the ground there in particular situations, [ was anxious to ascertain to what distance the cold penetrated in these regions generally, before it was arrested by causes very different from the sun’s heat. At Irkoutsk no one appeared to know more than every body knewat Krasnoyarsk,-which was merely, that in all this part of Siberia the frost remained perpetually in the ground in places sheltered from the direct beams of the sun. At Yakoutsk, however, I was shown a well sixty feet deep, the water in which was never frozen, but rose at all times two feet from the bottom. This depth, therefore—that is to say, about fifty-eight feet—must be considered to be here the limit of the frozen ground. Now, although very little may be inferred from this cir, cumstance singly, and though the truth may be very difficult to determine with exactness; yet, as the fact alone of the perpetual duration of the frost in the ground to most assuredly a considerable depth, is a circumstance calculated to throw light upon the theory _ of climate, a few remarks which it suggests may per- — haps be made without any danger of their being uncharitably interpreted.,

The excess of cold and its effects in Siberia naturally bring back to the mind of a traveller in that country, what he may have read with interest concerning the cold experienced by our navigators in the Arctic Sea. I remember when perusing the accounts of the voyages of Captain Parry in that sea, while residing in a cold climate in North America, being much struck with the proportionally small number of degrees in the difference of the cold between parallels of latitude so widely apart as that which I then inhabited and ‘hose of the observations of the navigator, and I have been no less so by the same circumstance while in thir country.
I did not obtain any actual register of the degrees of cold and heat experienced at Yakoutsk during the year; and not being there at the season at which any
observations could be made concerning the cold, I rely, in the statement to follow, upon the best authority that could be obtained at the time I was there..

The temperature of the atmosphere during the winter, was a subject of frequent conversation upon almost.all occasions upon which I met my friends, and especially at the government-house. There was at this time but one spirit thermometer in the place, hut there had been at various times several others, and it was ayreed by all who had ever taken an interest in this question, or made any definite observations, that there was during the severer months of the winter season here sometimes as much as: 45 degrees of cold of Réaumur for a fortnight together, and that there was not unfrequently 48 degrees, and’ that occasionally the thermometer fell even to 50 degrees. It will be” remembered that we are in the 62nd degree of north _latitude, and under the meridian of 129° 40’ east of Greenwich.

Upon turning to Captain Parry’s account of his several voyages in the Polar Seas, it will be found that the greatest degree of cold that he experienced during the first voyage occurred on the 14th and 15th of February, 1820, in Winter Harbour, Melville Island, in the latitude 74° 45’, upon which days the thermometer fell to 48 and 50 degrees below the zero of Fahrenheit.

During the first of two winters which he ee in these seas upon the second voyage, the greatest degree of cold that he experienced was 37 and 371 degrees, which occurged in the latitude of 66° 15’ on the 20th and 2Ist of January, 1822. And during the second winter of the same voyage, on the thrée first days of January, 1823, at Igloolik, in the latitude of 69}, the.thermometer fell to 45 degrees.
During the third voyage at Port Bowen, in Prince
Regent’s Inlet, in latitude 73° 13’, the thermometer on the coldest day, which was the 12th of January, fell to 37° 5’,

If we now reduce the degrees of the scale of Réaumur to those of Fahrenheit, we cannot, indeed, fail to be surprised at the difference of the temperature of the two regions, in which the distinct series of observations were made.* The greatest cold experienced by Captain Parry appears by the above account to have.been 50 degrees of Fahrenheit, although during two winters he did not experience more than 37° 5’. Now, upan the best authority that could be obtained, it has been above stated, that from 40 to 45 degrees of Réaumut is not an uncommon temperature at Yakoutsk, and that the thermometer -sometimes even falls to 50 degrees of the same scale. Now by reduction of the degrees of the scale in use in Siberia to those of that‘used by our ‘navigators, we find that 50 degrees of Réaumur is equal to 80} of Fahrenheit, which shows the cold at Yakoutsk, in the latitude 62 degrees (supposing the information upon which I have relied to be correct), to be 801 degrees of Fahrenheit greater than that of 74 degrees of latitude in the Polar Sea.-+ -

"74° 6 30” was greater by 15 degrees of Fahrenheit, than the greatest mentioned by Captain Parry, which reduces our above excess of 30} to 154. These

In contemplating this great difference in the degrees of cold in these two high latitudes, the question arises, Whence proceeds this apparently so great deviation from the ordinary course of nature in the lower latitudes? The first suggestion, in answer to this question, which might probably occur to most minds, would proceed

‘from the well-known inequality of the temperature . of the atmosphere, in the same parallels of latitude, in ‘the different longitudes, apparent in the most especial - ‘manner, between that upon the land and that upon the sea, but also in the variations upon the land, in proae tion to the distances of given places from the sea.

The effects of this great inequality are chiefly seen ‘ in the temperate zone, in the variation of temperature between: the eastern and western coasts of the two great terrestrial portions of the globe, proceeding from the prevalence of westerly winds, by which these coasts of both continents experience the influence of the higher temperature of the sea, across which the winds blow, even to a great distance, in the interior, with sufficient regularity to render to a certain extent differences of longitude the same in effect as differences of latitude, wherever there are no especial causes, such as the elevation of the land and the course of other winds, to counteract the general effects of the prevailing winds of the same latitudes.

The elevation of the land, indeed, would be the next cause that would suggest itself for the solution of the difficulty. But this is very partial in its effects, and we know that there are no very high lands," of any extent e despatches add, moreover, a new proof of the constancy of the law of the lower temperature of the land compared wit: that of the sca by the captain’s account that the greatest cold which he experienced was always with the wind 5.S.W., which was off the land, and that the thermometer invariably rose when the wind was from the Polar Sea.

at least, either in the immediate district of Siberia, of which we are speaking, or in the places of the above observations in the Arctic Sea. When, also, we consider the well-known causes which explain sufficiently the difference of the temperature upon the coasts of the continents, and that of the countries remote from the sea in the temperate zone, we are naturally led to apply the same causes equally to the higher latitudes,. Putting aside the former of these causes, and regarding the second and more probable, we ‘are ied to the pre- © sumption of there being an extensive open sea in the. direction of the west, feom the sites of the observations of our navigators. But we are here*met by the wellknown fact, that all the aqueous portion of the globe in the latitudes of which we are speaking, is covered with ice at the season at which the above observations were made. To other causes, therefore, we must look for this apparent eccentricity in the operations of Nature, in her arrangement of the different climates and the varied temperature of the globe.

Let us first then with this view, inquire whether it. be yet established, that the temperature of the atmo-~- sphere generally, or of that of the different parts of the globe, is wholly dependent upon the great external cause, the solar heat, regulated and modified by the inclination of the axis of the earth, and the causes before mentioned, or whether sufficient discrepance be not apparent in the conclusions drawn upon this supposition to admit at least of great probability, that the climates and the temperature of the atmosphere of different parts of the globe are considerably influenced also by internal causes., :

It is remerkable, that in observing the difference of the temperature between the higher latitudes of the southern and northern hemispheres, upon which the sun equally shines, we find that that which, for the

want of an equal proportion of land, we should, according fo the seemingly established Jaws above mentioned, have expected to find the warmest, is in fact the coldest. Now many of the greatnatural philosophers, for reasons which we must accept, suppose that the solid substances which we find upon the earth’s surface form only a crust of from thirty to 200 miles in thickness, over a mass of matter in a state of fusion. Nevertheless, though there should be no doubt concerning the staté of the interior " of the globe, the experiments which have hitherto been raade, seem to be wholly inconclusive in respect to the eéquality of the thickness of the crust of the earth, on accouut of- the contracted field of the experiments. The greater part of these appear to have been made in our deepest coal mines in Durham and Northumberland, where it has been observed, that the heat increases in - proportion to the descent, at the rate of 1 degree Fahrenheit for every thirty-four English feet. Other experiments have however been made, particularly in the lead and silver mines in Saxony, where the proportion of increase of heat with the descent has been found to be 1 degree of Fahrenheit for every thirty-five feet. But in other,mines in that country, it has been necessary to descend twice that depth.for each degree of increase of temperature. $ Now, our admirable Lyell in his great work on geology, after speaking of M. Cordier’s having made the ‘most extensive comparisons of the different results in different countries concerning. the internal heat of the earth, makes these remarks: ‘*M. Cordier announces as the result of his experiments‘on the temperature of the interior of the earth, that the heat increases rapidly with the depth; but that the increase does not follow the same law over the whole globe, being twice or three times as much in one country as in another, and that these differences are not in constant relation with either the latitudes or longitudes of places. He is of opinion, however, that the increase would not be overstated at about 1 degree Fahrenheit for every forty-five feet.” The same M. Cordier is of opinion that the heat of the earth’s centre is about 160 times that of melting iron.

" bet us now suppose, that the earth were eaneeaten in a hundred different places to an equal depth to that of the mines in which the experiments have been already made, or no deeper even than'to the point at which the cold is first checked and begins to diminish, and especially in the higher latitudes of the two great continents. From this it can scarcely be doubted, would arise new data concerning the thickness of this covering of our burning pianet: and if this were found unequal, then the variations of the temperature of the atmosphere might be found to be more or less influericed * by comparative distances of different portions of the earth’s surface from the grand internal heat.

Now, with regard to the probability of discovering that the crust of the earth is not in all parts of equal thickness, and the surface equally affected, let us make a further reference to the discoveries of science... The form of the earth, we are assured by the mathematicians and astronomers, is that of an oblate spheroid, which the greatest among them found to be the form that, by the established laws of nature, a chaotic mass, such as that of which our now beautiful world once consisted, would certainly take in revo.ving upon its axis. But it does not appear to have been shown by any natural philosopher, that che rotatory motion of thes earth would necessarily cause either inequalities in the thickness of the covering of its surface, or render this invariable ; or, which is the same thing, whether the portion of the earth which is still in a state-of fusion be or be not, by
that or by any other cause, precisely of the form of the external surface. ©

Our great natural philosopher and astronomer, Herschel, in treating of the-measurement and dimensions of our planet, calculates its deviation from the purespherical form, by which it becomes that of an oblate spheroid, to be the 5}, th part of its diameter at the equatorgor about twenty-four miles; which will bring the surface at the poles about twelve’ miles nearer the centre of the earth than that at the equator. Now, if that portion _ of the globe which is in a state of fusion, should not be gubjected equally to the effects of its rotatory move- _ ment, and,should not have taken the same form as its external surface, the lands in the higher latitudes will of course be proportionally nearer the heated material which forms the great bulk of our planet.

If we suppose, then, as appears probable, that upon making more.extensive experiments, it should be found that those portions of the earth’s surface which enjoy, so little of the sun’s rays, rest upon a thinner shell than that-upon which we tread in the temperate zone, we may reasonably conclude that the temperature of the atmosphere would be found to be influenced as well by internal as by external causes.

There is,.moreover, a phenomenon, whatever its cause or effects, which may be placed in conjunction with that above mentioned. This is the aurora borealis, What is the cause, we will ask, and whence pro-~ ceeds that light seen invariably in the north? If it be replied that it is electricity, we must demand again, How is it generated, and why always towdids the pole of the earth?

Moreover, if we would further multiply references to unexplained phenomena, we might even name among others that great difference in the temperature of the rivers of Siberia which has been herein noticed.

And again, asa last suggestion concerning the cause of phenomena and known facts and their unknown causes, though not the least important of those that present themselves, let us ask,.Who will explain why there are found in this region innumerable remains of animals similar in form to some, yet~more prodigigus than any, that now inhabit the torrid.zone, ‘and which lived: since the last great geological revolution, as is evident from the substances in which or amidst which they are found? All tiiose who have attempted to account for this region being once the country of the mammoth, have, for reasons which de not interfere with the freedom of our comparatively unimportant remarks, trod as gingerly at every step of their way, as reputation might walk upon the crust of a voleano of literary criticism; and their conclusions remain proportionally unsatisfactory.

Now, if amidst all this uncertainty concerning these several phenomena in regard especially to the past, it may be permitted to make a single step upon the tempting path of conjecture concerning the future, we would demand, Who is there among us who shall say that we may not by and.bye discover our long-lost and regretted countrymen, for whom we have sought so many years in vain, surviving in a climate ameliorated by a great Polar Sea, and in a land producing some fruits of the earth yet unknown to us, and which nourish other organised beings of which we know nothing, even up to creatures similar—(and who dare conjecture more ?) — to ourselves ?

The meruhant, upon whose movements I was in some degree dependent, was not yet ready.. We had no cause, hcwever, to regret this delay, on account of the condition and the character of the country through which we had to pass. Throughout a great portion of the way, we knew that we had to encounter many

obstacles to our progress, such as morass lands, bogs, and swamps, and rivers, and mountains; and this was the season at which the swamps could not fail to be full of water. Thus, as the-weather. was now fine, what we lost in time, we were sure we should gain in the decrease of the water in the swamps, which it was believed would be the greatest of the difficulties that we were sure ever ry step of our arduous journey would, in one shape or other, present.

The kind family which had followed us upon the Iéna, was ready before us. They had completed all their arrangements upon the ninth of the month, and were to commence their sad journey for Ayan, the place of their destination, upon the Sea of Ochotsk, upon the following day; and upon the morning of the tenth, I ealled to bid them farewell.

Upon arriving at Licutenant Rosenburg’s dwelling, I found his silo, and her child, and the young women that were with her, taking their last training lesson for their dreaded equestrian-journey. The lady seemed to have regained the confidence she had anciently possessed, and the young women were now thought sufficiently improved in the skill and courage that were deemed necessary to admit of their commencing their journey with the .good hope of happily concluding it.
