These are the glacial, districts of these mountains, whence the streams of the lower country are supplied with water, when the sun has its full force in the height of summer. This source, however, of these streams is cut off with “the earlier frosts, which usually occur towards the end of August; afterevshich the lesser rivers are dried up. In some places we found rents in the ice like fissures in solid rocks; and through these the water was running over the ground in winding courses just in the manner that the brooks generally flow; and to pass them was difficult, on account of. the ‘thickness of the ice, which was from ten to fifteen feet. But in some places these unsubstantial banks of the streams were so worn beneath by the passage of the water, that, upon the horses approaching the edge of them, large sheets upon which we were marching broke off, and let us easily down; while the noise they occasioned in falling, made the hills echo with the loud sound from one extremity of the vale to theother. But what was most remarkable to observe upon these glacial. fields, was the heat of the sun’s rays reflected from the ice, which was greater than any thing of the kind I remembered experiencing, except the reflection from the sand in the hottest climates,
. ‘ so kite upon the same scenes immediately around

Here, too, and far from the dry ground or trees, the quantity of the mosquitoes which swarmed untit five in the afternoon exceeded any thing we had met*with in the swamps. Altogether, the scenes and all we experienced during this day were novel in our travels; and the noise at all times of the ice melting stnsibly around us—the occasional deep sounds caused’ by the falling of masses of the frozen element. by the side of the streams—the crackling of the horses’ feet as they crushed the honeycombed ice beneath them—the murmur of the running waters—the clouds of mosquitoes, and the excessive heat,—Jeft an impression ds indelible as that of the more disagreeable portions of the journey already described.,

. While we were in the region of these glaciers, we ‘eek our accustomed hour’s rest during the day. After making a little fire in the stove of the samovar, for which the Yakoutes had provided fuel, we boiled water © without the least difficulty; and after placing some packages on the ice, sat down upon these, and partook of tea and biscuits.

Our march to-day was more rapid than usual; and, at the sixteenth hour from the time we left the last place of encampment, we halted in a deep and wooded valley, surrounded with high mountain peaks, which from their conical forms, were evidently of volcanic formation ; and we were now, by the estimation of our guides, about sixty versts from the spot upon which we had last slept.

I believe I may here notice the want to which we were now reduced, though so soon after the last replenishment of our stock of provisions, as alittle incident of the journy, and place the inconveniences which we thereby suffered to the right account, without any danger of setting down aught in malice.

Whet we came to-prepare our supper this evening, myself @t least was much surprised to find all the biscuits gone, which was certainly, as they had been hitherto the staple of our spare larder, a matter of not a little importance upon such a journey. However, I was toNrably confident, that among certain sacks that were yef untouched, there was something in reserve that would turn,out nearly as good; some treat perhaps, such as rye or barley flour, which our good caterer might intend to surprise the whole party with, whenever the need was most manifest. There was, indeed, nothing of ofr former articles of food left, save about half a meal’ of the dry chips of mutton for two of us; and I was. rather curiqus than anxious to see what would now turn up, quite determined to be satisfied with whatever it might happen to be. And I was the less inquisitive upon the subject, lest-I should chance to deprive my companion of the gratification, of which I thought he. might be anticipatiag the enjoyment, when he should produce his reserve. Not being myself at any time a great eater —and I may say, that at this time I had never met with any man of arfy race that could maintain his strength and spirits upon so little food, or so long upon nothing; as Ihave been able to do—I have generally been careless about the travelling larder, and more especially when not alone; for I would rather travel upon biscuit and water, and have no plague about it, than upon roast beef, and have the responsibility of satisfying others. For once, however, I now met my equal, if not in the accomplishment of which I have just boasted, certainly in negligence in meking provision for eveftual necessity; and I confess I was as much disappointed as astonished, when Ieheard upon the first hint that was given concerning the contents of the well-cared-for sacks, that they contained only tho merchant’s samples of fine goods, save indeed one alone, which was filled with parched peas. But ouf caterer was a young traveller, and probably myself of’ the two was the most to blame for the situation in which we now found ourselves.

Already the Yakoutes had had nothing from@us but occasionally a handful of biscuit dust betwetn them, since we left the last post. Some milk,which they procured there, and which they had put into a leathern bag, turned to a kind of cheese before w¢ stopped again, and had been eaten by them before they lay down, upon the first night..

Nevertheless, such is the.adaptation of the differcht tribes and classes of our varied species to the particular circumstances of their condition, and such the variety in the manner of life of men of distinct races, inhabiting different parts of the earth, that while we pitied the Yakouteg, whom we had reduced, as we supposed, by sad necessity to an allowance from our spare larder such as the same number of mice would have starved upon, these semi-wild men were actually living in luxury, compared with the manner in which we ourselves fared, and were feeding, which was much more, ypon food that could not, like ours, fail..

We had, indeed, observed our friends boiling their pot; but we had been so busy hunting the brooks for ducks, or the bushes for bears, or the woods for birds of any kind that we might chance to find, that we little regarded what they were about, or thought they were only making the most of what we had giventhem. But upon now eperceiving, as they sat round a cauldron, ~ dipping up its contents with wooden spéons, and cool ing broth with their breath, that they were at the same time crushing some solid article of food between the teeth, we examined their mess, and found it to consist of the bark of the spruce chopped in small pieces, and which did not exceed the dimensions of a nf ester
boiled With the glutinous tops of the young sprouts of the samd tree.

_ I had‘ certainly before heard that these men could live upon-such food;. but I thought it a fable at the time, and had before this, long forgotten that I had heard &. When I now, however: actually @aw them eat of thi® mess, I called to mind that I had read also in one of the works of our great natural philosopher Herschel, that sawdust itself was susceptible of con- “version into ae substance bearing no remote analogy to bread, and which, moreover, was both ‘wholesome aiid digestible, as well as highly nutritious; and without having read which, I should scarcely have ventured to ‘mention what we here witnessed, and perhaps at this time have thought, notwithstanding what I had heard, that I had been dreaming, when the note wherein this circuinstance is registered was written.*

Thus we now sat down over our mess of peas and last morsel of clip mutton, to eat ét entirely, ourselves with a very clear conscience, and in dracting that our guns might still aid us in time of greater need, in providing a better® meal than that upon which the Yakoutes were feasting with apparently as much satisfactfon as if they were over a mess of beef stchee.

We made to-night a little discovery, belonging rather to the moral than the physical incidents of the journey. Soon after our tent had been pitched, a thick mist entirely enveloped the grove ayound; and as the air was damp and disagreeable, while the Yakoutes reposed, or told tales to one another over the fire, we took our samovar withif the tent, and afterwards sat down over the chiboock, indisposed for conversation, are dozing like Arabs. Indeed, the wegther and the hour were such
* Herschel’s “ Preliminary Discourse on the Study of Natural

as tended more to inducé thought and reflection than ‘action; and even the time,.in relation to our past and future travels, was that which naturally disposes the mind as well as the body to relaxation and rest. The iron character of the journey seemed broken, in spite of our iaterial wants. We were encamped in a _ sequestered vale near the summit of the mountains, with the descent from which we should encounter the streams that fall into the Ochotsk Sea, on which myself, at least, trusted that I should soon erbark for other and sunnier climes.

After we had been seated for some time, indulgittg separate thoughts, our attention was called to tlie unusual silence beyond the folds of the tent, and we came out together to discover the cause of this. We found now a thicker mist.prevailing than that from which we had fled, concealing every thing beyond the distance of a dozen yards around us. We approached the fire to see whether the Yakoutes were sleeping. earlier than usual. But here we found only some redhot logs mouldering to ashes, or changing to a more volatile element;.and noone of the Yakoutes, either awake or asleep, was any where to be seen.

The absence of our guides surprised us; and after waiting some time, and seeing no one, we called out several times at the top of our voices, to give them notice wheresoever they might be, that we required their presence. But no one appeared, and no voice was heard in answer to this call, and no signal of any kind was returned. The mist was too dense to give us hopes of acearch for our friends being of any avail; so we sat ourselves down quietly upon soine logs by the fire, to awai‘ patiently the solution of the mystery.
The mist continued to veil every thing around us, save the faint outlines of the spruces, which were magnified to: great trees by the yapoury atmosphere,
through\which they were seen; and there was not the smallest motion in the ai to disturb the dead silence which reigned.

A fall hour passed, and we heard and saw nothing that Idd to any conjecture concerning the mysterious absence of the Yakoutes. They could not have’ forsaken us, or we should have wanted our horses also, which were all tranquilly dozing by our side. They could not have gone to gather wood, for logs were lying in abundance witltin a yard of the fire. Nor could they hgve gone in search of water, for a gentle brook “ made syeet music with the enamelled stones” at our very feet. We thought of the bears. But no beasts could have made® meal upon four stout Yakoutes, without a ceremony over their feast that would have dlarmed and brought forth fresh foes, whose eyes and ears had not even been closed, to dispute their right to mangle and devour human flesh. Were our hitherto feithful friends about to put on a new character’ and attack us? To suspect their fidelity in any particular was difficult. But so far from believing them capable of making war upon us, either open or covert, we knew that subjection to a degree’ of respect towards civilised men their conquerors, even beyond any thing perhaps ever before seen among men in a similar condition, was a remarkable feature in the character of the race to which they belonged; and we had no ground for thinking they might be an exception to the general character of their people. Yet where were they ?.e We called again and again at intervals, but received no answer. At length, after repeated calls with no better success,°we fired a gun, which echoed through thé mist from peak to peak, among the volcanic hills around vs, like the distant roar of many cannons. Yet no voice replied, and no one appeared.

While, however, we were still engaged in conjectures concerning the absence of our men, we ghanced to discover near the spot upon which the horges stood some loose white horse-hair lying strewed about upon the ground; and upon examining the horses, weefound it quite certain that some hair had been cut frgm the tails and® manes of more than one of them. At first this seemed, indeed, but to thicken the mystery; but when we now recalled to eur recollection having several fimes during the journey seen some locks of horse-hair attached to ‘the pendant boughs of the taller trees, and that, when we had inquired of the guide the cause of this, we appeared to receive onfy evasive answers, a stream of new light floated across our murky imaginations, and we remembéred having been told at Yakoutsk, that although these aborigines of the land were Christians by law, and even by outward assent while dwelling among men “ that with hely bell are knoll’d to church,” yet that. the ukase before mentionéd, which had effected this important step in their moral progress, had not had power to abolish wholly their ancient religious rites, which were still practised by them in’ secret upon every favourable occasion. And as the very place, the mist, and the hour, seemed all favourable to this purpose, we could no longer doubt the cause of the absence of the Yakoutes. After waiting very patiently for some time longer, we at length heard the cracking of dried sticks and other sounds of footsteps; and presently our friends appeared slowly advancing towards us, magnified to the size of giants by the dense mist through which they were seen. They evidefitly approached full of doubts of their absence being approved of, and probably suspicious of our divining the purjfose for which they had hidden themselves from observation, There appeared, in fact, a gloom and sadness upon their countenances when they were near us, that would itself have confirmed, if it had been ne-

cessary® all that we had conjectured. However, we felt bound to respect their religious rites, whatever they might be, and we made no remarks in allusion to their yetirement and their neglect to appear at our summens, lest the imperfection of the means of intercourse* we possessed might cause what we gaid to be misundesstood. For my-own part I have always thought it a favourable sign in any unenlightened portion of my fellow-men, when I have observed indications of their consciousness gf dependence upon some’Superior Being ; and I have, among the wildest races, always looked vfpon this in proportion to the sincerity which appears, and the moral which is attached to particular super-, stitions, ayindicative of the sooner or later ¢onversion of the people to the religion of civilised man. In general, indeed, the more ridiculous the faith of tribes among whom the more civilised nations have mixed, the more certain and speedy has been its destruction. And is it not, in the meantime, agreeable tg reason “to suppose, that even the worship of an idol, at least if it be not such as is excited by terror alone, but rather springing from a sense of gratitude, is more acceptable to the Creator than the orisons of the man of refinement whose actions do not correspond to the words which his lips utter, or who is moved by the terror attendant upon the uncertainty of the future rather than by thankfulness for the past, and for his hopes of a state to come?

Thus we went to bed, and took no account of the doings of our friends, nor presumed to judge whether they were evil or good; and it is scarcely necessary to add, that thefirst man of the Sclavonian race that we met, that was well acquainted with the gharacter and condition of the Yakoutes, informed us, that all our suppositions concerning the cause of the absence of the men were without doubt quite correct. And the same

Russian, who was. acquainted with all the sup¢rstitions extant among these people, informed us, that.the rites of their ancient worship consist, for the most part, in sacrifices to invisible spirits, which they suppose, dwell in the woods, and more especially in those that bound these and other mountains; and that portions of the horses’ tails that we had frequently seen attacked to the branches of trees, were there placed to, notify to these imaginary beings when they might chance to pass by, - that such rite had been performed, and that thereabout they would find the sacrifice offered, which it was thought in this case was probably something these men had saved from their last meal of good food. ‘ Perhaps of all the impressions upon.the minds of men that are not the offspring of a higher faculty than the imagination, nothing is more natural than that which peoples even this world with beings that are of a nature different from our own, and imperceptible to our senses ;' and accqidingly, such appears to havé been the belief even of some of the great departed among ourselves.
“ Millions of spiritual creatures walk the earth,” Unseen, both when we wake, and when we sleep,”

were not words put into the mouth of the first man by the euthor of dur great epic poem as opinions springing from superstition. Nor can Addison, when he asserts, in the 12th and other numbers of the Spectator, his. belief in this truth, be, any more than Milton, said to be conveying the opinions of others, or to be treating of mere superstitions.
CHAP. XXIL JOURNEY FROM YAKOUTSK TO OOHOTSK — continued.

Arter about six hours’ repose, including the whole time of our stay at this encampment, we rose and took some tea, and*ate only a few cold peas that were left of our supper of the last evening, and commenced the day’s journey at a very little later hour than on ordinary oc~ casions. The horses, also, had fared very badly during our stay here. They had found a few rhubarb plants, which they devoured very eagerly ; but they had chiefly eaten the buds and tender twigs of the young spruce trees,

The mornfmg was fine; and, as we proceeded, the scenery around us presented both grand and agreeable objects for contemplation. The vegetation was of the usual varieties of the fir tribes, including the cedar; and all the trees were in greater abundance, and of firmer growth, and larger dimensions, than the average of those of the same species that we had seen in the plains. But whenever we found ourselves wpon an elevation, by the rugged character of the ground, the hills and the magnificent voleanic peaks on ald sides seemed to enclose us within a bowl which had uo passage either to approach or to leave it; without«climbing some one of the rugged mountains around.

After about two hours’ march, we reached yet a higher elevatiom than that of the spot upon which we had passed the night. There was, nevertheless, here no distant view, on account of the narrower basin in whica we seemed now enclosed; and there was but littie vegetation around us, by. reason of: the rocky. character of the ground,

After another hour, we commenced, almost imperceptibly, our descent.of the principal range of these mountains. A thick mist received us, as we appeared to enter upen a new territory, but ‘this soon turned to a warm, drizzling rain. In another hour the descent began to be precipitous and the way difficult. We now crossed several narrow an rapid streams, which were the sources of the tributary River Aldan, which falls into the Léna. After this, the descent became gradual ; and at mid-day, we halted and took our samovar in another basin of the mountains, not dissimilar from that in which we had last slept.

The merchant and myself began now, it must be confessed, to be very hungry; and we no sooner alighted, than we took our guns in hand, and set off to perambulate the groves around, in the good hope of finding some beast or bird to shoot and make ~ meal upon; but finding none, we were forced to be contented with tea and sugar. The Yakoutes were evidently amused at our apparent impatience, as they sat very contentedly over their bark porridge. But they gave

us this ‘consolation, that we should not want food in good and wholesome flesh very long, if we liked that of the bear, astwe were approaching some of the favourite haunts of that beast in this district of the country.
We remained here but a short time. Upon renewing our march, we found the country rygged and undulatiag, and we crossed several rapid but narrow streams.

We did not again halt until near midnight; but: the road the yhole day had been so fugged and precipitous, and had so much abounded in torrents of difficult passage, that we did not suppose we could have made above thirty versts during sixteen hours of, actual margh. The place selected for repose was like that where we had passed the last night. But there was now a gloomier prospect before us than we had hitherto had to contemplate, on the score of food. Neither beast nor bird was to be found; and as far as the guides could*judge, we were yet above twenty-five versts from the next post. We had, indeed, nothing whatever left, save one or two lumps of sugar. Had a bear, or some bird of any kind appeared, however gross for food, it would have excited in us the spirit of chase of the eagle in pursuit of his prey. The prospect for our horses, too, was not much better; for there was here neither the rhubarb plant nor the spruce tree, The few shrubs that were to be found were larches, the - tender parts of which are inferior for animal diet to those of the spruce. But there was a little moss, which was probably all they would have to nourish them until the next evening. We, however, drank our tea, and retired ix#the full hope of being roused to hear of the approach of a bear some time during the night, or at least of hearing the -chirrup of some one of the winged tribes in the morning.
The night, however, brought us no such welcome

visitor as we hoped to make a feast upon, and the morning opened without any sound of birds; either of song or of prey. When we arose, the atmosphere was full of cold dense vapours. We took our usuab tea, and, fasting, once more mounted our horses, in the hope of reaching the next post before the day was fat adVanced.

As we proceeded, we found the country now abounding in larch. Sometimes we were ascending and some- “times descending; and as the way was difficult, our march was slow. Late in the afternogn, we reached the fourteenth post, called Allack Tinska, upon the River Allack, and about twenty-five versts, according to the judgment of the guides, from the place at which we had set out.in the morning, and at 150 vers{s from the last post.

The joy of the horses, when they obtained the first glimpse of the Yakoute hut and the green meadow in which it stood, with a Tungouse wigwam beside it, seemed quite equal to our own; and-as they increased their pace, they broke the silence of the smotritel’s dwelling-place by loudly neighing all together until we alighted at the door of the hut.

The debt of gratitude which we owed the poor beasts from which we were now to ‘separate, was scarcely less than that which we had felt towards those from which we last parted. Nothing, indeed, but the exploits of our horses in the swamps could have ex~ ceeded in devotion the patience and the spirits with which these animals had suffered hunger and fatigue during the passage of these difficult mountain passes. That which.I rode upon this occasion, was the easiest~- paced and gentlest of his species that I ever mounted. When we pressed their necks, in the same manner as with the last, as we handed them all over to the smotritel, with an injunction to let them feed as soon as possible, I remembered my distrust when I first saw

the shaggy coat and dwarf stature of that which I was to ride; and I could not help thinking of the difference we somefimes find between the first impressions made upon wusvby a new acquaintance of rough exterior, and the f@ elings with which we take leave of the same person, after attributes of a higher order than appearance have gained our respect and regard.

We would gladly have continued our march for four more hours, had we found any sort of provision here that we could have carried with us. Nevertheless, we had at our present disposition food for the whole party that was equal to the greatest luxuries that our imagiations had painted when hungry, and we could not, fail to syp to-night, and breakfast to-morrow most sumptuously, if we stayed. No sooner, indeed, was our condition known to the Yakoute smotritel, than his wife descended into a kind of vault by the side of the hut, and brought up a large bowl full of milk; and we were scarcely. at ease in the wigwam, wfich we chose to enter in preference to the hut, before a fine mess of cream, cranberries, and cedar nuts, was placed upon the ground before us. e Of bread, indeed, there was none. But this was a luxury that we had had no expectation of*finding. Our hopes had been chiefly set on beef, which the Yakoutes rarely want at any season, where there is any number of them together. The weather was wholly too hot during the middle of the day for the transport of cream to any distance, the thermometer being at 17 and 18 degrees; so we determined at any rate to remain here for the night. The dish upon which we supped was these good people’s only constant foode and both the berries and the nuts which we ate were the product of_the previous year. Sometimes the Yakoutes reduce the cream to a thick lumpy substance, which is similar to new cheese, and which we tasted the next day for the first time. For the present we ate of the dish above mentioned in a manner proportioned to our great appetites after so long an abstinence, with the security of the past and further horse exercise, and the mixture of berries, against the consequences of indulging, after sb long fasting, in food not the lightest and the safest for supper, perhaps, upon ordinary occasions. «

The next morning we rose very early; and after break fasting upon the same dish upon which we had supped, and feeling much the better for the two good meals, our Yakoutes filled some skins which they had provided for the purpose with cream, and another bag of some-
_what smaller dimensions with cranberries, and a third with cedar nuts; and with this good provision we recommenced our journey.

There was little chance of attaining the next post, which was at -the distance of above 200 versts, within four days with the most favourable weather; but as we were approaching a lower countiy, there was the greater prospect of killing something to supply our wants by the way; and if we should but be fortunate enough to meet with a bear, we had no doubt that we should be able to put an end to all our troubles on account of the condition of our larder. ¢

We began the journey to-day by crossing the River Allack in the smotrétel’s canoe, while our horses swam. But soon after this we encountered another of those obstacles to the passage of travellers through this part of the country, with which we were so painfully familiar; and for three hours we were wading again in one of the worst description of swamps, and which we estimated at about five versts in breadth.”

After passing this swamp, we found the country covered with the larch tree exclusively for twenty-five or thirty versts. About mid-day we stopped as usual, and took our samovar and a mess of cream. After

this, we recrossed the Allack lower down the stream, and continued our road along its shores until the evening, when we encamped-upon-a spot where we had a tolerable Pasture for the horses, and where, before we slept, i finished the remainder of our cream, now well churned to the kind of cheese above mentioned.

We altowed ourselves but yery little rest during this night, chiefly that we might have the greater chance of killing some ducks in the river in the morning. We had seen no birds, save a single blackbird, since the first days of our journey ; but the guides informed us that all the rivers in this vicinity were occasionally visited by wild ducks at this season; and we were fullof hope of getting a shot at some of them. Thus, after rising and taking our samovar at an early hour, and a few cranberries and cedar nits which we had reserved, while the Yakoutes took their bark mess, how flavoured with a few cranberries, the merchant and myself set off to trace the bankseof the river for two- or three versts, in hopes of catching some unwary prey tranquilly sleeping; but we returned without having seen or heard the voice of any living creature fit for food or sport.

Early in this day’s journey we crossed ‘several valleys filled with sow, through which.rivulets generally passed, and the courses of which we followed between walls of snow about twenty feet in height. In the middle of the day, we crossed a glacier of about five versts in breadth, and subsequently several smaller, honeycombed every where, and furnishing running streams, the beds of which were sometimes the ice and sometimes the solid ground; and we had here the same inconveniencéS as upon a previous occasion, from the excessive heat at noon and from the quantities of mosquitoes. The country around, too, presented the same bold features as that where we encountered the last glaciers, with several cones plainly of volcanic formation,

As we descended again very gradually towards the lower country, we found the vegetation much finer than any we had seen at the same elevation upon thetopposite side of the mountains. The trees, chiefly, «vhich we now observed flourishing along the sides of the hills by which we passed, were the larch, the mountain ash, and the lime. The larch was growing much mere luxuriantly than we had any where before seen it. We observed some of these trees now with trunks large enough for the masts of small sea-vessels.. The ash was small and thinly sown; but the limes most surprised us by their dimensions. Some of those that we measured were from forty-five to fifty-five inches in circumference. ; -

We had a little rain during this day; but our road upon the whole was good; and when we thought we had made above sixty versts, we deemed it time to stop ; and finding here a spot where our horses had by no means a bad paste, we pitched oak tent, took our samovar, and, for the second time during the journey, Jay down to rest quite supperless and very hungry.

Early the next morning we passed over several streams, and ‘several more broad valleys filled with snow. At mid-day we crossed the deepest stream we had yet met with, over a portion of which our horses had to swim, by which we were immersed, as on a previous occasion, up to our waists. This would have been a trouble to us at the beginning of our journey ; but we had at this tim seen too many similar, and still felt one that was much worse, to make any account of this —
” “ Where the greater malady is fix’d, The lesser is scarce felt,” ~
~= we were even suffering from the want of food, the greatest of all the evils that we at any time endured.

We found the soil of better quality, and the productions of the country more numerous, as we proceeded ; and among the varieties of shrubs which abounded near the streai$s, we observed the rose, which was now in full bloom} “We crossed however several more valleys filled with ice and snow, and similar to those we hgd before passed over ; and we waded several more deep and rapid streams. Towayds evening, we found the woods again wholly consisting of larch. At length, we encamped upon the bank of one of the streams, according to the judgment of our guides, about fifty versts from the next sfation.

*Our condition for want of food we could not now disguise fram ourselves, was becoming alarming, and as soon as the tent was erected, we held a formal council of all the party, to discuss seriously a question which we had already informally put to one another during the day, whether we should not kill one of the horses, to satisfy our crating appetites and escape all further risks; and I do not believe that any body of councillors of any crowned head in the world, whether full or fasting, or puffing the chiboock and dozing, ever discussed more dispassionately any vital question concerning the btood of their own species, than we deliberated upon and discussed this question, touching so nearly our own proper safety and interests, and the blood only of a single quadruped.

The Yakoutes pleaded the cause of the beasts upon the score of humanity, as we could not help thinking, by the manner in which they regarded our shaggy companions, while we talked of shedding the klood of one of them. Fo® themselves, they made us understand, they never killed one of their horses, uptil they had passed five whole days together without any sort of food. It would be a shame, then, we said to each other, that while we had tea anda morsel of sugar, and the prospect before us of better and more lawful food than horseflesh, to destroy one of the creatures given -us to relieve and lighten our labour, and even to refine and embellish civilised life, and not to devour. %t seemed as if it would be mere wantonness and gluttorfy. It would, at least, have been an act of which our semibarbarous companions were not capable. Q

’ This important question being thus,set at rest, the merchant and myself took our guns, and stole through the bushes by the side of the stream gear which we were encamped, with our thoughts full now of the blood of an enemy instead of a friénd of our species, and 8f£ that of the water fowl, both of which could not but Be lawful food, and very good if we could get them. And we determined to practise all the cunning we were masters of, in this attempt to supply, if it were possible, our natural wants.

As we advanced slowly and cautiously, sometimes approaching the edge of the wood upbn our hands and knees, and peeping at intervals between the bushes, to see if any thing were floating upon the stream, I thought I never enjoyed sport so keenly before.

When we rise twice or thrice a day from a full meal, we cannot be in a right frame ‘either of body or mind for the proper enjoyments of the chase. Our sluggish spirits then want the true incentive to action, which should be hunger, with the hope before us of filling a craving stomach. I could remember once before being for 4, time dependent upon the gun for food, and feeling a touch of the charm of savage life —for every condition of humanity has its good as well as its evil—but never till now did *I fully comprehend the attachment of the sensitive, not drowsy Indian, to his manner of living, which is found nevertheless to be so great, that though the years of his race, as he cannot but know, are already numbered,

by reason of his refusing to adopt the mode of life of the civilised man, yet he will persist rather than sow and rgap, or attempt to acquire any of the useful arts whicl, we practise. This; indeed, is a trait in the clfyacter of the wild man, which those who labour to reclaim and save his race from extinction, appear to have studied far too little. Touch but the passions which the chase excites, which are the very essence of his being, by other motives to action, and cease at the same time to fill his mind’ with revolting. terrors and with gloomy impressions of futurity, such as*are taught by very good, but often, certainly, vefy weak-minded men, and who shall say that all we wish to effegt may not be accomplished ?

As we skulked along the banks of the brook, under cover of the bushes, peeping out and surveying the stream at intervals, the slightest noise caused by the wind, or by the running waters, as it reached our ears, instantly filled our ¢qaginations with the Jiveliest images that hunger and hope could produce. One minute we thought we heard the splashing of the wings of a whole flock of ducks alighting upon.the water, aid the next we seemed to perceive, half concealed by the dusky firs that crowded the shores upon the opposite side of the river, a fine fat bear drinking securely at the stream. The most hungry wolves never sought more eagerly for a lamb quenching its thirst at a brook, nor the wiliest snake to catch a nobler prey sleeping, than we now sought if perchance we might find a bear drinking within our reach, or ducks floating tranquilly ngea the surface of the water.

While we wave thus intently bent upon our object, suddenly the sound of the voice of some biyd or other, whose note we did not recognise, reached our attentive ears, We now pressed the ground yet more gingerly than ever; and presently we observed a_ blackbird vOoL. If. U :
skipping from tree to tree and from branch to -branch,

-among the tall firs around us. Our attention thus drawn from the pursuit of worthier prey, was now fixed upon this poor bird; and lest she should esc ipe 1s, we determined that we would both fire at her t«gether. Whethe: it were that it was her hour of rest, and we had disturbed her, and she was not yet well awal:e, we ob- -served that she had not her natural voiee- and that shehad no fear of us. Witha note more like that of the magpie than that common to her own species, she flew towards us, and perched upon a tree within less’ than- half gunshot from the spot upon which we were standing. ‘et so eager were we to obtain _this delicate morsel for our supper, that we persisted still in firing st the same moment; and the triggers were no sooner pulled than the massacre was accomplished. But in the name of all the spirits of the wood, of what chagrin to us was it not tke cause! At the report of our guns, a brace of ducks from beneath the very banks of the river upon which we trod, rose from the water, and passing within shot of us, flew further up the stream, We seemed like merchants ‘who, upon the loss of a ship, should be found to have insured only her jolly-boat, which had floated safely on shore. And again, upon picking up our prey, we had the misfortune to find that one-half of the little bird was shot away into the air, and the other half so mangled, that it would not have made half a meal for a sparrow hawk; while, without making any account of the Yakoutes, we had to divide it between two men with more eager appetites than the most rave.ous eagles.

Renewed hopes and fresh excitemen., however, soon possessed us. We had at least seen a brace of fine ducks that, we agreed, appeared, as they flew by us, as fat and plump as if they had been bred in some royal aviary, or park; and they were still perhaps not

far from us. Thus we loaded again, and renewed our pursuit with increased cunning. and caution, excited by fresh anc greater hopes. Not a fox in the country could have excelled’ us in these necessary accomplishments Ser the ends we had in view. And now, after creeping for a few hundred yards, and peeping out upon the river at every opening, we again espied the object of our renewed Jabours, the two ducks, floating and stemming the current in the middle of,the stream. I never wished tg be invisible till now, nor longed to have even such wings only as those of Cupid, or of Afiel, or of some sylph, to lighten a little the pressure of the hands and knees upon the ground.

At length, after creeping on as close to the earth as serpents in sight of their prey, we reached an advantageous spot from which to take our aim, without having caused any alarm. AS we were not quite close together, and the ducks were swimming apart from each other, and we dated not speak for fear of disturbing them, we settled by signs which each of us should aim at; and in a minute the triggers were drawn, both shots were fatal, and the ducks*turned on their backs. —

But our prey was not yet secured. The current which the birds had been stemming while they were swimming was strong, and the instant they turned over they began to drift rapidly down the stream. But at perceiving this, we both plunged into the water, and after wading for a short distance, found ourselves swimming. However after a good ducking —a very appropriate term, from whatever it may be derived — we finally secured our prey, and we had the satisfactien to find they were two lack ducks, and quite as fat as they had seemed. Need it be said, upon what @ brave mess of séchee we supped this evening, and ‘with what new vigour we were inspired for the prosecution of our next day’s Journey ?
CHAP. XXIII. 1. rs JOURNEY FROM YAKOUTSK TOWARDS OCUOTSK —, continued.

AutnoucH it was long after midnight before we lay down upon the night of our duck feast, we rose at an early hour for the next day’s march; and while the Yakoutes were preparing the horses, we took our accustomed samovar. The grateful beverage seemed to us this morning more refreshing than ever; and we commenced the day’s,march under the favourable auspices of fine weather, and with the checring hope of attaining -the next post before the close of the day. During the first portion of this aay’s march, we passed over. several glacial plains similar to those which have been described. After. these, we crossed one or two. streams that were broader and deeper than any we had met with since we passed the highest ridge of

the mountains. The face 8f the country and the vegetation, also, were much changed, and our descent was now morg apparent. Instead of the varieties in kind among thy trees and shrubs of the climate, which had lately Pieen so great a relief to our weary sight, the larch here entirely covered the ground ; and the trees were of a finer growth than those which we had seen. mingled among, the varied productions of the better soils, or the more elevated lands.

At noon we geposed as usual for an hour; and after renewing our march, we found still the same country aftd the same obstructions of running streams and rugged ground, which continued to impede our progress, |

A single jncident only upon this day’s journey relieved the tediousness of the march. Our horses had been constantly raising alarm by their terror of the bears, and exhibiting to us the inconsistencies in the composition of their character. ‘hey daily faced dangers that were a thousand tines greater than any to be dreaded on account of the bears, and displayed attributes for which we deify our own species; and yet the. mere scent of their furred enemy of the forest reduced them to the most. timid of the four-footed tribes. Our chief guide’s horse, which was first in the order of march, now at a particular spot where the underwood was thick, was seized with more alarm than usual; and spreading his terror through: the troop by his snorting, and his determination to go no further in that direction, brought us all to a stand, The alarm of the animals was now indeed so much greater than at any time before while we were in their company, that, we thought we had got at mst exactly what we desired, and we made our dispositions to profit by the hazard. We turned a little back upon our steps, and tied all the beasts to the same tree, and left one of the Yakoutes to guard them and keep them quiet, while the rest of us returned ta the expected combat. Wich our various national arms, the Yakoutes refusing two pistols which we could spare, and offered them, we now scoured the wood around with every reasonable hope of the aeart of a bear for our dinner; for our number’ and our weapons were sufficient to leave but a poor chance to any animal not very quick indeed, of doing any one of us an injury, or of escaping after he might be within our reach. But after a full hour's search, no sign of any habitant of the forest whatever was to be seen or heard. Nevertheless, we had still great trouble in leading our horses past the spot at which they had taken the alarm. By coaxing and caressing, however, and firing pistols, which seemed more effective than any thing else, we succeeded. But we had no sooner remounted ‘them, after we were twenty or ‘thirty yards past the dreaded spot, than it required at least as much exertion to restrain their quick onward march, as we had just made to oblige.:hem to continue their way. The opinion of the Yakoutes was, that a bear had been sleeping at this place, and had gone off before our approach; but we found no signs of any thing of the kind; and as Nature had not given us the some olfactory sensitiveness that sh2 had bestowed upon our chevaline companions, we were still too hungry to allow of our losing the time that the pursuit would require without any such guide to direct our search.

The manner in which the Yakoutes face the bear has been before described. These men informed us, that it was very rarely indeed that any of theit people were killed by this ferocious animal, but that they were frequently slightly, and sometimes severely. wounded after they had closed with him and given him his mortal blow. One of themselves, indeed, had had his left arm lacerated and his shoulder scarred by one of these fierce beasts.,

At length, after four days of fatiguing march since we quitted the last post, at about six o’clock this evening we yeached the river and ‘station of Tudomo Krestowsxa. We found here a very obliging Yakoute smotrifel ; and as soon as our most pressing want was known, his wife, who was tq our.minds the prettiest as well as the best-natured woman we had seen® since we entered the Yakoute country, set immediately to work to provide for us the best fare in her power ; and after taking the usual leave of our noble beAsts, we entered the hut. ;

¢These good people were lodged in a rather curious ‘sdvt of dwelling, in construction and appearance something between a Yakoute ordinary hut and a Tungouse * wigwam. It was of the same hexagonal form of which we had already observed several, and open at the top of. the pointed roof; but in other respects it was like the wigwam. It was nevertheless divided into two parts; and of one, of these we were offered exclusive possession. We were not, however, disposed to take advantage of this; and before we had. time to seat ourselves upon the benches under the walls around the general apartment, the hostess reappeared with a plentiful supply of,the same. dish of cream, cranberries, and cedar nuts, that we bad so ‘much enjoyed at the last station, but which, though excellent, and ample for all our present wants, gave us but little hopes of finding a supply of more suitable articles for our next day’s journey.

We did not pass a very.agreeable night at this post, on account of the mosquitoes, which were here in such clouds, that tke good people were obliged to keep constant fires of cattle manure alight in the middle of the wigwam, the odour and half-stifling effects of which made us regret that we nad not pitched our own tent.

In the morning, although we had not had much hope of being well provisioned ior the next day’s march, we were a little disappointed, when over: the same dish at breakfast as that upon which we had supped, to find that there was nothing. whatever to be procured to add to the three components of which our late and early meal consisted. We did, however, obtain a few more of tlie cranberries to carry with us than upon the last occasion; and, although these are not very good food without cream, they conserve bétter than any thing else. Thus the beginning at least of the journey before us would be more favourable than the last. And besides this, the distance was happily’shorter, and, the rivers permitting, the journey would occupy a day

‘less. Moreover, we had here the satisfact‘on to learn, that the advance party of the merchant’s caravan had. only left this post the day before our arrival, which rendered it probable that we should overtake them in about two days at the furthest; and they, we knew, - had provisions.even among the articles of thevt merchandise. ;

We left this station at an earlier hour than we usually commenced our cay’s march, bent upon making every effort to overtake the merchant’s advanced party, if it were possible, before the close of the next day. During the first part of the morning we were enveloped in a dense mist; but as the day advanced the atmosphere became clear, and the thermometer at noon was at 19 degrees of heat, which was the highest to which it rose at any time during our journey. ;

Our progress was slower to-day, notwithstanding our efforts, than it had been during the two or three preceding days, owing tothe number o/stony streams that lay in our way. We had sometimes to follow the courses of these for a verst or two, as well as to cross at intervals from side to side; so that when we stopped to repose for an hour, after seven or cight hours of

march, our guides did no? think we had made above twenty versts. Our journey was, nevertheless, now ‘across afcountry less hilly than any we had seen since we airivyd at the foot of the western range of the mountains; and the distant view in our front presented hills of is altitude than those which we were leaving behind us.

During the latter half of this day, the obstructions to our march became greater; and for four or five hours we were enceemore involved in a low morass, to the difficulties of the passage of which, one instance only could be compared, among all those we had experienced, since the commencement of our journey from, Yakoutsk.e We had accomplished, however, as we believed, about forty five versts, when we encamped, as we were accustomed to do whenever it was in our power, upon the bank of a clear stréam.

We had this evening the opportunity of making a little experiments for the purpose of solving some -doubts in our minds concerning a report of the Yakoute character. A remark has been already made, upon the manner in which the very soul of this people seems to have succumbed to the genius and authority of their cénquerors. Such, indeed, is the apparent character of their submission, that an opinion prevails among even Russiaus that have lived among them, that they are arrant cowards. This impression, as we becaine acquainted with the men who accompanied us, appeared to be so inconsistent with our knowledge of their readiness to face the bear so badly armed, that it was a frequent subject of conversation with us upon the journey, and We had some time since determined, that in case we should find any opportunity, ye would endeavour to ascertain the correctness of the Russian opinion, or the error upon which it might be founded ; and a little circumstance which seemed to make the occasion favourable for the \experiment, happened this evening while we were over our samovar, and the Yakoutes were around the fire. i

Many, even of those who have lived or sojourned for a season in thinly-peopled countries, or in the woods, and have seen more clearly and felt more impressively the deperidence of man upon man, than those,who have not seen the phases in the varied degrees and shades of © human society which different modes of life exhibit, although they niay have-lost the superfluous portions of the arrogance of rank throughout its grades, and learned to respect equally every man who performs worthiby the part which fortune has assigned him, may neverthtless have experienced the inconveniences attending a - relaxation of self-importance, where the peculiarity of the case has not seemed to warrant what at other times might have been both politic and commendable. Our Yakoutes were at all times attentive to their duties, though’ they did not neglect their amusenients. During the time of leisure, and frequently on the way, they diverted themselves by singing; and though their notes seemed to us to be monofonous, and not worth listening to on their own account, we deemed them proofs of the cheerful disposition of the people ; and where there is cheerfulness, who shall fear treachery, or the consequences of any evil passion? Several times, however, during our sufferings from hunger, we had some suspicions that there was a little more than quite harmless cheerfulness in their songs. We thought, that we traced through indescribable signs, not merely exulta-- tion, but even some contempt of us, on account of the superiority they possessed in relation to the prosecution of the labour in which we were together engaged, in having a dish always at hand, by which they could at least escape the immediate consequences of hunger. But the manier in which they were singing and talk-

ing over their mess on th occasion, at the time we -were over our sa@movar in our-tent, convinced us that we had not been mistaken, and that our familiarity with our friends liad had the effect of so relaxing their respect, I to induce them to ridicule us in their songs, In fact, we were in reality offended; and | we éhoss the oppoy tunity to try the truth of the i impression prevalent concerning the character of their race, and whether they really had the awe they were stated to have of civilised man, such as we consfdered ourselves, or whether it were rather the: law in cool blood that they dreaded. * Our plan having been agreed upon, was thus put into, execution... We issued rather suddenly from the tent without our pistols at our girdles, and while we spoke some rough words to the men in our own several tongues, myself, as the least likely, from being a foreigner, to strike them with any terror of the law, advanced to where they were«gated, and seized the shaggy°hair of the heads of two of them that were sitting together, while my companion, not to make the menace too great, stood like a witness merely pf what occurred, though ready to aid in case of any opposition to this apparent violence. But the very instant the act. was done, the whole frames of these two powerful men shook, while the two men that were seated opposite to them sat still and seemed to experience hardly less trepidation than their comrades. Thus it was settled, at all cvents, that at so trifling a menace from two men, one of whom was not even a Russian, four Yakoutes were reduced to the condition of the lamb in the claws of the wolf. Inea future chapter will appear the reason for this particular account of this circumstance.

We allowed ourselves, upon this night, but a very few hours of repose. Hunger disposed, and hope stimulated us to make all possible exertidns to come up with the party we were following; and as our horses had here very good pasture at night, there was no let to our efforts upon their account.

The district through which we now passed bounded in stony torrents; but in other respects, the travelling was better than it had been at any time since we encountered the first obstructions to our journey ; and the face of the country began here to wear a more cheerful and agreeable aspect.’ For the endless firs, sown ovér the whole‘surface of-the ground, in larger or smaller quantities depending upon the character and quality of the soil and the elevation of the country, aifd exhibiting only the little varieties of colour and foliage which their several tribes admit, we had now around us a mixture of the several perennial green-leafed trees that have been mentioned as growing in spare quantities in different parts of the ‘country through which we passed during the journey, with a larger proportion of the limes of more luxuriant growth. ~ Along the banks of some of the brooks, we now found strawberries ; and here and there we perceived open spaces covered with a variety of shrubs, among which were mingled currant bushes, the fruit of which, though not sufficiently advanced to exhibit colour, was cvidently of the red sort. Our men were in raptures of delight at the sight of this fruit even in its present state, and they picked and ate quantities of it: but we reserved our appetites for something more solid in prospect. A variety of flowers were also seen flourishing here among the brambles and underwood, amidst which the rose and the flag-iris were predominant.

This change in the appearance of tk2 country and the vegetation, was as unexpected as it was agreeable to us, seeing that we had yet scarcely recrossed the GOth degree of latitude, and it seemed to make some amends Tor our physical deprivations. It was easy to

perceive from the timidity dnd fretfulness of our horses, which now required constant encouragement to persuade them to, proceed, that the bear had also a particular inclination, if not for the beauties of nature here exhibited! in the vegetable world in so much greater profusion than generally in this snowy land, at least for the fruits, with which the country abounded. ”

We reposed to-day at an earlier hour than usual, upon the banks of a fresh torrent, which abounded on both sides with, the shrubs and flowers above-mentioned, in full bloom; and such was the weather and the t@mperature of the atmosphere, that it was difficult to réconcile our experience of the past and that of the present, and the latitude in which we were, which, if we did not take into account other influences than those which at first appear, seemed full of contradictions and inconsistencies. Perhzps, this fine portion of country, which we found afterwards of limited extent, may owe’ its verdyre to the prevalence of calm$ arising from ‘its position being that at which the winds from the sea encounter those from the mountains, which in several other countries it has fallen to my lot to observe, has a remarkable influence on climate.

Early in the afternoon we came to a stream, the bed of which we made our road; and after crossing it four or five times with not much difficulty, we were once more well immersed in attaining the bank, where we’ resumed our direct path towards the coast.

Before the fourth hour after noon on this day, a strong, chilly, damp. wind blowing from the south-cast, met us, and was the first announcement of our approach to thesca. ‘Bhe country continued to exhibit the same aspect and the same vegetation as we advanced; and after a march of seventeen hours, we had the satisfaction of. coming up with the advance of the merchants’
caravan which we had so° anxionsly longed and so ardently striven to overtake.

The men had just discharged their beasts, and were preparing their meal as we joined them: The meeting upon our side was one of unmingled satisfaction, until we perceived the whole party which had crowded around us, were under the influence of some lively trouble, for which, indeed, wé soon found that they had full cause. They had lost no less than two of their men and one of their'horses, upon the previous day, by thebear, and had another of their men still missing, who they feared had experienced the fate of the otlier two?

The tale of woes, as it was related to us, was ds follows: —Upon the party, who were ll natives, mustering their horses in the morning previous to that of the present day, they found one of them missing, and to search for which one of the men remained behind after the departure of the rest. But as this man did not make his appearance «3 expected, ‘soon. after the departure of the party, two of his companions returned, in order to discover the cause of his detention or aid his search for the missing horse. In the mean time, the rest continued their march until they stopped for their accustomed hour of repose at noon, when, neither of the men that had returned upon their steps appearing, the cause of their absence was discussed, and there being little doubt that some accident or other had happened, three more of the men, as the rest resumed their journey, retraced also the steps of the caravan, determined at all events to solve the mystery. These men saw and heard nothing either of the missing man or the rest, until their arrival at te spot where the caravan had passed the night. But after now commencing a search in the wood around, they very soon stumbled upon an enormous bear, occupied in tearing aud eating one of the men. Horrified at the sight,

they attacked the ferocious) beast without an instant’s hesitation, and two of their poniards were fixed in his breast before he had time to spring from his hind legs, Upon which he had raised himself to meet his enemits. "The bear was no sooner dispatched, than they found the body of another of their companions, whose internal parts had been drawn out and “devoured. The two slain men proved to be the one that had remained and one of those that had first returned.

‘Moreover, at a few paces from the spot upon which they found one of the men, lay also the carcass of tie missing horse. But of the other man of the fifst two that had returned, they found no trace, and, no one knew any thing about him up to the time we joined them; but it was supposed that he had met the same fate as his companions, from some other bear of parallel strength. Nor had he, indeed, been found, dead or, alive, nearly a month after this, when the last detachment of the,caravan reached the coast.

After what [had heard of the dexterity of the Yakoutes in their combats with the bear, I was much surprised at this account of the death of two of them, who had evidently not wanted courage, and killed, too, by the same beast. But when the skin of the animal that the conquerors had brought with them was shown to us, it appeared that their enemy was of such an enormous size, that we wondered rather at the courage of any man whatever, in attacking him with nothing but the miserable native weapon. The.Yakoutes themselves acknowledged, that this bear was of a size that many among them, single-handed, would not have attacked. Butethey conjectured, that the first man that was killed, enraged at seeing the animal devouring his horse, had, under too much excitement, used his weapon awkwardly, while the bear was probably more furious than on ordinary occasions, on account of being at the time over his prey; and th¢\same reasons, exa’ zerated they thought in the case of the second man, by his seeing the animal tearing his companion, had produced similar results. It appeared, however, that the bear’ had received one wound only previously to that by which he was killed..

After we had heard the gloomy tale of this unfortunate accident, we supped with the captain of the party, upon the real luxuries of biscuit and the very same sort of dry chips of mutton which we had despised until we had none left, and peas; after which, We pitched our tent near one of the fires that were blazing, and lay down to rest.,
