Not only were we now furnished with such coarse necessaries as we had a just right to claim, but at the moment of our departure, the qaptain of the detachment presented to us a portion of a great sterlet pie, with which his wife had provided him for his own use, before he left Yakoutsk; saying at the same time, that he had been unwilling to tempt us when we arrived, with what he VOL. Il. x was sure we should, under fhe effects of hunger, have used as intemperately as his horses would their food, were they put loose in a fresh pasture upqn ending a day’s journey, and suffered afterwards the bad consequences which always attend excess. _

The firgt fifteen versts of out way after.we renewed our journey, lay across the same fertile country as that over which we had passed on the preceding day. But our progress was greatly impeded, in some places by pits of mud, and at others by the streayas which were full of larger stones, and deeper and not less rapid than those over which we had passed upon the more elevatéd

After this, we ascended another range o§ hills of no great altitude, but where we found several narrow plains locked in by surrounding peaks, and full of snow and ice. They appeared lik® the beds of ancient lakes from which the water had been drawn off, after some change in the geological configuratiat of the country.

After descending this range of hills, we came into a vale of extreme fertility. ‘The green and broad-leafed trees that chiefly flourished here, were the lime and the birch’; of the hardier species of the fir tribes which were more familiar to our eyes, we observed only the larch. But the forest was the more remarkable from its affording the first instance which we met with of any trees indicating age. The wood was open, and the trunks of some of the limes were from three to four feet in circumference, and the branches were much larger than the proportion which is usual to that size of trunk iw most forest trees, but they had very few small boughs, and very little fresh foliage.

Along thegbanks of a slow rivulet by which our path lay, we observed shrubs of varjous kinds in full bloom, and growing with such luxuriance as in several places to obscure the view of the stream. Among these, the
rose-trees were predominant} In many instances they reached to seven or eight feet in height.

In the,evening, we pitched our tent as usual by a running stream. But we had much trouble on this occasion until midnight, arising from the terror of our horses of the- bears. The poor beasts seemed to have their natyral enemies continually in their minds. Ié was our custom to make but a small fire until the time of going to bed, in order that if any of the ferocious animals, after gpeeping out of the wood, should be curious to know more of us, they might not be deterred fr8m approaching near enough to give us an opportunity of*trying the superior virtue of our arms over those of. the men ofothe same forest in which they were bred. But as the underwood was here much thicker than’ usual around us, this seeming want of caution did not meet: the approbation of our quadruped companions, and we were tormented by their fears until wg made two or three good “fires. °

The first part of the next day’s march was across a country similar to that which we last passed: over. After five or six hours’ travelling, we came to the banks of a broad part of the River Ora, which we had several times previously crossed where it was but a shallow and narrow stream. We found a Yakoute here in one of the little huts of sexangular form, and with a canoe, in which we passed the river while our horses were driven across in the usual manner.

There was another hut of the same description, upon the side of the stream upon which we landed; and the good man who inhabited it, invited us to enter, and partake of a nftal of the best refreshment he had to offer.

The arrangement of this Yakoute’s Ageing excited our curiosity, on account of its differing from that of all of his race that we had hitherto seen. It was of the ordinary form, and was fijrnished with the same kind of mud benches asthe rest. But instead of the usual emptiness of the huts in which we had previously reposed, the walls of -this were hung with all sorts of trophies of the chase. Bears’, wolves’, and foxes’ heads, and the branched horhs of rein-deer, were suspended around; upon lines. drawn across the hut above our heads, was hanging a quantity of dried salmon; and upon several shelves were placed water-vessels made of birch-bark, and perfectly similar to those used by the North American Indians. The meal to which we now sat down, consisted -of . salmon soup or stew, which had been cooked out of doors in the lid of an iron pot, and was,served up in the same remnant, probably of a perfect vessel, which these Yakoutes had once possessed. This novel mess, hewever, was a great luxury to us, and with the use of wogden spoons of our host’s own handiwork, we made an excellent meal. a The confidence with which the swallows take up their abode in the Yakoute huts, and the Tungouse wigwams, that are open at the top, is remarkable.. Here four families of this species of the winged tribes had built their nests within,our reach; and they were so much accustomed to human company in the dweliing which they had chosen, that they continued to fly backwards and forwards, to bring food to their young ones, which were unfledged in the nests, while we stood close by them. We observed that their colour differed from that of the several varieties of their species commonly, seen in Europe. Instead of being of the nicely mingled hues of the blue, and bhick, and purple of our swallows, their dark plumage was universally tinged with a dusky red., The more than ordinary approach to comfort that we found here, caused us to make some inquiries before we

quitted this. hut; and we I¢arned that its inhabitants were especially expert, and had been very successful, in their hunts for the bear in particular, by which they had always an article of commerce to exchange with the mefchdnts that passed by.

Upon renewing our march, we found precisely the same country as that over which we had passed during ‘the earlier part, of the day; and in the evening we reached the post of Metinska, at 200 versts from the fast at which ye had changed, and within fifty-four versts ‘of the haven in which were centred all our hopes ofthe termination of our arduous journey.

The Yakoute smotritel we found here, was lodged, in a hut of the usual hexagonal form, and deeply set in the ground; but he had opposite his door two other huts, which, unaccustomed as we were to see even two houses together, presented t6 us quite the appearance of a litile settlement. | But if-this people want the advantages of soci&ty of their own species, they certainly live, whether that want be the cause of this or not, upon the best terms with the winged tribes we have just seen, which are found every where. within and without their dwellings. Here the swallows were as abundant as any where; and they were still tamer than those we saw at the last Yakoute dwelling at. which we had stopped. Several of the little winged’ families had their nests within and without the huts, no higher than five feet from the ground; and they were so familiar with our species, that-when. we took some of the squalling unfledged ones in our hands, it seemed to cause no alarm to the parents, which continued to make their flights b&ckwards and forwards through the air, and ever and anon to return and feed their crying offspring that remained in the nest, while we stood by with the others in our hands.

But there was here a greater novelty to us than this, a regular‘pack of jhe travelling dogs of the country, which we now suw for the first time. The dogs are not, indeed, generally used for travelling, further westward in Siberia than the foot of the mountains over which we had passed. Lor

T shall only at present remark concerning these animals, that it appeared to me that the Siberian dog increased in fierceness at every town as we advanced eastward, from the time of crossing the: Ural Mountains -until our arrival at Irkoutsk, where none are upon any‘account allowed to run loose. In general, even in Western Siberia, the dogs are tied up in-the yards; but tlas practice was not there universal. These dogs, however, are of a different race, as we shall aftexwards more fully see; and those we now first saw were loose, and were lying strewed round the house; and whether asleep or. awake, took no notice whatever either of ourselves or our horses,

As the Yakoutes’ huts here were by no means inviting to enter, and the weather was fine, we preferred pitching our tent to passing the night within either of them;. and after partaking abundantly of the truly national dish of the Yakoutes, the cream and the berries, with which we were now becoming quite familiar, we reposed, as we were accustomed to do, upon our fresh beds of spruce boughs...

The next day, some difficulty about our horses delayed us, and we did not recommence our journey before a late hour in the morning. Soon after leaving this post, we ascended a range of hills, that form towards the north some ridges of considerable altitude, which are known by the name of the Ocheta Mountains. When we were at the highest elevation we attained during the passage of them, we had a far fairer and more extensive view than we had at any time obtained while we were in the mountains over which we had

previously passed. In the direction of the country into which we were advanciig, appeared a fine wooded plain as,far as the bounds of vision, in which the deep green foliage with which it was covered, was relieved ‘by ‘the occasional view of some part of the River Ochota, while the rest remained concealed by the serpentine gourse of the stream and the undiflations of the ground. In the direction of the north, the high and irregular form of the above-mentioned mountains terminated the view; while in that of the south appeared an undulating country; and towards that from which we came, a wooded plain, which seemed bounded bf an irregular range of mountain peaks.
After a,difficult descent from these hills, we encamped in the plain which commenced at their base, according to our invariable custom whenever in our ‘power, by the side of a fresherunning stream.

The next morming, as we advanced we found the fertility of this plajn greater than that of any portion of the country through which our path had hitherto lain. Early in the day we passed by several Yakoute huts, where we were plentifully supplied with cream, The distances from one another at which the several families that inhabited these houses were dwelling, in the midst of a country where there is no scarcity of pasture to maintain their cattle, which furnish the sole means of their subsistence, seemed indicative of their race being of a gloomy and.unsocial disposition. We believed this, however, not to be the case; and we made inquivies of them why they lived so far apart. But in reply we heard only the same teasons that are often given in very different countries, for the conservation of usages that ought long since to have been. abolished, that such was the custom of their fathers.

Attached to all the houses that we passed by, after crossing the last hills, there were larger portions of pasture-ground than we Had before seen; and the grass, though of a coarse description, was heregrowing most luxuriantly. By the stream, the abundance of the wild productions of the several kinds with which we were familiar, still more surprised us. “he rosebushes, which were every where in great plenty, were in some instances from six to nine feet in height. Early in the day, we crossed several times a stream of a chalky colour; and we observed that, wherever the stones broke its smooth course, appeared a foam like soap-suds, which covered the surface of the water as far down as the eye could reach. :

Before noon, we arrived at the bank of the’ mai stream of the Ochota, the entire waters of which were of the same colour as those'of the streams just mentioned. It was necessary for. us to cross the river at this point, on account of the country on its right bank abounding in the same morasses and swamps from which we had suffered so much duringrthe earlier stages of,our journey, although it would be soon equally necessary to recross it to, avoid the same obstructions upon the opposite side, and afterwards even to cross it for a third time, before arriving at the termination of the journey.

We found a hut here inhabited by one of the natives, who was living quite alone, and who had no cattle whatever, and was almost in‘a starving state, with a pack of dogs that were as nearly as possible reduced to skeletons. And this, too, was by the side of a river that had probably more salmon in it at this very time, as it will be afterwards shown, than any river in the world has of any fish at any season. But the Yakoute. had neither néts, nor hooks and lines, and obtained only such fish as the current threw on shore. How he lived through the winter we could not learn from him; and his appearance and the reception he-
gave us, were,not such as te make us feel much interest in his affairs.

We ercountered here some difficulty and some detention, on account of the state of the river. The Ochota is"subject'to sudden swellings, arising from two very different causes, and which are not on that account ta.be foreseen. If the rains are heavy on the higher lands, the river swells with rapidity ; and if the sky is without @ cloud, the-same effect is produced by the melting of the,snow and the ice in the elevated. valleys from which the sources of the river proceed. Thus, the Water will rise to a great height, and fall again, sometimes twice in the course of the twenty-four hours. But the seeson of the full influence of these causes and _effects is but of short duration; for with the first nightfrosts, which usually take place in the middle of August, the condensed mists which thang over the mountains fall in snow, and the glaciers cease to melt, whea the river becomes ldéy, and its breadth equal, save for about four of the twenty-four hours, during which the waters still rapidly rise and fall, from the effects of the mid-day sun upon the snow amd ice in the less elevated lands: The breadth, generally, of the Ochota at this pass is less than a verst; but it was at this time more than two versts, and the current was running with such rapidity that the horses could not be put into the stream without great risk of losing them.

After three or four hours’ detention, however, the river rapidly fell, and the current was so much diminished in force, that’ we crossed very easily in the halfstarved Yakoute's little canoe, and swam,our horses without much@lifficulty of risk.

Soon after passing the main stream of, this principal river, which falls into,the Ochotsk Sea, we crossed several torrents of the kind to which we were well accustomed. The soil and the vegetation which we found:

after passing the Ochota, were the same as those which have been last mentionea. Here, however, we remarked that the most venerable of all the trees were the birches. The larch was equal in size to any to be found upon the western coast of the continent of America in the latitudes between 47 and 50 degrees.

As we proceeded, the stony streams continued to obstruct our progress, and the waters in them were now increased in breadth and strength. About two hours before the time at which we usually encamped, we came to the second pass of the Ochota, where we found the river divided irito two channels. Here thete was neither native nor canoe; and it was necessary that

‘we should find a ford over which we might pass with our horses, But before we discovered a favourable place for wading, we met two of the natives mounted, who, though they pointed out to us a ford, informed us at the same time, that-one of them in crossing had been swept into the broad waters, where the channels unite, and had with difficulty saved his horse. Partly, therefore, to avoid the risk of losing ours, and partly on account of the-sickness of one of our men, from which he was suffering much, we determined upon encamping here for the night, in the. hope of there being some diminution of the flood, and that our sick man would be better the next day. Thus, after marking the line to which the water now reached, that we might know in the morning how much it had risen or fallen, we pitched our tent.

The complaint of the Yakoute was very similar to that by which the captain of our boat upon the Léna had been attacked, and is supposed by tho natives to be peculiar to the country. It manifests itself in a swollen throat and tongue, which, when exaggerated, prevents respiration. This man’s tongue was so swollen that he was unable to speak ; but it appeared to me that he
had but very little fever: his disease was probably the influenza. <

The immediate spot which we had found the most convenient for our encampment, was about twenty paces from ¢the‘high bank of the torrent, and was a perfect bed of flowers, composed of the several kinds which have beep before mentioned as abounding inthis plain. It proved, however, to my companions and myself more like a bed of thorns; for we had very little rest, owing to the more than ordinary alarm of our horses, on account of their ferocious enemies of the forest, both Wefore and after they were tethered to feed. We had bten so often, as we thought, disturbed without reason, that we had grown indifferent to the claims of our beasts to our care. Neither was it very prudent to be hunting for bears amid the dense beds of underwood and shrubs and flowers that*surrounded us, even with any weapon whatever; for that savage animal is not without a portion,of the attribute in which thé fox has the credit of excelling all the beasts of the forest, and must be cautiously dealt with, whatever may be the weapon by which he is to be encountered. Our Yakoutes upon this occasion, however, were doubly careful -in regard to the security of the camp; and after the horses had once or twice disturbed. them, they lighted fresh fires among the underwood on all sides.

In the morning we were the first stirring ; and when we came out of our tent, we found all the Yakoutes sleeping. They were very snugly rolled up in their accustomed wrappings, and the fresh flames of the fires were burning around them. Assoon as we,had aroused them, our firgss business was to descend the bank of the river near which we had pitched our tent, in order to discover how much the water-had risen or fallen. But we no sooner reached the beach, than our attention was attracted by marks upon the muddy ground, by which we found that a bear of no mean stature had been here promenading wuile we were asleep; and that by our unpardonable indifferencé to our horses’
plaints, which were no doubt on account of the too near’ approach of this very animal, we had lost the best chance that could have occurred of a satisfactory shot. -

When We came to examine the height of the water, we found it to be about six inches less than it had been when we arrived; and as the current must have proportionably diminished in rapidity, we now determined to attempt the passage. It was the strength of the current, indeed, rather than the depth of the water, that was at all times to be regarded. Thus, after making our preparations at perfect leisure, we trace the shore of the principal of the channels somewhat ‘higher up than the spot at which the Yakoutes that we had met upon the previous evening, had crossed; and when we thought we had found a convenient pines we plunged into the midst of the current,*and soon gained the opposite shore, without experiencing any other inconvenience than such as we were too well accustomed to to regard. ”

After passing this river, we found the plain at every verst less and less fertile. Of flowers there were now none; and of shrubs, save the stunted scrubby spruces, we had very soon scarcely the merest bush to vary the’ monotonous prospect ; and for the torrents that had so much embarrassed us for so large’ a portion of our journey we had now nothing but sluggish streams, slowly wending their way through a morass in which there were cccasional ponds, that were the resort of the curlew, the plover, and the snipe, which wele every where in great abundance.
At length, upon the seventh day of July, after a journey of twenty-four days, of which the chief incidents have been recorded, and after a last trot acrossa barren

heath of a few versts in extent, we reached the banks of the Ochota for a third timd} now within three or four versts of its mouth, and immediately opposite the good town of Ochotsk, that had been so long in our thoughts by da’, if not by night also, as the happy place of our repose.

The breadth of the river is here about two versts and ahalf. From where we now stood, we had a peep at the sea through a narrow break in the sand hills which form the coast, and through which the waters of the river find a passage to the sea. The town appeared to éonsist merely of.a small collection of black huts; but this dull picture of our so long wished for place of repose was,a little relieved by the view of a brig lying near the mouth of the river.

There was no canoe upon the banks of the Ochota where we arrived; but the fring of guns and the lighting of fires soon brought ‘us aid ; and we now took leave of the last of the noble race of animals ‘that had served us so faithfully, and of the last of our additional guides, who returned with his beasts freed from their burdens; and before the close of the day we were snugly housed in a Yakoute hut at Ochotsk.

I shall hera further add only this remark, that the obstructions and difficulties which we met with upon this journey were greater than those which I had encountered upon any previous occasion ; and that this was the first journey I ever made, where the accounts given by those to whom the road ought to have been known, of the difficulties and dangers to be encountered, have not proved to have been greatly exaggerated.

We were new upon the coasts of the Ochotsk Sea in the Pacific Ocean; and our distances by the measurement of the Russian government were from Yakoutsk, .1045 versts; from Irkoutsk, 3774 versts; and from Moscow, 8883 versts, or about 665U miles.

Tue town of Ochgtsk lies in latitude. 59° 15’ N. and longitude 143° 10’ E., and is situated a little eastward of the point at which the coast deviates from the northeast and south-west directions in which it stretches for several degrees further southwards, and now lies nearly due east and west, by which the country is laid open to the full effects of the south winds. It is a naval port, and has both ‘an arsenal and shipyard, and a naval school. Its population consists of the officials, comptising the commandant, who is always a captain in the navy, and usually of the first grade, five or six other officers, and about 300 seamen, witli several officers in the civil service of the government, and a few,merchants. The little town stands at about a verst from the entrance of the harbour, upon the inner,side of a long peninsula or neck of land, formed entirely of shingles, on one side of which is the sea, and on the other the River Ochota. Its buildings consist of about 150 loghouses and huts, a government-house, a barrack, a church, and a hospital, bes_des those of the arsenal andshipyard, which are ae a little below the rest of the town,

Nothing can be more desslate and wretched than the aspect of this remote town and the country that surrounds it; though to our eyes, after our arduous journey, its meanest hut was most grateful and refreshing. Upon the occasion of our first walk among its buildings, we ouserved that they were not placed without some of that regard to order whica distinguishes all the Russian towns and villages. There- was even, notwithstanding its inconsiderable commerce, a double row of buildings containing a few shops, and though very badly supplied with merely a few articles for domestic uses, yet representing the gostinnoi dvor. The barrack was of two stories, but was fast falling to decay. The hospital was better. But the church is the most lone and wretched imaginable. It stands apart from the houses upon a little elevation of the ’ shingles, and has a burial ground attached to it, the rails of which were, however, fallen down for want of solid earth to support them. Moreover, we heard afterwards, that it was impossible to place the remains of the dead out of reach of the wolves, by which they were continually raked from the shingles amidst which they were laid. 5

The importance, as well as the support, of the town of Ochotsk, are derived from its character of a naval depdt, and from its being the channel of intercourse between Kamtschatka and the interior of the country. Formerly, it enjoyed also advantages arising from its being the port of the Russo-American Company, which has been removed to Ayan. Two vessels have been built in its shipyard; but neither of whicn is fit to navigate the seas of these high latitudes.

The great disadvantages under which, the town labours, arise from the exces of cold experienced upon this coast in these latitudes, and from the sterile character of the country which borders the coast, but above all from its extreme unhealthiness. These drawbacks, indeed, to its progress are so great, that were it not for the salmon with which the Ochota abounds, the expense of the maintenance of the town would be far greater than any benefits which it returns.

The unhealthiness- of Ochotsk is more the effect of the position of the town with respect to the sea and tle surrounding country, than of its latitude and longititle. Placed between the ocean, and lands which | in, summer are,heated by so many hours of sunshine, it is exposed during the best months of the year to almost perpetual cold and damp winds from the sea; while in the spring it is subjected to the effects of an impuye.air, proceeding from animal matter in a state of,decomposition, which cavers the morass along the Opposite shores of the river. _Here, great quantities of salmon take shelter in the autumn, and are frozen, and lie embedded during the winter and when the sun melts the ice in the spring, the swamps are found covered with the pestiferous animal matter. Thus the little settlement, as often as the wind is off shore, is exposed to all the effects of the malaria; and fevers and diarrhoea now prevail. The causes, indeed, of the pestilence are not of long continuance; for as the rivers begin to swell, by the melting of the snow at their sources, the morasses which border them are cleared of the intolerable nuisance. But scarcely, however, dogs this take place, before the town is subjected to the winds, almost as destructive to health as the pestilential atmosphere from which it has been so lately relieved. °
It is said by the inhabitants, that Ochotsk, so unblessed by nature, wants, in effect, three out of the

four elements which compose the material world and - support life elsewhere. ‘Sheir houses, they say, are built upon loose shingles, amidst which their dead sleep; and thus they must needs want the proper element that composes the earth. For their water, they say, that in summer they have to send ten or twelve miles up the current of the river, which flows. in a brackish stream by their doors. And when the state of the ice in spring and autumn prevents their’ so doing, and the snow which they melt i in winter is gone, they have to drink of a single impure spring, from which flows all the water they possess. And their avr,

.the element denied to no living creatures that walk the earth, is at one season rendered insufferable by the causes above mentioned, and at another loaded with drift snow, and at a third a mere blast from the ocean, almost as inimical to life as the malaria with which it is loaded in the spring. Fire, they say, alone of the four elements comforts them.

This picture, which the people of Ochotsk draw of their own sad condition, is but little exaggerated, From sixty to sixty-five, out of about 300 sailors, were sick in the hospital the whole tithe of my stay here, and nearly the same proportion of the constant inhabitants of the town were suffering from complaints incident to the climate. The Russian government does much to repay the officers for the inconveniences to which they are exposed at this remote station; but they cannot do too much for men subjected to so many trials of patience in so bad a climate, for the interest and advantage of their country. Their term of service is usually five years, during which they receive double pay, with a ey of promotion at the expiration of. the term,
.On the morning after our arrival at Ochotsk, I-sent a letter, with which I had been furnished by the

Governor-general Mouravief, to the commandant, Captain Voulalarski of the imperial¥ navy, and I soon afterwards called at the government-house. I found the commandant of this distant outpost of the empire in the chi&f apartment of his dwelling, which was a neat and humble building, very suitable to the character of the place of his command; and I met a polite and hearty reception, The gallant officer was very curious concerning the country between the seat of his government and the more populous districts in "the interior of Siberia, none _of*which he had seen. His road to Othotsk, as well as that of all the officers and chinovnik thit were under his command, had been upon his own, element, ronnd the great continent which comprises the three old quarters of the globe; and it had been a very long one, on account of their ship, though she was built in England, being one*of the worst sailers that ever floated upon the ocean, which had caused them, indeed, to be about, eighteen months on. the voyage. When a few other ordinary matters had been disposed of, I commenced my inquiries concerning the projects ‘T entertained of continuing my travels as far as the peninsula of Kamtschatka; and I now learned from the commandant, that the ship which it has been already mentioned, passes annually between Ochotsk and the great peninsula, was expected to arrive here in about a fortnight, and thatshe would sail again to return to Kamtschatka after a very few days’ delay. The commandant also informed me that, in the meantime apartments would be provided for my residence in the officers’ barracks, and that, on the ship’s arrival, every agcommoda~ tion would be afforded me for undertaking the voyage. Before I retired, the commandant reqyested that I would dine with him the same day, that he might have an opportunity of introducing me to his family, and also to the officers with whom he was about to domicile me. ¥2

Upon coming to the gororminen house at the appointed hour, I had the pldasure of meeting Gospojah Voulalarski, as well as several of the officers of the port. The lady was quite the wife of a sailor, full of kindness and affability; and she seemed almos: as much at home here, as if she had been native born, and unacquainted with more favoured portions of the globe. Since their arrival, tgo, she had given birth to five fine children.

Among the gentlemen present, were Captain Poplonsky, an officer who had lately explored a part of the south coast of the Ochetsk Sea, before unknown to navi- ‘gators, and very little known to geographers, who “have almost entirely depended upon the reports cf the natives in the interior of the Manchur country. There was also Gospodin Yakovenko, ispravnik or judge of the province, and Gospodin Malinari, naval architect and surveycr, and an officer of engineers from one of the German provinces of the empire.

The dinner was purely Russian, plentiful as far as the table was concerned when the climate is allowed for, without: being deficient in the ceremonies which the inequality of ranks among the guests in regard to one another, and their relations to the host upon such occasions, naturally engender. There was, nevertheless, a touch of that warmth of feeling and friendship among all parties, which will appear whenever a few individuals of similar pursuits or breeding are separated from the rest of the social family to which they belong.

The day after this dinner at the governor’s, I took up my querters at the officer’s barracks, where ample rooms were assigned to me, with a coupte of sailors for domestics. T'was rather fortunate in respect to the time of my arrival here, as far as regarded the spare amusements which the members of the little society of the place are able to enjoy. Gospodin Malinari, above

mentioned, had had the good fortune to find a young lady of Russian, descent upqp the male side, attractive enough tg determine him to fulfil the natural as well as the scriptural law, which commands us to increase and multiply, and the celebration, of the marriage took place a few days after my arrival.

Among the Russians, the union of a young couple is at all times an affair of interest to a wider circle of the relations and friends of the parties, than the same event is with us, and of course this marriage was a cause of joy to the whole of the inhabitants of Ochotsk. The pure Russian blood is estimated in this part of Siberia in? about the same degree that probably the Roman was estimated in our island when Agricola taught out progenitors, of one at least of the several races from which we trace our origin, that rational amusements and enjoyments contribute to cleerfulness, and that cheerfulness tends to produce that disposition of the mind which is most favourable to the advance of kndwledge, and of all the refinements in which civilisation consists; and just in the same manner the Russians, as far as opportunities favour them, follow this wise as well as humane course for the improvement of the dull races they have suhdued, and certainly with every prospect of arriving at the same results in Siberia that the Romans happily attained in Britain.

The day before the marriage, the papa of the young lady, who was the otcoopstchik of the department, gave a suitable entertainment, at which all the officers and chinovnik of the place were present; and I had the pleasure of being a partaker in the amusements of the evening. The good folks of Ochotsk enjoyed themselves upon this occasion much in the same manner that a party of mixed ages are wont to do among ourselves. Some danced, some conversed, and some did nothing. There was, nevertheless, at least one novelty, but which was not necessarily connected with the immediate cause of th> entertainment. This was the appearance of a younger sister of the bride, who had been dressed until this day in quite child’s clothes, but now appeared in very marked woman’s attire. I believe among all nations, ancient and modern, that have or have had any manners at all, it is and has been the custom to distinguish the period of life that we look so anxiously for during our under age by some ceremony, or by some change in our relations by law ‘to the community to which we belong.

It was not permitted by Augustus that girls shouid marry before they had attained their twelfth year. “Marriages at nine and ten on the side of the girl are very frequent in Eastern countries. Whether climate or race be the cause ‘of the difference, certainly our species are much more precocious in some countries than in others ; and perhaps in all countries the period fixed for manhood and womanhood, or, more properly speaking, the period at which the matrimonial alliance should be permitted, ought to be determined by laws framed in accordance with Nature’s more hasty or more tardy performance of her good work. This period is not determined in law.in Russia any more than in most other countries. But custom among the people in this part of the empire has established the age of seventeen for the full-grown period of the woman; and the moment is made manifest to the world by an immediate and very marked change of dress ; and on this occasion the child of yesterday appeared set off to the best advantage in full woman’s attire. But certainly, if this instance ware a fair one, the conventional law has here by some years anticipated Nature; for the appearance of the young lady was that of a child that had put on her mother’s gown, or that of a badly dressed doll, I made now this discovery, how-

ever, that,[ must, upon several previous occasions, have spoken to girls that ware at any rate just bordering upon, womanhood precisely as we address mere children. I am disposed to think, that a girl of twelve years of are in Egypt, and a girl of seventeen in this part of Siberia, are in general as nearly as possible equal, as well in regard to the material as to the imma~ terial portion of our two-fold nature; but I do not think that the duration of the: full bloom of the one is longer than that of the other. :

The first act of the ceremonies, as they were epee oft this occasion, was one_ of ancient usage among the Rissians, but which is not now practised § in Russia Proper, or at least not in the great cities of the empire. When the celebration of the marriage is determined upon, a married couple, not ‘being very young, are selected by agreement among ‘he parties to perform the little offices which belong naturally to the parents on both sides; and,in the present instance thé gallant commandant and his lady played this important part, which was as novel to a stranger in the manner of its performance, as the appearagee of the parties in this character was novel in the ceremonies. Upon the day selected for the celebration of the marriage, the substituted parents gave a grand entertainment, which com-~ menced with a dinner, at which, in addition to the best viands of the country (which cannot indeed be much praised), were served the preserved meats and fruits and the choicest wines of Western Europe. But the young couple in whose honour all were assembled, were not yet present. Soon after we rose from the table, however, a heraldeformally proclaimed the approach of the bride and the bridegroom ; upon which, the substituted parents took possession of the upper end of another room, which was to be that whcre the first portion of the ceremony of the marriage was to be performed.

The young couple now entered the dining-room, and the guests of the commandént stood back, to admit of their advance towards the inner room. ‘The bride was prettily dressed in-the chastest white, and the young officer was in military attire. Having passed through this room, they entered that appointed for the first part of the ceremony, followed by all the governor’s guests, who remained at the lower end of the room, as spectators of the scene. The parties on whom all eyes were bent, now advanced towards the elder couple, who were standing to receive them, but with the slow and solemn step which a due respect to the representativés of the parents on both sides appeared to demand ; and the little ceremony which followed wes the more interesting, from its being a relic of the customs of the Russians of the more purely patriarchal age.- The substituted parents. bore in their hands typical signs at once of our relations with heaven and of our necessities upon earth, The father held with Loth hands before him the picture which was designed to furnish the holy corner of the sleeping-room of the happy couple, and the mother laid her left hand upon a loaf of bread, that had, on account of its immense size, been placed upon a small table by her side instead of in herhands. When the young couple stood in front of the elder,. the bridegroom informed the substituted parents that he was about to accomplish the marriage, for which he had already obtained their permission, with the lady who was by his side; and that he now came, accompanied by his bride, to ask the blessing of their united parents before the celebration of the more important of the ceremonies of their final union. Upon this the substituted father made a sign to them in silence to kneel; and as soon as the young couple were on their knees, he made the sign of the cross with the picture over the head of the bridegroom, and then placed the little holy symbol to his

own breast. At the same time, the substituted mother, with her left hand still upgn the bread, made the sign ‘of the cross with the right hand over the head of the bride. As soon as these signs were made, the bridegroon® bowed his head to the ground, and touched the floor three times with his forehead, while the bride remained kneeling. Then they both rose fipon their .feet; and after having kissed the little picture which was extended to them severally, they twice again repeated together the same genuflexion’ as before, and the bridegroom ¢he same bowings to the ground, and the parents the same eyenhene signs ‘by which the blessittg is conveyed.

The -bevediction being complete, the picture was presented by the aubstivated father to the bridegroom, and the bread, though not removed from the table, was presented by the substituted mother to the bride, the former aS an appropriate memorial of the event, and the latter as symbolic of worldly prosperity. The presentation was accompanied also by a few words of solemn admonition, pronounced by the substituted parents separately, and which were translated to me as follows : —‘* So long,” said the father, as he presented the picture, ¢ as you both can look without shame upon this holy emblem, which will sanctify your chamber, your sleep will be tranquil, and your days will be happy.” * Then,” said the mother, ‘ while you are virtuous, neither yourselves nor your children will want the fruits of the earth, typified in this loaf.”

At this moment two stout “pailors, that had been placed in, some corner unseen, advanced and took up the enormoua loaf, and bore it to the future home of the young couple, svyho now retired accompanied by their substituted parents, to proceed ‘together to the house of the true parents of the bride.
Shortly ‘after this, the rest of the commandant’s

guests took the same road. When we entered the apartment in which all parties were assembled, we found the relatives of the bride and all who were most interested in the union, seated at the upper side of the room. We took our seats upon benches that had been placed around; and in.a very few minutes after this, a ceremony-of quite another kind to that last mentioned commenced, by way of preparation for the solemnitiesof the church, consisting in large doses of champagne accompanied with appropriate toasts.

From the father of the bride’s louse, late in the evening, we all set off together on foot for the churclf; for there is'no description of carriages in use. in ‘summer at Ochotsk, except a few talashavi, or small carriages for the dogs to draw water from the boats by which it is brought down the river, or from the brackish springs above mentioned, io the houses.

This part of the ceremony of the marriage was commenced by an exchange of rings between the future husband and wife, each party, according to the Russian custom, presenting a ring to the other. This ceremony, however, is performed'in Russia Proper some days previous to that of the celebration of the marriage. On this occasion, the officiating pope. carried these symbols of the sacred contract within the ékonostass ; and after having there, unseen by the company, by some rite of the church, infused them with all necessary virtue, he returned them to the parties, who now made the exchange. The rest of the ceremony was the same as that of the marriages in the Russian and Greek Churches in Europe.

A whimsical incident occurred during the performance of the ceremonies, which a little relieved the weariness inseparable from an attendance at a Russian marriage, on account of the great length of the offices which the priests perform.

At a certain moment, when the happy couple stood with the crowns, which ayg used in the ceremonies, lightly pressing their heads, and with their eyes fixed upon the pope, who was reading, and when, doubtless, all othern eyes were set with admiration or curiosity upon the bride and some maidens of mingled blood by her side, we were all startled by a gninsh Within the sanctuary, that, would have awakened a bear from his December slumber.. Every eye was now turned towards the holy place, the whole vicinity of which was well hung with lamps and candles, and presented a kind of fairy show ; ; but the cause of the alarm was concealed fidm our view. The officiating pope, as he stood and looked with apparent astonishment upon the screen which concealed the ékonostass, scemed to hesitate whether to throw down his book, and fly to the scene of mischief, or to pregerve the dignity proper. to the time, and continue his sacred duties. Nor did any of his several assigtants move from the spot, on which they seemed to stand entranced. But while all eyes remained bent in the same direction, a little boy in naval uniform, with cocked hat and sword, presented himself from within at the door of the sanctuary, as if another bottles like that which imprisoned the diable boiteux had fallen, and given liberty to some spirit in the form of a general of Lilliput. It would have been impossible for the droll apparition’to fail to set a party of stoics in a roar, and it was not therefore wonderful, that none of our party, from the pope to the sailors in the back-ground, were able to maintain their gravity on the occasion. The Lilliputian hero tyrned out to be the son ofethe commandant, at the time playing so different a part. Finding what was passing in the open church rather too wearisome for his temperament, he had entered the holy of holies, when all the attcntion of the company was occupied by the ceremonies that were performing, and had accidentally committed some mischief that produged the alarm, but which, however, turned out to be of not much more importance in point of cost than the smash of the bottle that set at liberty the prying déable boiteux. And what might have been sacrilege among a less sensible people than the “Russians, and. deemed worthy of excommunication in the church whose priests separate themselves from the rest of the world, :and remain unacquainted with the true feelings of humanity, was by the intelligent and good family pope of Ochotsk, looked upon just as a wise parent regards a piece of mischief practised by a spirited: boy.

Besides -the gaieties which were incident to the Ochotsk marriage, one or two féte days of some of the good folks of the place occurred during my stay here ; and among these was that of the wife of the commandant. It was celebrated in the same manner that® the Russians are wont every where te keep this sacred epoch of their particular history ; yet two little incidents of the evening were adapted to attract.the special notice of a stranger. While the dance, cards, and chess, were going merrily on, a gentle tap was heard at the door of the room in which the young folks were dancing; and presently in marched four seamen, staggering under the weight of a cake of enormous bulk, made of white flour, and which they brought to present to the lady on the part of the whole of the seamen of the port, as an acknowledgment of their gratitude for her interference in behalf of several of them, both at sea and on shore, by which they had obtained pardon for offences and escapeé the floggings which the strict discipline of the service had seemed to demand.
The other incident will tend to show that the means of advancement, both in the Russian service and in the

grades of rank which are not so nicely defined by law, is not confined-to those yhose fortunes have placed them im the more populous and richer towns and districts of the empire. It was the presence of a cadet of thesschpol above mentioned, who was a son of one of the ordinary seamen of the port, and was that day advanced to the rank of an officer in the imp€rial navy. He was a fine youth, and of course in uniform, and J was informed that several other seamen ‘of the port had sons among the cadets, who were in the same way of advancement.

A REMARK has been inade in a previous chapter, concerning a disease which is peculiar to this. part ofthe country, and to which it.was conjectured, at the same time, the apparent feature in the charactet of the Yakoutes, which is generally supposed by the Russians to be want of courage, might more justly be attributed. - I was but a yery few days at Ochotsk before I had the opportunity of witnessing some decided cases of this disease; and I shall report all that I was able to observe in two of these instances in particular, just as the facts present themselves to those who, have no knowledge of the medical art.

The disease is called, in the language cf the natives, mereyachichit; but the Russians merely term it the Yukoute disease. The first of the afflicted persons whom I saw was a native lady, the wife of a merchant of this place. This was not a bad case; but, as the
manner of my, introduction to the invalid forms a circumstance in the only,account of the complaint which it js in my power to give, it will be first mentioned.

It was a thorough time of merry-making at Ochotsk, on account chiefly of the marriage above mentioncd ; and the soirées and suppers’ were nightly? and the strangers ‘in the place were never forgotten. On my arriving one evening at the door of-a house of rejoicing, in the company of one of the oflicers béfore mentioned, Captain Popl&nsky, who had preceded us, and with whom I had previously had some cofiversation concerning the disease, came out to say that the lady above, alluded to was aniong the guests within, and that he wished me to follow in his “ wake,” and close to him, in order that he might give me the opportunity, by suddenly introducing me tosher, when I had not been previously seen, - of witnessing some of the curious effects of the disease. Thg lady, he informed me, knew very well that there were strangers in the place, and, upon hearing that I was to be one of the guests of the evening, she had becomg very uneasy, and wished to retire, but had not been allowed so to do. I confess, when I heard this, and remembered what had been related to me concerning the disease, I feared that I should be a general] ‘disturber of the harmony of the evening; and I, therefore, begged I might be rather allowed to return to my quarters, contented with what I had heard, until a better opportunity might oceur for observing the effects of the disease. But this was as peremptorily opposed as the request of the lady had been; and I therefore followed the captain, by whom I was closely covered. The lady, nevertheless, easily perceived the attempted deception ; and, in considering the effects of the introduction that followed, it is necessary to remember this. When we stopped in front of her, the captain bowed politely, and, after one or two words of course, suddenly started on one side, and, in a tolerably loud and rough manner, at, the same instant, uttered some interjectional phrase equivalent to, “ Behold!” In an instant, the lady was absplutely deprived of her senses; and, with a countenance which exhibited} as it appeared to me, at the same time, jhe passion of terror and the expression of laughter, she fixed her eyes on me for a few minutes, but neither said nor did anythifig. This produced, strange as it will appear, until all has been said of the odiSease that this case and the other's to be mentioned suggest, a hearey laugh through the whole room. Upon this, the reason of the lady seemed gradually to returg; and her countenance now expressed neither sorrow nor anger at what had passed, but rather perfect good-humour and simplicity, with smikes, almost like those of approbation. But it will appear doubly strange that this lady was subjected severq) times during the evening to the same treatment, which had always the same effect. ° The next instance of the disease which I had occasion to witness, was gq much more confirmed case. The afflicted person was a man of the mingled blood, and was a ship-carpenter in the service, of the government. I was led by the commandant and the captain to the spot where the man happened to be working in company with several other men; and I was told by my conductors, on our way, that I was about to see the disease in its full vigour, and a case in which the means taken to exhibit it would not only deprive the sufferer of his reason, but reduce him to such a state of subjection as to allow of his being made tp perform any act whatever that he was told to do by the party that terrified him, however unlawful or absurd it might be. ‘When we came to the place where the men were working, the commandant called to the sick man, who

Was engaged in his ordinary labour among the rest, to approach him, just as if ee merely some instructions to give about the work in hand. The man came from among the rest, and stood in front of us, without seeming to, take any notice of the presence of a stranger, which at least, seemed to prove that the terror of foreigners that “appeared to have had so strang@an effect upon the afflicted lady, even before I came into the room, was not a’symptom of the disorder. But while the commandant was conversing with® this man, the captain suddenfy started as he had done in the case of the lady, and bawled out again séme interjectional phease. At this, the man started also, and called out, the same or gimilar words to those used by the captain, and then stood and stared like a madman arrested by his chains. Before, however, the afflicted man had been a minute in this condition, the captain roughly commanded him to beat the commandant, which the man now commenced doing immediately., But the commandant, being on his guard, had scarcely received a blow, and which was luckily not such as a John Bull might have given under similar circungstances, before he started also, and shouted at the same time, and, by a fresh command, set the affrighted man to beat the captain, who, by frightening him again in the same manner, left him stupified and standing inactive. He did not remain, however, in this condition for a longer space of time than about a minute, when, being no further tormented, his senses returned, and he smiled as good-naturedly as if he felt rather satisfaction than anger at the condescension of his officers. a

Of the manyether cases of this malady that I saw, the effects were always the same. But what most of all surprised me, was the good-nature with which all the invalids bore the barbarous treatment which they ap peared to receive. I saw even urchins treating men of

middle age just as the officers had served the carpenter, and without receiving any other reproach than a very gentle check indeed, éither from the witnesses of the apparent outrage or from the invalids themselves.

Many accounts, Rowers: were related,to me of the effects of the complaint seen under other circumstances, some of which were droll and some tragic. A woman afflicted was, while gathering wood, at the sight of a plume of feathérs upon the cap of an officer just arrived at Ochotsk, seized with such a sudden Yrenzy as to be “ frighted out of fear :” and in this mood, in which “ the
_ dove will peck the estridge,” she attacked the offiter so violently that his gallantry was rather sorely tried on the occasion.

Two officers who had been some time here; upon the dropping of a stone before them, fell to beating each other, and did.not recover their senses until after they had been pinioned by the sailors at the command of a superior officer.

In most cases, when the afflicted person isin the act of doing any thing unlawfu} or ridiculous at the command of another, he will immediately desist if so commanded by the same person; but when the immediate cause of the derangement of the intellect is accidental, the temporary madman is not so manageable. Several children had been killed since the time of the arrival of the officers, that were now here, by their mothers letting them fall when they were suddenly alarmed.

Nothing seemed to be here known of the origin, or of the immediate causes, of this disease. It is said to have been prevalent among the natives at ‘he time of the conquest of the country. The Russians, after a few years’ residence, are as liable to it as the natives; and its effects upon both races are the same. This seems to indicate that it is at least an impartial endemic, origi-

nating most likely in the air and climate; which appears confirmed by the fact that aj] who are afflicted recover -very shortly after leaving the country. Nevertheless, if the observations before made.upon the strange contradictions in the Yakoute character be recalled, this may lead to a doubt whether that very submission of this people to their conquerors which has converted them all at once into,a semi-civilised people, and the terror of. civilised men of which an example has been produced, do not proceed from the prevalence of some sleeping portion of the disease in the very blood of the rate. The name, indeed, which has been given to the distase by the Russians, by whom it is called, as before, mentioned, the Yakoute disease, seems to indicate that this has at some time been the prevailing opinion among them, As for any such symptoms of the extraordinary malady as might lead the physician to a proper knowledge of it, I am only able to say that I fgund no one that pretended@to know more than might be judged from similar effects to those which have ‘been shown. I heard it, indeed, described while I was here, by some who had not been long in the ¢ountry, as an affection of the nerves. But unless it were said, at the same time, what it is that effects the nerves, and in what manner these delicate links between the material and immaterial nature of which we appear to be composed are affected, this seems a very unsatisfactory explanation of the mystery.

Although the annual vessel from Kamtschatka had been expected in a very few days when we arrived upon the 6th of June at Ochotsk, she did not appear before the 2¢tlwof July, having had a passage of forty days, which was double that of the average of years; and there was now no prospect of her being able to sail again before three weeks or a month. After what has been said of the climate and the scanty population of

Ochotsk, it need hardly: be said that, in spite of an occasional outbreak, such ag that caused by the wedding, which was simultaneous with our-arrival, there was a great want of means to relieve the tediousness of the time to all those who had been accustomed ta, Evropean society. rhe officers, however, have several sources of amusemeft which are suited to the seasons of summer and winter, without including cards and chess, at which the Russians-play at all hours, and generally well. In summer, salmon- -fishing and shooting, occupy their leisure hours; and in these pursuitsp which they now followed, I was able,to join them. As to the fish- .ing, however, the fish, indeed, were in far too great numbers to afford a lasting pleasure in catching them. I have already mentioned the quantity of salmon with which the rivers in this part of Stberia abound. Upon one occasion that I joined in the profitable sport, several of us together, with the use of a net, filled, a canoe which carried, ‘about a hundred salmon of the ordinary size in three hours. During’ that time, however, we worked hard, and were very wet; and, moreover, on:landing we learned, what was at least not calculated to stimulate further enterprise, that two of the servants of one of the. officers of our party had filled two canoes in exactly the same time that we had taken to fill one. The same two men had, indeed, in four days caught 2000 fish ; and it was not an uncommon thing for four men to catch 1000. in one single evening and night.

But the shooting at Ochotsk was quite another thing. Though th2 weather was continually bad, we were out almost daily upon the long banks of shingles and sand which reach for several versts upon both sides of the harbour, where the curlews and the plovers, though plentiful enough for good sport, were not so numerous or tame as to leave no motive for emulation. The

ground, too, being formed in ridges. which afforded occasional shelter, was very favourable for this sport ; and three or four of us together were ordinarily able during the afternoon to bag thirty or forty brace or more of Jarge curlews, without counting the smaller species and the plovers.

Several times we mounted the stream of tle Ochota, well prepared for the bears; but these animals are rather scarce within twenty versts of the coast, in consequence of the greater paucity of thcir*food here, more especially of the ehoicer kinds of which it consists, such a$ berries and cedar nuts. We shot, however, some ditcks upon these occasions. But as we found them generally iny ponds unconnected with the river, and as we lacked proper dogs, those of the country being worthless for our purpose, this.sport was not very attractive, :

Captain Poplonsky had built a little pavilion about a mile from the towy, above the beach, where the officers sometimes met in the afternoon to take their accustomed tea; and I was generally with them during my stay at Ochotsk. We had one day garried the commandant’s atlas with us to suggest subjects of discourse, and our conversation fell upon the power and extent of dominion of the different sovereigns of Europe; and I was led to speak in the strain not uncommon among us at home, remarking that the sun never set on the British dominions. Upon this being said, my friends began to glory in the same manner in their pride of dominion; and once of the party said, “ Neithcr does the sun ever set upon the Russian. empire., When it is noon in our mid-territory, he surveys the Czar’s dominions in one unbroken mass, save af the Straits of Behring, as far as his beams can reach, both in the cast and the west, and, he is drying up the dew iv the early morn at Sitka, our capital in Ainerica, at the same time that he is darting his evening ray against the gilded domes of St. Petersburg.”
Another time, when thé officers were regarding the

. vast proportion of the earth over which the Czar held absolute sway, they fell into exultation very-nafural to men of the. profession of arms, but which, ott of delicacy tothe foreigner, they expressed in their own tongue. It happened, however, that my acquaintance with this, was quite sufficient to enable me to comprehend what was said, with the maps before us and the previous turn of the discourse for a guide ; ; and I was much amused with their nationality, when I fouid them in imagination stretch out the line of their fleets of the Baltic and the Black Sea, until,: compassing Europe, they met in the Atlantic Ocean, masters of the coasts at least of all- the civilised world. What could be more harmless, more tiatural, or more loyal ? Not willing that they should be taken by surprise and too soon awakened from their pleasing dream of universal dominion, ‘did not for the present attempt to deaden their exultation by any suggestions that would have been as natural on my pnrt as their thoughts were on theirs. I took an early opportunity, however, of expressing my doubts of the possibility of the Russians carrying out any great enterprise before a reform took place in their manner of life, more especially in the excesses in which they indulged in the use of wine, vodka, and tobacco, which were gradually undermining the constitutions of the people.-and subduing the mental and bodily energies of the nation.

I did not find the Russian officers whom I met in any part of the empire great students uf the political or commercial, relations of different countries to one another. My exccllent friends here, thought that- England only subsisted by such supplies from Russia as could not be procured elsewhere. They were, also,

under an impression, which is not uncommon in the great countries of Europe, as every one who has mingled much with the people on the Continent cannot have failed to observe, that all our national enterprises.
and international transactions were peculiarly selfish compared with the more cosmopolitan acts of the French.

Captain ~Poplonsky had been engaged for several summers in surveying the coast of Siberia, but more especially that portion which lies between the port of Ochotsk and the-eoast of China; and he had discovered a‘new port two degrees south of Ayan in which ships might anchor in perfect safety “in six fathoms water. But as no selmon, the great support of Ochotsk, was to" be obtained there, and as the coast was more open to the dvift-ice in spring than that of Ochotsk, it was not believed that this discovery would lead, as it was at first expected, to the removal of the present port. The captain had also “discovered the meuth of some large river, not laid down in any map, and which he believed to be an outlet of the waters of the Amour, that had not been before known. It seems extraordinary that, at this day, this part of the coast of Asia should be almost unknowa, and especially when we remember that we have so many ships, commanded by able naViEntars in the Pacific Ocean.

I called one morning with one of my friends to visit Gospodin Samiloski Temopha Evanoff, a merchant of this place, who was reported to have a watch that wasa great curiosity. We found the “merchant at home, and he exhibited a watch marked Bayley & Son, Londop, with the figures 1424 in three places. It was very large and had a steel face, and was not unlike that shown formerly in Westminster Abbey for Oliver Cromwell’s watch. The figures, it was not doubted,
indicated the date, yet it may be that they marked the number of the watch.

While I was at Ochotsk; a deputation arrived from a large party of the Tungouse tribe, who were encamped in this vicinity, to pay their yasac to the government in skins, which they brought with them. The similarity in featuré and form between these people and some of the Indians upon the eastern coast of North America, between the latitudes of 45 arid 50 degrees, has been already noticed. This was particularly remarkable at this place. The same form of face, tiie same colour of skin, the same lank hair. "We endeavoured, while they were here, to carry on some kind of intercourse with them by the aid. of the Yakoutes of the town, who knew a little of their language ; but nothing could have been more unsatisfactory. We contrived, however, to get a few of their words, which I think were put down with tolerable accuracy. They will be found at the end of the chapter.* *

In winter, the sole out-door ainnasment of the Russians of Ochotsk is dog-sledging during the more temperate days that occur. The draught dogs of the coast should form a feature in any full account that might be given of,the customs and manrer of life of the inhabitants of this part of Siberia, They are, generally, a cross race between the savage animal of the interior of the country and the sledge-dog of Kamtschatka. But as enough has been said of the difference between the two races now naturalised in their several districts on the continent, and as an opportunity will occur to speak from,experience both of the qualities and the use made of the parents of those of the ‘toast in their native clime, all further remarks may be deferred until the narrative reaches the traveller’s arrival in Kamtschatka.
The day after the ship dibived at Ochotsk, I had the

pleasure of meeting the captain, Domitti Rudakoff of the imperial navy, who commanded her, among the usual party of officers at dfoner at the commandant’s; and, after dinner, the whole party walked down to the port, at the distance of about two versts from the town, to inspect the forty days’ storm-beaten “ thing of life” and most welcome visitor to every one a® Ochotsk. Such, indeed, had been the weather upon the coast during the greater part of the time that we were expecting the ship, that much anxiety ‘had been felt by the friends of tle officers and seamen on board, who Were all of this place, save the captain, who belonged properly to the fleet of the Black Sea; for they knew well the dangers attending the navigation of this rude coast and stormy sea. ‘The apprehensions entertained, indeed, during a violent tempest which had occurred immediately before the ship’s arrival, and which had’ damaged the buildings on shore and destroyed a garden that had been forrped with incredible labour by placing mould upon the pebble-stones upon which the town stands, had induced the commandant to send exploring patties along the coast on koth sides, in the hope of relieving any part of the crew that might have survived the shipwreckswhich the vessel could not have escaped had she been near the coast at the commencement of the tempest.

The good ship, that was a sight of so much joy to myself in particular, was called the Irtysch, after the great river of that name in Sibcyia. She was, nevertheless, an English north-country built vessel, and had been once an humble collier, though now ayrived at the proud rank ef a man-of-war and store-ship in the imperial service, carrying eight guns, apd officered and manned like vessels of the same force in the Black Sea and the Baltic, and sailing without a rival in these scas,
There was not much to see on Yoard the Irtyseh ;

and her crew were on shore for a day’s relaxation after the fatigues of the voyage. The captain entertained us after the mode of his country.’ The braxe. collier was as much transformed below as upon deck. She had two cabins, the larger of which was before the smaller, and was that of the captain, while the smaller was appro} riated to the rest of the officers and passengers in the government service. In the captain’s cabin there were two state rooms, into one of which I was at once introduced, as that which was to be appropriated to my use, and at the same time hospitably, invited by the captain to mess with him during the voyage. -

On the 15th of August the Irtysch was ready vo cross the bar. Leaving and entering the harbour of Ochotsk are equally difficult, on account of the shallow waver upon the bar, which does not at full sea at spring tides exceed two fathoms; -and as our vessel drew more than this, when laden, it was necessary she should take in a portion of_her cargo in the cpen roads. But besides that it requires full sea to cross the bar, as the channel is narrow, it is equally necessary that the ship should have a leading wind, and, moreover, that there should not be much.sea running at the time of the passage. Thus, so many things being necessary at the very same time, the passage of the bar in vessels even drawing no more than nine or ten feet of water may be considered half the trouble of a long voyage. It is much to be regretted, by all who are concerned in this dangerous and difficult navigation, that a vessel peculiarly adapted for the port and the voyage, possessing above all things two qualifications in which the collier man-of-war was wanting—a light draught of water, and quick sailing capability, was not sent to perform the duty of these seas,
The new moon was upon the 16th; but, the wind being foul and the weather bad, there was every reason

to expect another fortnight’s delay. It happened, however, upon the 21st, which was the last day that the depth of water might be sufficient, that a sudden gust of wind came down from the mountains in the interior, just at the moment of high water; and our watchful captain, being ready on board, took instant advantage of it, and cast off his holdings, affd ran his ship over the har just at the time that every one, had made up his mind for another fortnight’s delay at least, and whiJe some other intended passengers by his ship, as well ag myself, were comfortably seated at dinner at the commandant’s. ‘This was accomplished with no other accident than two or three thumps upon a bar of lose stones, to which sort of usage the transmuted collier was no doubt well accustomed. _

The next day an attempt was to have been madé to despatch two lighters to thé ship, now lying at anchor in the roads, to complete her cargo, and the passengers were to have takég this opportunity of-embarking : but as there was found to be a very heavy surf running upon the bar, the attempt was abandoned; and as a strong wind directly on shorg sprang up the same afternoon, and there was no shelter inthe road, and the holding ground was bad, the vessel was obliged to get under weigh, and haul off the coast, to return when the weather might permit. Fortunately, however, the wind was the next day moderate, and in the afternoon our good ship hove in sight again, and preparations ‘were immediately made for our,embarkation.

The following day, at noon, the hour of departure was at hand, and there was a little party of the friendly inhabitants ofOchotsk assembled at the commandant’s 3 and, while we were engaged over sparkling champagne, in expressing our hopes of one day again meeting, and in exchanging our good wishes, and in speculating concerning the issue of the voyage, the amiable lady of the commandant was occupied in preparing a box of luxuries for their foreign guest, consisting of wines, spirits, sweetmeats, and preserved soups, which wes- kindly presented to me on our departure.

At the hour appointed for our embarkation, the whole population of the town, from the commendant downwards, moved in a mass along the beach to the point at which the boats and lighters were lying. We were to have two ladies of the party, one of whom was a sister of our chief pilot officer, or sailing master, Chudinoff, whose duty in the service upon this coast embzaced also that of the first lieutenant in our ‘ships; the other was the wife of a pope some time since employed in missionaty labours among the unconverted Kamtschadeles: and we had also an officer of artillery who had lately. arrived frofu Russia by land. All the officers, with the exception of the captain, and all the sailors, and also the two ladies, belonged to the place. Thus, if the proportion, as it was stated fo me, be correct, of one-third of the voyages attempted between this and Kamtschatka since the passage has been known having ended in shipwreck, our departure was very naturally an affair of great general interest.

Besides the passengers, half the crew were now to embark on board the lighters and the boats appointed to tow them; and I must confess that such a scene of embracing and kissing I never knew hallow any beach before. And if benedictions, “ with tears watering the ground,” could appease the winds and waves, before the raging of which poor mortals must cede, we thought, as we embarked, our voyage ought to be fortunate. My own feelings were a mixture of triumph :at the attainment of this step in my travels, which had been of doubtful accomplishment even to the moment the Ixtysch passed the bar, and of regret at quitting the society of the hospitable and worthy men with whom
I had sojourned for six weeks on terms of the utmost confidence and friendship.

The two lighters were toe towed by four boats, in one of which we embarked; and casting from the beach, we now committed ourselves to the mercy of the current, over the effects of which oars have no control. We had much difficulty in crossing the bar, upon which the sea was still breaking. Finally, however, with the use of the oars after we gained the open sea, we reached our ‘ship without damage. The goods were sooft hoisted in, and the shoremen thet had aided the transport of the wares left us, and our captain. now looked’ only for the signal fiom the commandant on shore,*to weigh and depart.

The next morning at break of. day the signal wa’ flying which gave us permission to get under weigh. But,althongh we could perceive by the flags that there was a good breeze on shore, there was not wind enough where we were, to counteract a current which continually sets to the westward upon this coast, and by which vessels, when exposed to its influence, are drawn into a position from which they cannot extricate themselves, in case of a strong wind arising in the same direction, and which was the quarter from which it generally blew at this season.

In the evening a light breeze sprang up from the southward, which was dead on shore. Our captain now perceived the necessity of taking the earliest opportunity of creeping off the coast, and immediately weighed, and putting the ship’s head to the eastward made all sail possible. The breeze continued during the night ; but the land was still in sight in the morning. By noap, however, upon the day after we weighed, the wind had hauled two points; and wher the sun set the same day, the Siberian mountains were fast sinking bencath the horizon, and we were now at length fairly on our voyage.
