CHAP. XXVII. VOYAGE FROM OCHOTSK TO KAMTSCHATMA.
Character of our Becollections of 2 Voyage.— Auspicious Omens,

Tux sea, commorly called that of Ochotsk, isa great gulf shut in from the North Pacific Ocean by a chain of large and small islands. It is bounded on the west by the continental coasts of Siberia and China, and on the north, the east, and the south, by the peninsula of Kamtschatka and by the Kurile Islands, belonging to the Russians and the Japanese. It is about 1200 or 1400 miles in extent from north to south, and between 700 and 800 ftom west to east; and our course was towards one of the passes between the Russian islands. Those who have travelled much by sea are well acquainted with the manner in which the days blend and confound themselves with one another, and the indistinct recellection that the traveller retains, after his arrival in port, of what severally distinguished the greater part of them while he was at sea. When, indeed, there are ports and islands to.ouch at, where there may ‘be even the smallest objects of interest to observe, or where there may be enemies, civilised or barbarian, to encounter, both the tediousness of the: voyage, and of any narrative of it that may be written, will be proportionably relieved. Or when a. sailor writes, his knowledge of the noble art by which his ship is conducted over the trackless seas, gives hima power whizh it were in vain for any one not thoroughly conversant with both the theory and practice”of naviga. tion to attempt to excel. During the voyage on which we are now embarked, such few incidents as are thought worthy of notice will be set down in the order of time in which they occurred. The first remark which appears in the note-bouk which I kept on board the Irtysch, apart from latitudes and longitudes, and other every-day matter, is precisely otie of those which show how great our interest when at sea in trifles that afterwards even escape our memory, when they have not been written down at the time of their occurrence. On the morning after we left the land, we saw very near us one of those monsters of the dcep in which the ocean abounds in every latitude —
——-' that sea-beast Leviathan, which God of all his works Created hugest that swim the ocean stream.”

He was observed ploughing up the sea, as he held his course majestically along, with a grext portion of his enormous body above the surface of the water, and spouting up at intervals one or two great fountains of the liquid element upon which we floated. All attention was directed to the great sea-beast, which was ‘by some prcnounccd to be a spermaceti, and by others a black whale; none of the first of which kind, nevertheless, I believe, have yet been found in this sea. This question, however, was not the cause of the interest that the great fish was to usat this moment. It was rather ds an omen and messenger of good or evil, that we
regarded the monster of the deep; ajid in this light leviathan was an especial object of interest to us.

The ancient superstitiors of sailors navigating the Atlantic, which doubtless originated in, or was nourished by, the hopes and fears natural to our position when out of sight of land, and the uncertainty concerning the length of our voyage, have been perhaps as stiupletely subdued by the introduction of steam navigation, asall ° ‘that kind of enjoyment commonly called yomance, which belonged a few, years ago to a journey from one end of our island to the other, has been destroyed by our railways. But since the Tritons and Nereides, and all the rest of the brave subjects of the supreme deity of the. sea, have not»been disturbed and frighted from this part — of their sovereign’s domain, we must not expect to find

‘natural causes sought for to explain every event here, just as if Siberians and Kamitschadales had navigated our European rivers, or lived in our material, world, or were accustomed in any way to the investigation of truth.

‘Chief officer,” said our captain, as he stepped upon a gun-carriage, and, while supporting himself by a stay, he regarded the movements of the monster, though he was probably rather a conformist to, than a believer in, the superstitions of the seamen, “ go aloft‘and report in what direction thg whale is swimming.”
‘* And, second officer,” continued the captain, *‘ look at the compass, as the officer aloftespoints qut the course which the whale is taking.”
And in a moment the chief officer was at the masthead, and the second officer was over the “ binnacle ” with his eyes fixed aloft.
« But first, what manner of fish does it now appear to be?” demanded the captain of the officer aloft.
* Most certainly a spermaceti,” replied the officer.
‘* And how does he head? ” then said the-captain.
“In this direction,” repsied the officer stretching out his hand.
“Which is,” said the second officer, as the. captain turned his eyes towards him, ‘exactly west-south-west.”
** Nothing could be better,” then said the captain. ‘* Has he two ‘spouts or one?”

“Enough: check thé yards there, men,” the captain now called aloud. ‘‘ Officer of the watcli, keep the ship a point free, and let her go through the water. Quartcrmaster, nothing to windward during the watch.” '

“It is impossible that any thing could,be more favourable,” now said our worthy commander, as he paced tis, deck with an air of satisfaction which his features had not previously worn. ‘The wind will soon be west-south-west, and we shall have a favourable voyage.”

As to myself, I make a point on,these occasions of not discrediting any thing that it is agreeable to believe, and of not troubling myself about the reasons or proofs that things are what they seem to be, so long as the omens are deemed favourable. But I nevertheless claim the privilege at all times of doubting, whénever the signs appear to point to things evil. And, therefore, I rejoiced with the rest at the good hope with which the leviathan had inspired us, of a favouradle passage across this unfrequented sea.

We dodged on very well for some days, without seeing any thingpsave spouting whales, which were very plentiful, and happily generally sailing along in the right direttion, and a few birds, among which were a duck and a hawk. The hawk, after hovering about us for an hour 6r two, towards evening alighted to rest himself, and roost upon one of our yard-arms; but nothing was prognosticated from his presence, though

certainly it indicated that the wind was off the land, and moreover, that it was very strong upon the coast that was nearest to us, which was “hat from which we came. But the duck, which came late in the evening for his night’s vest,also (for he was not of any of the species which float continually on the sea), settled upon the deck, and nothing whatever was divined fronf his visit, and no one knew the direction from which he came. We put him under cover for the night, and in the morning it was proposed to make a stchee of him. This was, however, frbidden by our captain, who said that thé duck came, sent by whom we know not, to seek our hospitality, which we had given him, and that now we, could not lawfully destroy him.‘ So he was set loose, and he settled upon the water near us.

Some other fowl, however, of the many species’'n which this sea abounds, kept ‘us daily conjecturing and speculating, though in a very indeterminate manner, upon our future prospects. There was infact a great deal of difference of opinion about the indications and omens ; and one saw good, and drew the most favourable conclusions, and was certain that he was right, when the birds flew high or low, or sat on the water in clusters or apart; while gthers were full of apprehension, when they observed the very same signs, which they were just as positive portended evil.

There was, however, a nov elty to myself among the sea-fowl which we continually saw. There were two species of gulls keeping companys and living, as we were well able to perceive, in a strange relationship to each other. In some respects they might he said to very much resemble honest men and thieves among ourselves, though the plundered party of the winged tribe certainly bore their injuries more patiently than most honest men do at all times bear theirs; and this, notwithstanding that the kind of robbery was of

a more vexatious description than often falls to the lot of men to suffer. The injured par ty of these two winged species were gull¥about the size of ‘the larger sort of the common gulls upon our coast, and the other party were of another species much larger, The smaller sort were sitting upon the water in groups, in each of "which there were frdm about thirty to a huudred birds, and the larger sort were hovering over these'in the proportion of ‘bout one of their kind to twenty of the smaller sort. The smaller birds, as they sat in the water, were engaged i in catching fishes, which appeared to be abundant and to be about the size of smelts, and the larger sort were occupied in darting at and snatching the fishes from the mouths 2f the ‘smaller before there was time to swallow them. The Russians cait the birds of the voracious species by the very appropriate term of morskoy-naz-boinik (sea-robbers or pirates). Both the species were abundant; and they afforded us some amusement in watching the dexterous thefts of the robber birds, and the apparent indifference of the dupes, as long as we had fine weather, during our passage of this sea.

Early during the voyage, a little matter occurred which regarded the comfort of the three tenants of the captain’s cabin, the commander himself, and his servant and his guest, which I cannot forbear mentioning. The religious, and, at the same time, tolerant spirit generally prevalent among the Russians has been sufficiently dwelt upon. The. captain’s servant, Antonio, though remarkable for the best qualities that any man of any country, in his capacity, might possess, was nevertheless among the less enlight2ned of his race, and was an_exception to ‘the general prevalence of religious tolerance, at least among the Russians of the orthodox church, of which he was a member, and not jess a stranger to the light, thoughtless, and gay

temperament which is among the more remarkable characteristics of the humbler grades generally of the Russian people. He was, h@wever, a genius, and very skilful in several little handiworks; and, being much valued for his strict honesty and faithfulness, he was upon more familiar terms with his master than is usually the case with Russian servants. But he had two inveterate prejudices, or passions, from which the captain had not been ableg to wean him. He was a great hater of the fair sex, not one of whom he would so much as look upon, and not the less so ofe all foreigners, not because they were not Russiaf's, bat because he did not believe that they were Christians. « :. On account of this latter prejudice, he had during the figst few days of our voyage conceived so bad-an opinion of myself, that he had not even entered my particular cabin to perform such little necessary offices gsare among the duties of a domestic; buf with this negligence the captain had not been made acquaiited. On the first Saturday evening, however, of our voyage, while I was upon deck, after we had taken tea, it happened that the captain, who remained below, in conversing morg familiarly with his servant than he had before done since we sailed, gave the good man‘an opportunity, and the courage that he seemed to have before wanted, of asking a question which he said he had for several days wished to put concerning the foreign guest. Ie was still very cautious, however, in his approaches to the subject of his inquiry, and prefaced his question by saying, he trusted, he would be pardoned, ow account of the question being, as le believed, upon a subject that concernedgevery one in the ship as much as himself. And upon full leave being given to him to ask any question hie pleased, he said that he wished to know whether his master really Asa 3 was, as it appeared to him, entertaining, and eating and drinking daily with a heathen,

But it is necessary hefe to remark, thats generally among the Russians of this class, not one of the’ numerous sects, bearing a common’ name, into which the religion of civilised man has been divided, save those into which the Russians thewiselves are divided, has been so much as heard of; and the omission of the outward signs of the Christian faith, which are in universal use among the different sects in Russia, ranks the nonconformist to these usages in fne eyes of the less enlightened of the people, with the Tartars, the Buddhists, and the Worst pagans, none of whom they consider to be.fit to sit at table with Christian men. Thus, my omission of the ceremony of crossing myself befrre and after eating, and bowing to the, little picture which hung in our cabin and sanctified one of its corners, in the same manner that it is found to do évery where, from the chambers of the palace to those of the humblest cottage, on shore, had so shocked Antonio’s susceptible religious feelings, that, as he declared himself, he could not sleep tranquilly on board, until he had ‘ascertained whether his master’s guest was or was not what he seemed to him to be.

Our worthy commander, who, as I had many opportunities afterwards of observing, posfessed eminently the two points in religion which I found so prevalent among the Russians— strong conviction of the truth of what ‘is taught, and unlimited tolerance—made an attempt, in reply to the question put to him, to enlighten his servant, by giving him some general account of the true state of the Christian world, with a few particulars concerning the more remarkable sects that were not generally known in Russia, and the differences between the external symbols which they used. But
he remained, as he afterwards informed me, for the present uncertain whether what he had said had been either uncerstood or wholly eredited. —

In the meantime, not a word of the conversation between the captain and his servant was for the present communicated to me. But it happened the very morning after it took place, while [ remaiged quite ignorant of the relations in which I was thought by the pious domeStic to stand to all the good Christians on béard, that I very wrfconsciously tstablished my claim to the ri®htg belonging to all the members of the Christian family. To refuse to conform to the external signs especially of religion, wltenever this course is productive of ill-will, or liable to be misinterpreted,* provided the conscietice is not violated in so doing, and especially where there does not seem to be any thing. in the religion in question that is contrary to our ideas of morality, and where we do not thereby give any just cause for an accysation of hypocrisy, I confess has always appeared fo me to be unreaSonable; and I should, for my part, have no objection at any time to make.a thousand crosses at a single meal, if it pleased any body to see them made, dr if the neglect of making them hurt any, one’s feelings in the manner it did our Antonio’s; but’I should be sorr. y to say that I thought that the viands would nourish the body the better, or that the soul w6uld receive the smallest benefit from them, since men’s conduct towards one another, and not external symbols, the Author of Christianity certainly taught, is chiefly regarded by the’Creator. Thus it happened, that when the captain, over our breakfast, informed me that he would to-day read prayefs, to serve for mass, in the presence of the sailors, I told him that if it were agreeable to him I would attend. And if any one among a tolerant people were to do otherwise, it appears to me that he would disgrace any
Christian church or community whatsoever to which he might happen to belong.

Be this, -however, as git may, after the hour of prayer to-day, at the expense of mingling with the officers and seamen while engaged in the act pf worship, and listening for a short time to, prayers read in the Sclavonic language, of which the reader himself knew buta very little, and myself not a syllable, my position was quite changed; for I soon found that - I had thus easily establisheda Christian character, and gained the good will and good service. at*the same time of the honest man that attended in the cabin, and, moreover, secured my comfort for the rest of the ‘voyage.

On the 29th of the month, after dark, we observed a great fire in the direction of the south, which our officers and crew knew very well proceeded from one of several whalers, belonging to merchants of the maritime nations,*which had lately found their way into this sea. As they melt their blubber in ciormous cauldrons upon deck, wherever they appear, they illuminate the ocean during the night for many miles around them.

The 30th was the /éte-day of a relation of. our captain, which we all united in keeping. Nothing is more characteristic of the Russians, than the manner in which they keep the féte-days of their relations among all classes, even from the prindé of the land to his meanest subjects. Our officers were on this occasion equipped in their full-dress uniforms, in their newest gloss, and wore their side-arms, and the seamen were mustered, and the champagne sparkled upon the binnacle; and if there were no other afvantage to be reaped from the display, it was at least calculated to beguile a portion of a tedious day. It happened that it was the cause, however, to myself of a little revelation that it was agreeable to receive. Our captain alone of

the officers came upon deck without his sword, and Antonio, seeming to perceive that this was not quite ship-shape, brought up hgs master’s weapon, which being of a description to attract curiosity, caused an examipation to take place, that led to the discovery of ap inscription beneath the hilt, which upon inquiry I found signified that it had been presenged to its possessor “For his bravery in an affair on shore at the Caucasus, under General. Ryeffoki..

Ffom this time, until the 4th of September, we had variable weatlfer and changeable winds. Thus in spite of the auspiciousomens at our sailing, our progress wasslow,. and we were yet but little mote than half our passage across the sega. Our transformed collier, too, was a bad sailer, and under the most favourable circumstances we had not yet got out of her above six and a half knots. But she was worse than an erdinary bad sailer; for she was unequal in her rate of sailing upon different tacks. It was the first Jnstance of the kind I ever met, on board any ship of any nation, and I felt confident that some mischief must have been done to her keel. When, in fact, we got six knots out of her upon one tack, we could not get more than four*and-a-half upon the other, with the same breeze, and with the same canvass spread, and sailing under the same circumstances in relation to the running seas. There was no suspicion, however, on the part of* the officers of there being any other reason for this than that kind of want of skill in her constructor, go common among the architects of Russia, : which has left nine-tenths of thé church-steeples of the empire absolutely lop-sided..

On the 4th of the month we experiented a tight gale, which, as it was from the eastward, obliged us to lie to under the close-reefed ristnefopaail. In -this position, however, the’Irtysch behaved admirably, and made some amends for her bad sailing. Although the waves, as in all narrow seas, were short and quick, and knocked rudely enough against her weather bow, she sat, as seamen say, like a duck upon the water, an scarce a drop of the element upon which we floated came on board of her.
CHAP, XXVIII VOYAGE FROM OCHOTSK TO KAMTSCHATKA—ontinued.

On the 8th of th8 month we experienced a little relief to the every-day occurrences of the voyage, which we had not anticipated. At day-break in the morning; while we were scarcely lyfng our course, dead on a wind, with a light breeze from the southward, a sail appeared in sight to windward, bearing down upon us under a press of canvass, The telescopes were imme-~- diately in han@, and we soon perceived the American flag; and our captain had no doubt of her being one of the several whale-ships which had lately found their way into this‘sea. In less than two hours the ship hove-to within gun-shot of us, upon our weather quarter; and as we fajlowed her example, she lowéred her boat and boarded us, when she proved to be the whaleship Marcia, Ellison master, of New Bedford.

I cannot refrain ‘from being particular in the relation of this incident and break in our voyage, on account of the interest excited by the contrast between the two parties encountering upon the waters of this little-frequented sea. :

As the whaler’s boat came under our lee quarter., the’ telescopes that had aided in scanning her as she approached were placed under the arms of those who had been using them, or upon their rests on the capstan, and all the officers, save the captain and such as were on duty, and all the passengers, now hung over the quarter-rail, to scan a little closer the visages of those they were about to see for the first time, hold a moment’s intercourse with, and then see no more.

I do not know a more interesting. moment, upon # long voyage especially, when we have seen no strange faces for some time, than that at which the officer of a ship we fall in with, jumps upon the deck upon which we stand, or that at which we mount on board another ship, as it has often been my lot to do, and exchange mutual inquiries about the accidents of our veyages, and concerning the last news of importance at the ports from which we severally came. In the whaler’s boat sat six rowers and a steersman, all in their red shirt sleeves, and as they put in their oars, and the boat reached the waist of the ship, the steersman sprang up to the gangway, and was, in spite of his red sleeves, easily recognised as the commander of the ship. In the meantime, though he ought not to have been surprised, as he must have seen our guns peeping out at the port-holes as he vame alongside, he appeared for a moment taken * aback” at the ceremony of his reception by the officer of the watch, with the gay uniforms which he saw about the deck. After an instant’s pause, howver, he was conducted by the officer who received him to the quarter-deck, where he was introduced to our captain.
Of such a character had so far been the ceremony on one side, and the impossibility of imitating it success-

fully in shirt sleeves upon the other, that it seemed as if the intercourse of the two ships was going to be very unsatisfactory. Buté@t was gratifying to see how easily good sense set aside etiquette, when its observance would have stood in the way of the agreeable intercourse that the time promised. The gallant captain of the manof-war, decorated with his ensigns of ranl@and authority, now offered his hand to she master of the whaler in his red shirt sleeves¢ and the two appropriately dressed monarchs of all * they daily surveyed,” shook hands as heaftily together, with the eyes of the whole ship upon the scene, as if they had been two ancient friends.

The invariable first questions which pass upon the occasion of a parley with the speaking-trumpet betwaen the commanders of two ships at sea when a mighty wave stili rolls between them, are well-known. ** Whence came ye?” ‘How long have you been out?” - Where are you bound to?,’ and, * What is your longitude ? 2® The same subjects, somewhat amplified, usually form also the first portion of a closer intercourse of the two parties on board one of the vessels, The commander of the whaler had not expected to find any one on board the Russian ship to act as interpreter; and he had boarded us chiefly for the purpose of making a little break in the sameness of his own constdnt avocdtion; and, moreover, as he had no doubt that we were lately from the land, to inquire at the same time our longitude, the badness of the weather having prevented his taking any observations of any of the heavenly bodies for several days. Before, therefore, any dif§culty seemed to arise to render an interpreter useful, he demanded our longitude, and was easily understood. And as the day’s reckoning had just been completed by the chief officer, who was present, the question was answ-red by presenting the slate which had been lying on the companion with the figures that resulted from the work. Upon this, the ‘master of the whaler took his pencil out of his waistcoat pocket, and wrote down our longitude upon the palm of his left hand. Certainly, the Chaldean shepherds could not have had a simpler means of registering their astronomica! observations. Then taking the slate in his hand, he put down for our information the longitude by his account, which differeé but little from ours, and which, as he had’two chronometers and we had none, was most likely, notwithstanding the little use he had “been lately able to make of them, nearer. the truth thaw ours. ‘, - But now that the intercourse could not by the same simple means proceed further, the time was arrived for the intervention of a third party; and upon my,addressing our welcome visitur in our common mother tongue, the hardy sailor took the opportunity before every thing else, to apologise as handsomely as possible for boarding a man-of-war in his red shirt sleeves. Then followed some such questions as those above mentioned; and as the weather was fine, and the two ships were now sailing in the same direction, our cap~ tain invited the master of the whaler below, where over a glass of good wine, we entered upon other subjects which afforded us a most agreeable hour’s conversation. :

The last dates from the countries that play the lead- ‘ing parts, whether in comedy or tragedy, upon the wide stage of the world, usually upon these occasions precede our more particular inquiries concerning the most important news,.And when it is found which of the parties encountering has the latest accounts, the next inquiries proceed from the other side. What was the great international play in course of representation when the last accounts came away? Who were the

actors? Who the “robustious and periwig-pated” princes, that were tearing the passions of the nations to tatters? And which of tle monarchs were tranquilly beholding the last scene of the mighty drama, always enacting in farce, tragedy or dumb show, with neverceasing plot, and counterplot, on the great theatre of the world?

‘As the*whaler had been two years out, it wag our fortune upon this occasion to have the latest news, and moreover, as it happened, to be the brief chroniclers of the first scen@ ofthe serious play then opening upon the eventful year of 1848, I had quitted: Irkoutsk just after the intelligence of the flight of Louis Philippe had reached thgt capital; but all that we could say for certain was, that France was once more a republic.

If sailors are not the most ingenious and, subtle reasoners in the world, they are not the least remark-, able as a class of men for their general good sense and correct judgment, If they are not profound politicians and political economists, they are freer than.any other body of men from those motives to a narrow judgment, which necessarily influence those who sit continually too near the scene upon which ‘men’s eyes are chiefly bent, to leave them at liberty to generalise their thoughts. Perhaps the ‘very space which is continually before their eyes may aid in resisting the tendency of the mind to circunfScribe its thoughts within the sphere of its own particular experience. Be these things, however, as they may, I was curious to note how the sailor citizen of a republic, turned for a moment from his whale-fishing, would receive our European news, and what observations he would favour us with:

The sailor reflected but for an instant, and then exclaimed, “ France a republic! The French people are not of a character to maintain such a government, Even in America, we, who have known no other, and who are the offspring of a people who are free as ourselves, find it as much as we can do to weather the storms of the presidential election. How, then, can a nation of the most excitable people in the world, be expected to ride out the quick succession of political tempests which must necessarily follow the establishment of sugh a government?

In return for the pithy intelligence whigh excited these observations, we recelved the news of the sea upon which we were floating. The’ captain of the whaler told us that he believed that about’forty vessels,

‘~for the same objects as himself, had found their way this year for the first time into this sea, and that théy were chiefly French and American; byt that, owing to the bad weather that had prevailed during the greatet part of this season, notwithstanding the wkales were plentiful, he believed there had not been the average number of them, of one year with another in the northern fishery, yet taken. He informed us, that of thirteen whales which he had killed, he had lost three by the bad weather before he could secure the oily portion of them; and that when the last gale came on, which was the same that we had experienced, he had thirty barrels of oil on his deck, which he saved with great difficulty. He still wanted, he said, fifteen fish to fill his vessel with oi], but which number he’ hoped to make up in this sea in the course of the next summer. But he was somewhat surprised when he heard from our captain that the Russian government was contemplating, or “had determined upon sending some men-of-war a little more formidable in effect than the Irtysch, to take absolute possession of the sea, and prevent the vessels of all other nations from entering and fishing without a pass from the Russian govern ment, This, however, seems a measure that it is hardly likely can be contemplated, seeing that a large porti o
of the coasts of this sea are Japanese and Chinese, and that the sea may be entered without even approaching the Russian territory..

The master of the whaler also informed us, that one of a number of ships from the same port as himself, had been wrecked upon the coast of Japan with 3000 barrels of oil on ‘board, and that he himself hag narrowly escaped dviving on shore during the same gale. He gave us an account likewise of the shock of an earthquakt, which he had felt i the middle Of this sea upon the 8th of Jane, and which was so severe that he thought for a moment that his ship tad struck upon a rock. All seanien, indeed, with whom I have conversed, who have witnessed the effects of this phenomenon at sea, give the same account of their sensations. I was on board a ship in the port of Valparaiso on the night of the 4th and Stheof June, 1849, when a shock was felt; but I was asleep, and quite aaeonscians of it. Others, however, were awakened ; afid some thought that the nfovement they felt was caused by the grating of the hawser from our ship across the hawser from another; and others, that we had drifted foul of another ship, and were thuthping against her by the motion of the water.

After an hou:"s agreeable intercourse, the commander of the whaler left us, and the two ships soon parted company. At sunset, we were not by our reckoning above 110 miles from the Kurile Isles, which form the south-eastern boundary of the Ochotsk Sea; and as we were lying our course with a spanking breeze, we had every reasonable hope of seeing some of the islands (many of which are visible at the distance of ninety miles), or of even being very near them at day-break the following morning.
The bicese continued, and we were not disappointed. As the next day broke, our captain came to my cabin,

to give-me notice that the land was in sight at no great distance from us, and that the view of what was already visible, afforded such a magnificent spectacle, that he was desirous I should. not lose the opportunity of seeing it before it might be obscured by the mists which hang almost perpetually about these islands, and * upon - the eastern coasts of this sea.

Those who have made voyages in high latitudes especially, will not readily forget the agrceable sensations which they cannot fail to haze experienced, when after looking for many days only upon the. sky and the water, divided by the unbroken line of the horizon, with nothing but the clouds to vary the one, and a change in the motion of the sea the other, they again behold the firm land. Probably, indeed, there are few travellers by sea who would exchange the feelings that have _ possessed them at this moment, with those they have experienced upon entering port, if allowance be made for the pleasure of meeting our friends, when we chance to have any at the place at which we acrive.

It was hardly full day, when I came upon deck; but there was light enough to sce plainly the cone of a mighty volcanic mountain, forming the island of Ahlehead, which appeared towering above a stratum of vapours that divided the mountain about a third of its’ full height from its summit. The breeze that had brought us within view of tlie Jand dur:ng the night, had now died away; and there was nothing to interrupt our calm contemplation of the scene which the increase of. light was rapidly presenting to us. Our distance from the island by cross-bearings taken from its points at the base, was found to be twenty-eight miles, though it did not appear to be above eight or fen. The floating mists which divided the mountain “were drawn out in a long and straight line, without any variation of colour; while from the top of the cone above them,

ascended a still subtler element, proceeding from the burning substances within the crater of the volcano, and which atsthe limits of its algtude formed a curling cloud of deeper hue, which by the constant succession of the floating particles that were taking the place of those that were lost to the sight, appeared as motionless as the vapours below. But our view did not long yemain ‘con~ fined to the objects that were at first visible. As thé light increased, the larger i¢land of Pero Muchan, which is aout forty miles in len&th, gradually came into view in the same Hregtion, about fifteen miles more distant fsom our place of observation, and presented a series of’ velcanic mountains with cones and peaks of various forms and ajtitudes. From one of these alone, which towered high above the constant stratum of still vapours that divided all the cones and rude summits from the bases upon which they rested, ascended a volume of dense smoke, which the winds dispersed at a great height above the mouthsf the crater from which it issued.

As we stood cohtemplating this magnificent display of some of the mighty natural objects which so vary the scenery that adorns.our fair planet, the far greater object of wonder, and the gréatest that we are permitted to look upon, was on the point of coming into view, and the eastern sky already exhibited the livelier colours and deeper shades which in all lands proclaim equally the return of dy. But now-as the rays of the bright orb fell upon the peaks and cones of the mountains, all that caught the direct beam became streaked and shaded with lines of varied colours, which the snow in the ravines and the deeper shades of the bare earth which divided themgseverally reflected. But before the great source of all we enjoy became visible frgm our deck, the floating vapours also received his direct rays, and the magnificent spectacle which we now beheld, was extended to the limits of the vision on both sides,

I shall here mention, upon the authority of our captain and two of his officers, a remarkable phenomenon which is frequently observed in these seas, and which is called by the natives of the coasts spolocka. Its most common appearance was described to me by these officers with the aid ofan old sailor who had navigated this cea, and lived upon its coasts for fifty years, and to whom it was consequently much moré familiar. A bright speck of white ligltt or lumindus vapour first appears upon thé horizon in‘the north, afd presently seems to rise in a column of about 6,or ‘7 degrees in “breadth; which continues to ascend, and to increase it. length until the upper end reaches. within a few degrets of the zenith, at which time the lower portion appears to separate itself fromthe horizon. It continues however, to advance, in falling towards the south, until what. was the upper end as ‘it rose, becomes''the lower as it approaches the southern horizon, beneath the watery line of which it now gradually sinks’ until it’ entirely disappeat's. The whole time of the passage of this remarkable light across the hemisphere, from the time of its appearance until it is lost sight of in the south, does not exceed three minutes.

I have seen many different appearances of the aurora borealis in the higher latitudes of both continents as well as at sea, but [ never saw any thing that resembled this light. Yet I am disposed to believé that it is but a variation of that unaccountable phenomenon, arising
"from causes yet unknown. Those, however, who gave me this account, and who were of course well acquainted with the varied appearances of the aurora borealis, were not of this opinion, "

While we arg considering what appears peculiar to this sea, I must mention, that I remarked during this voyage, that that sparkling light seen at night in the water when agitated in every sea, and formerly supposed

to be phosphisrie, prevailed te a much greater degree in this, than in any sea I had befove navigated. If it really proceed, as. I believe it is' now stated, from any form of animated nature or of organised being, at what a profound depth must the secrets of Nature yet ie ‘hid from eux observation !

- The remarkable chain of islands of which we have now seveoat under our view, whether we régard their pesition, or thre natural wonders they exhibit, belong in part to the Russians and in’ part to the Ji lapamese, two people probably athat of alll the varieties of the human Species the least'vesemble each ether, yet they"are not iathabited cither by the one or the other. Some of them are. inhabited by men, nevertheless, of two yaces almost as distinct from each other as the two people by wham they are governed, or more properly speaking, to whose dominion they have been severally subjected, as their inhabitants axe described as. scareely living in a state of society. ePhe Russian islands are six in noniber, without taking those inte aceount which are little more than the cones ‘and eraters of volcanos, or those, of which there are seyeral, that ate formed of mere rude and barren recks, “They ave all, indeed, ef volcanic formation. The most northern of them is that of Sumshie, which lies between the larger island of Pero Muchan, in sight of which we are now sailing, and the southern point of the grand peninsula of Kamtsehatka. The most southern is the island of Urup, which for ms one side of one of the passages; of which there aye many, connecting the Ochotsk Sea with’ the ocean. The south peint of this island is in the, latitude of 45° 35’. @
Sea, consists of two long islands called Iturup and Kumoschir or Ischikstan.

The Russian islands onl are at this time Inhabited by portions of the two distinct races. The race which inhabits the most northern’ are called by the Kamtschadales(who themselves have been long subjected to regular governmen®, and are comparatively a civilised people), simply Kurilians, after the general name given to the islands. They resemble the’ inhabitants of the sougiern districts of Kamtschatka both in feature and in their language, and they have doubtless @ common origin ‘vith that people. But. the inhabitants of the more southern of the Russian islands, are called by the Kamtschadales Kurilian Mahnali. These’ @eem to be quite an original people. A Russian that I afterwards saw, who had been at astation that has been establighed by the Russo-American Company upon the north side of the island Pero Muchan for the furtherance of their commerce in furs, and who was wel}*acquainted with them, informed me, that they did not certainly resemble the Chinese, whom he had seen, in the slightest degree ; and, as it is supposed that the Japanese are closcly related to that people, probably none of, the islanders are related to either the Japanese or the Chinese. The same gentleman informed me, also, that the last mentioned of these inhabitants are such a hairy race as to have obtained a name from the more northern inhabitants of the island, equivalent to that of ‘¢ hairy men.” Neither of these races of these islands have fixed abodes, and both live chiefly upon seals, sca-cows, or the walrus, and a species of the same genus called by the Russians by a term that-would signity in English sea-beaver, and of which we saw several as we passed through the strait. They have both now, however, begun to trade with the company above named in the skins of these animals, from which intercourse they will
no doubt, in time, receive the same advantages that are enjoyed by the other races which have been incorporated with the subjects of the empire.

The Japanese islands were till very lately inhabited by the same race of men as those which occupy the more southern portion of the Russian islands. But their population has been withdrawn by tke Japanese government, in order to.separate them as far as possible from their brethren inhabfting the Russian islands, so as entirely to cut off all iiftercourse between them.

We had baffling winds and variable weather during the whole of the day on which we made the islands, settling in the evening in an east wind, with a densely loaded atmosphere. “Our course had been directed during the day towards the strait which fo-ms a passage from “the Ochotsk Sea into the ocean, between the islands of Pero Muchan and Ownekotan, which is the third navigable channel south of the point of the peninsula of Kamtschatka, and the safest in the northern portion of this chain of islands, on account of its superior breadth; and before dark, we obtained a sight of the islet of Sherjnska, which lies near the nor entrance of the strait.
During the early part of the night it blew a gale from the east, and we were driven some leagues to the westward of the islands; but as the day approached

the wind veered to the northward; and as it now became more moderate, and the thick clouds and mists began to, disperse, we made all sail towards the strait, through which-it was our intention to pass. But as we approached the land again, we found the atmosphere as loaded’as’ before with vapours and thick clouds; and nothing was’ visible around us, when wg supposed eiareclves at the very entrance of the strait. Suddenly, however, the high and rocky islet of Sherinska, which we lfid seen on the previous evening, &ppeared on one side of us. ateabout thirteen miles’ distance, and ina fgw minutes afterwards, another similar islet upon the, opposite side, at the same distante, called Monkuruska. These two islets stand out on either side before thé entrance of “the strait, the very mid-channel of which we thus now found we were approaching with admirable exactness. But for two haurs after this, we yet saw nothing of the coasts and mountains of the larger islands. = These two congpicuous islets are no more, indced, than tthe mere cones of the craters of volcanos; and they are appropriately called by the Russians Karaooli (the Sentinels), because, in thick weather, by reason of their less attracting the clouds and fogs than the larger islands, they ave seen in time to warn the navigator (as it happened, indecd, in our own case) of his near approach to thé strait, where he might, without such notice, be subjected to the influence of dangerous currents before he was sufficiently certain of his position to direct his course through the passage. They were not, however, now sufficiently well seen to enable us to distinguish their volcanic character. But the officers on board informed me, ‘that as they passed them by on their voyage to Ochotsk, the one that was on the south side of the entrance was diséorging a broad volume of dense smoke.

As soon as the two Sentinels were plainly enough seen for our purpose, our course was set with confidence; and as the wind now veered to the scuth-west and blew a gentle gale, we fairly enteréd the passage between the larger islands, which we were not yet able; to perceive, under. full sail, with as much security as if we had seen the land upon both sides of us.
As we advanced, the,two Sentinels became again obscured from our sight. But we were assured of our position by the“smoothness of the waters in which we were now Sailing.

I do not remember any where on board ship being placed in a more curidus position than that in which we now found ourselves. With a stiong, breeze and under crowded canvass, we were sailing with the utmost confidence between two rocky shores, through a channel about sixteen or eighteen miles in breadth, and without any fixed object visible in any direction around. And as the diy advanced the sky became clear overhead, and we could see many miles astern, and towards the ocean almost to the horizon; while the land, with its peaks and mountains, was enveloped in dense clouds, which entirely concealed ‘it from our view on either side, so that we appeared to be sailing between two vast walls of condensed vapours and dark clouds.
While we were gliding gently, yet rapidly, through the smooth water of the strait, Anfonio made his appearance upon deck, loaded with bottles of champagne.

' These I supposed to be for the purpose of greeting worthily the sovereign of the ocean, into whose wider domain we were now launching, or such of his brave subjects as this portion of his watery,empire might especially acknowledge; but it turned out to be an offering of our captain to the manes of his parents, in commemoration of his own birth, which took place in this very strait on board a ship of war, which his
father commanded at the happy epoch, about thirty years sinée,

While’ we were occupied in aiding the captain in honouring his parents and hallowing the place of his birth, a favourable omen, as if some of the Tritons and Nereides of the sea took the compliment to themselves, greeted us. One of the sea-castors or beayers before mentioned, with which the seas that wash these islands aboynd, popped his head Yabove the water and stood erect, with at least as mifch as three feet of his body exposed to dur siew, as if he were a sea-god that was dntemplating us approvingly, on account of our loyalty, as’we passed by. There was af least not a man among us that did aot augur from this visitation a speedy and happy termination of our already too-long-protracted voyage,

We were now going rapidly through the watér; but at what rate we were passing the land we could not tell, owing to tle uncertainty of the, currents in the passages between these islands, which depend chiefly upon the winds, and they had been variable. But about two hours before sunset, the peaks and summits of the higher mountains up$n the northern, and soon afterwards these upon the southern island, began to appear, though still confounded with the dark clouds which wholly obscured their solid masses.

After sun-set, thie land became visible on both sides of the strait. And as we launched into the ocean, we distinguished very plaiply the most eastern capes of the two islands, from which we shaped a course towards the south-east coast of the peninsula of Kaintschatka with o spanking south-west breeze, and in full hopes of reaching the Bay of Avasha, in which the Russian seat of government is established, in three or four days.
Upon the whole’ of the day after our entrance into the

Pacific Ocean, we were sailing parallel with the chain of islands, witha strong wind fram the west-south-west; but, though the atmosphere was clear around us, the inna was not visible, on account of the clouds and vapours that still hung about it.

The next day we obtained the first sight of the coast of Kamtschatka which presented an irregular line of rugged mountains, the higher of which at their summits’ were covered with snéw. We appeared here to have got quite ifto the ‘region of the whales. At one part of the day no less than five were blowing around vs at the same time:.

The fine weather, with a strong westerly wind, cchfinued until the early part of the third day 1fter we left the Ochotsk Sea, when we ‘obtained a’ view of the mountains in the vicinity of the Bay of Avashz, to which we were bound. Tle scenery of this particular part of:the coast is of the grandest description. A wide range of tude and elevated land presznts itself to the spectator as far as the eye can reach, from the midst of which three enormous mountains, whose summits terminate in voleanic cones, rise above the rest, and add that finish to-the wild magifificence of nature, which the domes and minarets when seen from the same clement upon which we were floating, high towering above the irregular buildings of a great metropolis, add to the most remarkable of the works of men. I cannot forget the raptures with which we looked upon this display of the prodigality of. nature in her gublimest works in the material world.

As we approached the land,a lower country in advance of these mountains seemed to rise gradua'ly out of the water, and by and by presented a bold, high and rude coast, amid which we were able to distinguish the cutrance of our desired port, which appeared like a rent in the rocks dividing the rugged table hills of the

coast into two parts. But while we were dwelling with transport upon the grand natural scenery upon which our eyes restetl, and cherishing hopes through the agreeable prospect before us of entering the port that very evening, and while the breeze “and the weather were fair, our prudent captain communicated his suspicions as to the fulfilment of our expectations.

It must be remembered what sea we were navigating, and upon what ¢oast we had%rrived. And now, although the wind was dead into the port, a doubt-had arisen in the captain’s Mind, upon measuring the distance by the bearings of the capes and headlands upon either side of: uspand the rate of thé ship’s salting, and marking the hour, whethgr, in case we should persevere in running” down, we could with certainty enter before the close of the By 5 ; and; after some hesitation, the accomplishment of our object did not appear to hinr sufficiently probable to admit of our running upon the land with the wind directly on shore, without great imprudénce and risk, until the next day. The east wind, which was blowing, is usually accompanied upon this coast by a misty atmosphere and bad weather ; and in case of its thickening in before we reaclfed the mouth of the port, we might hardly expect to find.our way into the strait; while with a “considerable increase of the wind, it might be impossible to work off the coast. The vessel’s head was theref$re reluctantly placed in the opposite direction, and, to those who knew the nature of the winds and the weather upon this coast, without much prospect of our being able again to approach the port for some days.

Up to this gime, I have set down all the incidents that seemed to offer any variation fromthe every-day experience of most voyages. After this, we passed no less than sixteen days more in perpetual contest with the winds and the sea, before we were able to accomplish our entrance into the Bay of Avasha. -A very brief notice of the occurrences of that period will suffice.

It was not, indeed, two hours from the time our ship's head was turned from her port, before she was under close-reefed topsails, and such ‘storm staysails as she could bear, with the wind due east, with thick weather. And it, was, soon clear that had we run down upon the land, our safety would have depended entirely upon the chance of very nicely hitting the entrance of the port ; for such was the violence of che wind during the night, that we could not keep even the course of the coast; and when the next day broke, we were not able, by reascn of the thickness of the atmosphere and the uncertainty of the currents, to tell how near we were-to the ironbound shores that were under our lee.

From this time we were alternately running spon the land, and hauling off uader storm sails, just as the almost incessant gales and the direction of the winds favoured or oppased us. ‘We had even a second time a view of the entrance of our port, and were again driven off. Twice during this period of uncertain and tempestuous weather, we were lying to under the closereefed main topsail; and at one time we were by the reckoning no less than 340 miles from the port which we had actually twice seen, and once been so near entering. Such is the uncertainty and such the delight of navigating these seas.

The chief occurrence which varied our every-day ex~ perience during this long and tedious struggle with the obstinate elements, was an alarm of no ordinary character, which threatened us with even a worse fate than the wreck and total loss of the ship and all on board upon the rocks so often beneath ourlee. One morning, after the cabin had been several times half full of water, and the partitions between the departments were broken to pieces, and the furniture was nearly all destroyed, the

captain and myself were sitting upon a sofa, which, from being placed in a niche, had escaped the general wreck, and were very composedly @pjoying a favourable change of weather that had occurred, and the fumes of the chiboogk, when suddenly a seaman in his shirt entered with a woe;begone Countenance to inform us, that, upon turning out of his berth, which was uyon the halfdeck, he fad found the floor’so hot that he could not stand upon it ‘without his’shoes ; and he had rushed to the cabin just as he® stood, to convey the awful intelligence 8f his fears, which he communicated in a few brief words. 7

“Upon receiving this intelligetce, our captain, before hastening to the half-deck, as one of less presence of mind might have done, summoned ‘the officers who were on “duty to the cabin, and then with admirable coolness issued his orders. To one officer was given the charge to sce that all the hatches were sg battened down and made tight, that not the smallest portion of air could escape from the hold; and to another was given the order to cause to be drawn from the sea, and handed below, as large a quantity of water as possible.

By the time the officers* returned to the deck, the alarm had reached the whole ship, and all became now activity, but without the slightest breach of order. A few moments only elapsed before several casks of water had been filled and secured on the lower deck, and a number of men placed around with buckets of water in hand to await the opening of the hatches for the discovery of the true cause of our fears.

The heat was now so intense here, where the greater part of the oficers and crew were gathered, that it was scarcely supportable, though the deck beneath our feet was already wet with sea-water. Yet there was no appearance of smoke, which, if there had been flame, could not but have appeared semewhere. It was therefore theecaptain’s impression tliat the heat proceeded solely from the cargo, ané had not yet broken into flame. Thus it was above all things necessary to avojd admitting such a current of air upon opening the hatches as to cause the bursting out of flame below, which, as there was a quantity of spirits among other things in the hold, would have been instantly attended with the dreaded consequences. All communication bet:yeen the external air and that between decks was therefore carefully cut off. And it was now #2 trying. moment when the hand was placed to lift the hatch; it would reveal the certainty of our destruction, or fill us with hope, if not assure our ‘safety. The captain and his chief officer stood one on either side of the portion of the hatch to be lifted, while two of the other officers ‘yradually removed the tarpaulin which covered it without any consequences yet appearing. Then the two firstmentioned officers gingerly lifted tht portion of the hatch which they held; and the instant the air found a free passage, a damp vapour rushed up, which was so intensely hot as, if possible, to increase the alarm. Prudently, however, the hatches were now still very gradually further opened, and.the water withheld. And now after a few minutes thé vapour diminished in quantity ; and our alarm ceased, and-all the injury we sufferec. after all was a good scorching from the vapour which had proceeded from the lower hold. But it is certainly my impression, that had the hatches been suddenly and fully removed, and those of the upper deck kept open, the rush of air thereby caused would have been followed by the bursting out of flame from the cor.bustible ma~ terials in the he'd, from which the heat turned out to proceed, that would have been attended with all the consequences which we had dreaded.

As much as possible of the cargo was now hoisted between decks, and wherever else it could he safely disposed of; and upon exaynination, it was found that a large quantity of rye flour that we had on board, aided no doubt by the spirits which were near it, had heated during the time that the hatches were necessarily closed on account of the long continuange of bad weather; and in an hour or two all went on again as steadily as befofe.

Athong the troubles we experienced Guring the long suspension ofeur hopes of gaining the port, wasascarcity ofwater. The voyage under favourable circumstances-> ought not to exceed a fortnight. Thus, after three weeks, we were reduced to so small a supply of this ne~ cessary of life, that our captain had to put us upon short, allowance ; and after the thirtieth day, he thought it necessary to reduce this to a most incon¥enient quantity, and at the same time to communicate his doubts concerning the prudence of our remainihg much longer upon the *doast, should the same weather continue. This question was, however, one of great difficulty. If we should abandon our attempts to enter the port of Avasha, where were we to find the shelter and relief of which we were in search? One of the Aleutian Islands was the first place of refuge which would naturally occur to a Russian, where the Russo- American Comffany have a factory. But to leave a port to which we were so near for another in a similar climate, and from which we were at least three weeks’ sail, when we had not water enough for ten days more, without immediately reducing the allowance to the smallest quantity upon which we could subsist, was not a step to be hastily taken. In the meantime, a few days’ longer delay would render it impossible that the | step could upon any account be had recourse to with any chance of success. VOL. If. ce

There was, however, still another course possible, and for which there was at least a precedent, Only a year or two ago, the annual ship making‘ "the same voyage from Siberia, found herself in the same position with regard to the weather and the season, although she had still a sufficient quantity of water in’ board; and after striving against the tempests until all hope was abandoned by her commander, she bore up for the Bonin group of islands in the latitude of 27 degrees, and after wintering in one of these made goo her voyage in the spring. This was, however, a much longer passage than that to the Aleutian Islands, and offered proportionably less hopes, on account of our want being that of an absolute necessar y of our existence. All things thus weighed, therefore, it was determined to persevere to the utmost in our struggles to gain tne port of Kamtschetka.

At length, upon the fifteenth day after that upon which we obtained the first sight of the Bay of Avasha, we saw the mountains above mentioned for the ‘third time, now quite covered with snow, at the distance of fifty-three miles, bearing nearly due west of us. The wind was northerly, and te circumstances were deemed so favourable, that we made all sail a third time directly towards the haven of our hopes; and in the evening we were within ten miles of the entrance into the bay, when the wind drew out, »vut without any such change of weather as to endanger our hopes of maintaining our position during the night. ‘

Before this day closed, we found ourselves in company with another ship, which was evidently a whaler, and which we passed upon the opposite tack ; for she was striving like ourselves to gain the entrance ofthe bay. This was to me a most welcome incident; for considering the time we had been out, and the length of the ship’s previous long passage, I had but faint hopes of
any whaler coming into the port during the season, and upon which I knew all my hopes depended of escape from the A ius before the setting in of the winter.

After tacking several times during the night, we found ourselves in precisely the same position the next morhing that we had been in at sun-set the previous evening; and the weather being still fine, wg, continued to beat up towards the port until mid-day, when it fell calm. At*one o'clocls, however, a fine bréeze came*in from the sea, andewith all sailset we entered the narrow passage leading to the bay, which we found a gnere gut,.as it had appeared at a‘distance, between. meyntainous table lands on both sides. The whaler, which we had missed in the morning, had beaten in, or® been favoured by the wind, and entered the gut before it was well day. But she had. been caught by a breeze that came from the bay, and.had anchored in thé gut; and she now got under weigh again, as she f00k the breeze that we brought up with us.

At two o'clock, We passed three rocks called the Three Brothers, rising above the surface of the water on the right hand, as high probably as our topmasts ; and after these, we passed also a rock en the opposite side of the gut, called the Grandmother.

The winds wére light, and they became less favourable as we proceeded. But as soon as we had passed through the gut#the fine Bay of Avasha opened before us. This bay is about ten miles in breadth; and «within it at its north-west side, there is a little inner ‘ port, where now appeared the” Russian seat of the government of Kamtschatka, Petropavlovski (or the town of St. Peter and Paul), off which we anchored early in the night after our passage of thirty-six days, during more than half of which we had been exposed to the most tempestuous weather.

I will only add, that I left the Irtysch with a strong’ impression of the superior skill and seaman-like qualities of the Russian officers on board; and with 4dmiration of the perfect discipline that was maintained without recourse to severity. After having been accustomed to voyages in almost every description of vessel,“with and without that essential instrument, the chronometer, I am able to say that.I was never on board a ship where the results of the reckoning without a chronometer were more precise than on. this occasion. ‘

It is impossible to speak, however, in the same terms anf the seamanship of the men generally on board. About half a dozen of them, who were accustomed Jike the officers to the navigation of these seas, were, as far as I was able tojudge, equal to any, save the best of our own seamen, with whom I have sailed; but the rest, the greater portion of whom bad marched from the Black Sea, and had. been three years on their journey, were the worst I ever sailed with. Our chief officer, Chudinoff, who added the qualifications of an artist to those of his profession, before I left Kamtschatka, presented me with a drawing of some of the Kurile Isles, which he had made during, our passage.

eo KamrscHaTKA comprises the whole of that great peninsula which stretches out from the coast of Asia at its north-eastern. extremity, and is washed by the Pacific Ocean on the east and the Sta of Ochotsk on the west. It lies between the 5lst and 64th degree of north latitude, and between the 155th and 164th of east longitude. It is between 700 and 800 miles in length, and about 250 fh breadth at its centre near the latitude of 55 degrees, but not above eighty or ninety at either of its extremities. The most remarkable natural features of this great peninsula are its voleanic mountains, which rise at intervals throughout a vast range, which stretches from its southern to its northern extremity, and appears to be but a continuation of the volcanic range which forms the Kurile Islands, and extends even to Japan and the islands along the eastern coasts of the Asiatic continent. It has only éc3
one navigable river, called the Kamtschatka, which falls

‘into the Sea of Kamtschatka near the cen{te of the peninsula, but it has many less considerable streams. The coasts and all the rivers of Kamtschatka abound in fish and water-fowl. _ The sea is frequented hy whales of several species, and -by walruses and seals in great abundance, besides cod and herring; and in the rivers are found great quantities of salmon, ” Geese and ducks, also, of several species frequent the coasts and the rivers during the authmn and spring in great numbers.

The peninsula is inhabited by three Sosigivel tribes, ‘the Kamtschadales, the Kouriaks, and the Ohlutors. “The first of these occupy the southern, end the other two,the northern districts of the country. But the whole of the native population is not supposed to ez:ceed 4000 or 5000 souls.

The climate of Kamtschatka is much milder than _ that of the continent in the same perallel of latitude, owing, without doubt, to the influence of the sea on both sides of it. The maximum of cold in the southern districts does not exceed 20 degrees,

The country politically Yorms a part of the government of Ochotsk, and is comprehended within the grand province of Eastern. Siberia. 1t¢ capital town is called Petropavlovski, or the town of St. Peter and St. Paul, and is seated in the Bay of Avasha. ’The government of the peninsula at the time I visited the. country, was administered by Captain Machin of the imperial navy.. Its chief provincial towns or villages. ate Bolschiretsk, Tiguilsk, Nijhni Kamtschatka, and Verchnei Kamtschatka.

‘When the passengers on board the Irtysch came on deck on the morning after our arrival in port, we found the captain had left the ship at an early hour, to deliver his despatches to the- governor or com-

Mandant, and report the passengers and freight which hQ had brought with him, previous to our landing, which left us at Igisure to take a particular survey of the harbour of Avasha, and the surrounding scenery.,. :

The view which is here presented to the eye of the spectator far surpasses in magnificence any thing that is to be seen throughout the mountain districts of Siberia. The.nearer lands around donsist of rude and befrren iiills; but at a greater ér less distanée within thirty versts, appeaf the mountains already mentioned, while at the sign of the existence of nien in any state af soviety, or of the means of thei? subsistence, is to be seen througkout the vast extent of country under view save only a little assemblage of a dozen or two of black huts set, apparently, at the very base of the volcanic mountain of Avasha, from the crater of which was now issuing a column of white vapour.

The highest oft these remarkable mountains, and that which is the most conspicuous when “they are viewed from the sea, is called by the natives Karatski (the Giant), in Russian Villikanin. It appears from this point, as if it rose immediately from the shores upon the opposite side of the bay, whereas its base is at a distance of thirty versts ‘from the place where we lay. The name of the second is Velutchink, and of the third Avasha. a 3

On our captain’s return, he informed me, that he had presented the letter which I brought with me to the -commandant, among others, and that he was commissioned to tell me that apartments would be immediately prepayed for my reception during’ my stay, in one of several small buildings set apart for the accommodation of the officers of the station, and that the commandant wished to see me on shore as soon as possible.

The five passengers now descended to the ship’s boat, well pleased to leave the storm-heaten Irtresch ; for though nothing could be better than the gallant manner in which she had weathered the gales, the anxieties of the passage had been greatly augmented by the aincertainty which we had been under during the last sixteen days, whether we should reach the port, or have to bear up, after all, for some distant country.

We found the inner harbour, as we rowed up it, perhaps the most perfect little haven that is to be met with on the coast of any country in the world. It is formed bv a peninsula of elevated land, which stretches out into the noble bay, and inakes the harbour by approaciing at its extremity within 200 or 300 yards of the opposite land. But again, even within this, there projects from the main land a bank of sand and pebbles, which furms a third harbour within the second, with a narrow passage to enter, but with depth of water to admit vessels of any burden, and capable probably of containing fifty or sixty large ships at anchor at the same time.

We landed at the bottom of this harbour, at a little fort, belonging to which were some storehouses. My fellow-passengers now made their way towards the apartments that had been severally assigned to, them, to wait for the ordinary hour to attend on the commandant, while I took my road immediately to the governmenthouse, in order to respond -as early as possible to the invitation which had reached me while on board the vessel.

Oa arriving at the government-house, 1 found a low but neat wooden building, with a garden in front of it, where the humble birch stood in the place of fruit trees. Upon gaining admittance, I was shown through several doors similar to those which enclose the tenants of the Siberian houses, to the audience apartment of
the commandant, who, after receiving notice. of the entrancQof a stranger, soon appeared.

My reception from thg remote representative of his sovereign was polite and warm, and wus accompanied with the offer of his aid in every object I might have in view. After a short conversation concerning the voyage and its several incidents, and pon the news we brought from Siberia and Europe, the commandant conducted me to an inner apartment, dnd introduced me to his wife, from whof also I met’a kind reception. The lady w&s amative of St. Petersburg; and she was Pleased with the opportunity of conversing with one eo lately, as something more than*a year appeared to, her, from her nasive town. She had married very young, and had now been between four and five years in Kamtschatka. All I was able, however, to communicate to her only amounted to a traveller’s passing infpression of the modern capital of Russia, and must have been of little value. ° Ow the other hand, the lady cotld not. fail to excite great interest in a stranger, from the solitude in which slie was residing.

She was still in the very bloom of youth; and with no ordinary degree of beauty, she possessed all the accomplishments common to the more refined portion of her sex in Etrope, which served but to heighten the contrast between the daughter of civilisation, and the women of this rude and inhospitable land. Taken so young from the contracted confines within which continental delicacy coops up the younger portion of her-sex before the matrimonial alliance, and brought here by sea, the knowledge which she had acquired concerning the world wore more the air of romance than reality. She made no secret of her feelings. She said that for the first two years after her arrival at Kamtschatka, the ennui which she suffered had been scarcely supportable ; but that since that time, habit and the, occupation which two children gave her, had not only reconciled her to the country, but Vad even made. her now look with something like regret to the time of the commandant’s recall to fill some other post.

Before I took leave, I learned from the commandant. that an American trading véssel that had visited this port for several secsons, had this year left her master Mr. Knox, behind, who had established a little general store for the purpose, more particularly, of trading with the natives in the interior of the country’; and after receiving an invitation to return to dinner, I was now conductéd by owe of the commandant’s servants in search of Mr! Knox at his little American store, in hopes of beitfi able to obtain the information which was so important to me, respecting the whaler that entered the port with us, and was now at anchor in the bay. - o

On my arrival at Mr. Knox’s, I found the master of the whaler had already been on shore. The ship proved to be the Josephine, Captain Hedges, of New Bedford; and I found to my great satisfaction, that she was bound to the Sandwich Islands, the very place to which I was most desirous of prosecuting my travels, and that she was to sail as soon as she had refreshed her crew by one or two weeks’ repose, and pro cured wood and water, which were chiefly the objects for which she had entered the port. After this, I was condueted to the quarters provided for me, where I found a servant already in attendance, with instructions w remain during the time of my stay.

On my return to the commandant’s at the dinner-hour that had been named, I found Captain Rudakoff already there, and some of the chinovnik residents in the place. Upon the entrance of the lady, we sat down to a dinner little differing in viands, and nothing in ceremony, from that of the pure Russian repast which has been before the subject of remark. But as the captain had
duties to perform this evening, and my own little affairs fequired attention, we retired together at an early hour after this our figst dinner on shore.

The next morning the ee as well as the whaler, the oyly ships in the port, entered the inner harbour ; and went on board the whaler to make the acquaintance of my doubtless future captain for a longer voyage than that which I had just accomplished. The captain was on board; and it was no sfnall relief to me to fitid the hardy navigator of these eold and storrhy regions, a free, open,:and fhorpugh sailor. He was much delighted, also, to find that he had the chatice of a companipn during perhaps another month? or two of fishing, as well as during ghe voyage, which at once relieved me from the anxiety I had felt from the time of leaving Irkoytsk, on account of my being, for the reasons before mentioned, so ill proyidedwith the means of tiavelling. Our arrangements, therefore, did not cost a moment’s time, nor more,breath than would have been required to throw a harpoon into one of the monsters of the deep with whose blubber the good ship was nearly loaded.,

The next morning at @ very early hour, I went in search of another foreigner of my own nation or race. At the dinne? at the government-house the day before this, I had been informed that the lady of the commandant was ‘acquainted with the English language. Upon questioning her, however, she informed me that she had been instructed in English at school, but thas she had not made much. progress in speaking for lack of opportunity, and that she was now afraid to attempt it., But she informed me, that*there was an honest man here, whose native tongue at least was English, who had been left behind by a whaler that had put into this port many years since, and who had married a*Kamtschadale girl, and had now a grown-up family,,and that she had endeavoured to maké some use of him as an instructor. But she said slpe found his pronunciation so different from that of thé master by whom she had been taught | at school, that she supposed he must be an American, as she had jheard that the Americans spoke the language differently from the English | themselves; and in the meantime, as he was not very rapt at distinguishing the parts of speech into which philologists divide language; she had snot been able to make much use ef him.

In search of this man, therefore, not without some curiosity concerning what he might turn out to be, L was now led by my servant to a little dwelling amorg tle scattered huts of the place. As we approached his door, the good man appeared; and while I was full of expectation of hearing some backwoods-man’s elegant discoursc, behold, quite as,elegant a string of cockneyisms of the style of the quarters of London the least frequented by the schoolmaster, and such as would doubtless as much have startled any home-keeping American of one of the Atlantic cities, as they surprised myself at Kamtschatka,.The Anglo-Kamtschadale, however, had been a bricklayer before he became a sailor and a wanderer so far.

The next day was a féte day among a'l the civilised inhabitants of the little town. The Russians of every race, and the Italians, notwithstanding th. great contrast in their characters generally, which is scarcely exceeded hy that of the climates in which they live, have certainly one point of resemblance, which lies in their nearly equal love of holidays or fétes. There is, nevertheless, a remarkable difference in the days and the occasions for which these dissimilar people severally pass their time of rejoicing. If in Italy you inquire what ‘is the occasion of the féte you find celebrating by masses, processions of wooden or stone images,,and other

appendages to the pomp of Romish worship, you will most probably hear, that it is the day of some wonderfal saint that has stood voluntarily chained to the top ofa pillar till he died’ of starvation or the heat of the syn, or of one who enjoyed the somewhat dirty luxury” of being eaten up by vermin, or perhaps, of one that flogged himself often and well until he died, and for whom heaven has ; ‘@Open’d wide Her everwduring gates ° On golden hinges moving,”. » and appointed him to be an intercessor for all penitents, oahigh. But if you inquire*the cause of a féte you may happen to find celebrating at any place from ofie end of this empire to the other; you are almost sure to heay that it is the natal, or wedding, or name’s day of some near relation of the parties rejoicing ; or, when the holiday is general, of one of the imperial.family. The present féte was kept to commemorate thé exchange of rings -betweeh the Grand Duke’ Constantine, the second son of the reigning Emperor, and the present Grand Duchess, the news of which we brought with us: and the rejoicings indeed ow account of the same event IT had already witnessed at Irkoutsk.

The commtndant gave a dinner on the occasion, at which I had the honour to be a guest; and I had now the pleasure o? meeting the deputy or civil governor of Kamtschatka, Gospodin Stetzenkoff, and my fellowpassengers, the officer of artillery and the ispravnih'; and also several of the chinovnih of Petropavlovski. The officers were for the most part from the Black Sea. It may be gasily supposed. that the service of these coasts is not popular in the Russian navy. Those, however, who engage in it are compensated in a manner our admiralty might do well to imitate. The service is voluntary, and the officers engage for only three years as a fixed period. During this time they have double pay, and at its termination they receivegpromotion.
