Ifthey remain five years, they are allows a halfyear’s pay for the expenses’ of returning; and if ten years, they may retire on full pay of the rank they have attained, or continue in the service, and receive a “pension equal to their full pay when they quitted the coast, in addition to that of the rank they actually hold,

The governor's dinner was°of course a little too much under the influerize of official xestraint to be very Bay: but after retiring for an hour or two, and-qeturning in the evening, according to Russian custom, we had cards, and music and song from. the amiable lady of the houss, aud finally a cheerful supper and the loyal toasts, and such conversation as the time suggested.
Character of the Country.— Capabilities —Obstacfes to Progress.

As I continued to be daily a guest at the governmenthouse, and the character and capabilities of the country, in regard especially to agricultural pursuits, were often discussed, I had the opportunity of obtaining some information on these subjects, as well as of confirming what * heard upon other occasions. 7

A grand obstacle to the progress of the peninsula in this particular must ever arise from its generally mountainous and sterile character. Very little progress has yet been made in changing the mode of life of the inhabitants generally. The Kamtschadaies, however, live in villag@s like the Russians in winter, when they hunt and procure furs, some of which they exchange with the traders for-useful articles, but the most part for vodka and tobacco. But in summer many of them continue still to live more like the independent tribes. At that season they remove to the coasts, where they inhabit fishing stations called yahkolas, and Vve upon any fish they ean procure, from the whale cast on shore, to the cod and herring caught by the line and the net.

Yet there are extensive districts that are exceptions in this respect; and the imperial government, advised by several patriotic commandants at this station, has become aware of this, and. in conjunction with the Agricultural Society of St. Petersburg, hag established two superintendents of agriculture, who travel and distribute seeds sent from,Russia, and collect information concerning the condition and capabilities of the country.

On one occasion at the government-house, the commandant, whose interest seemed fully engaged in the advance and prosperity of the country under his government, exhibited a specimen of cloth manufactured by two Kamtschadale girls of the interior of the country, and also some specimens of the plarts from which it was made. The cloth was not very fine, but was said to be extremely durable. The plant which furnished the raw material is called krapeva by the natives. It very much resembles our stinging nettle, but is of larger growth and of a fibre much strenger. Those which were exhibited were upwards of six feet in length. Specimens of the cloth had alrzady been sent to St. Petersburg; and the agricultural society there had forwarded some rich presents to the two ingenious girls. I could not learn whether the art thus unexpectedly discovered in a land so uncongenial for the growth of ary thing springing from original conception, were a relic, as I strongly suspected, of a xnowledge of the arts once more widely spread, when the country may have been more populous, cr whether it were an extraordinary instance of modern Kamtschadale genius.

At any rate, it may be hoped that it is the incipient germ ofa staple of*commerce, hereafter to develope the resdlirces of the country, which the states now springing into existence around the Pacific Ocean, and the ingrease of the trading of the Chinese must eventually produce.

There are two rivers in Kamtschatka in which oysters and mussels are found, and some pearls. The governor on fhis occasioif exhibited several of the pearls, but they were not remarkable“for size or form. These rivers9are the Goligninor, which proceeds from msmall lake near the southern point of the peninsula, ard the Outkator, which lies further north.

The government has not been unmindful that morai culture, if it do not precede, must at least march hand in hand with material progress of any kind; and the true elements of proper ccivilisation, the means of instruction, have been afforded the natives of the southern districts, of the peninsula. Two Scliools have in effect been established; one at Milkova, 320 versts from Petropavlovski, and the other at Clutchifskoi, G00 versts from the capital. And besides these there are no less than eight other small schools for young children, attached to the same number of churches, which have.b&en erected and endowed in different parts of the country.

The Russian$ of Kamtschatka have not imbibed the inclination and taste of their countrymen at Yakoutsk for the tongue of the natives. of the country they inhabit, and these schools are all expressly for the instruction of the Kamtschadale boys only in the Russian language, and, through that means, in other branches of general. knowledge.
At Pctropavlovski there is only a small marine school, and the boys ‘are chiefly Russians, or of the mixed race. The master of this establishment has a
end of twelve years. The following’ are Ka

salary of 115 silver rubles a year, with a retirement on half-pay at the end of six years,‘or on full py at the the chadale words :— ~God, Ducetaschutch ;. Chinovnik, Herme ; Sun or Moon, Khiht (very guttural); Boy, Patel ;” ; Man, Tatach ; River, Keeiche.

The extreme poverty of the language may be gathered from its having but one term for thé sun and the moon; but stitl more frotne the circumstance that it has scarcely any names for fish or jbirds, which are merely distinguishéd by the moon in which they age most plentiful. Almost all words end with the sognd formed by the syllable iche. ~ Several of the officers stationed here fad been in the northern and mid-districts of the peninsula, and they umreservedly communicated to me all the observations they had had the opportunity of making concernitfy “both the natives and, the capabilities of the country.” Their accounts did not differ in any thing essential from those generally given by ancient travellers in Kamtschatka. They informed me, however, that a second tribe.called Ohlutors,. numbering about 1000 souls, in addition to the Kouriaks, inhabit the northern districts, which have ¢herefore been placed among the native tribes mentioned in a previous page. Their mode of life and théir customs are similar to those of the Kouriaks. Both live without settled habitations, like the Tungouse, and subsist wholly by hunting, and their sole beast of burden is the reindeer. They pay a small yasae in furs to the Russian gévernment; but, save in this formality, they may be still considered as independent tribes, I saw none of either of them; but from all I heard, I am disposed to believe that‘ in feature they equally resemble the Tungouse; but they are declared to be
of a much less docile disposition. Captain Rudakoff,

who had) visited all parts of the shores of the sea of Ochotsk,* informed me that the Russians who; with some Kamtschadales, were settled at the little town of Tighilgh, for the purpose of trading with the natives, were occasionally greatly troubled to keep at peace with them ;.and that during’a winter which he himself spent at a little fortress, fifteen versts north of the small settlement calléd Ijiginsk, at the head of the gulf of the same name, consisting of only 150 men 4nd 250 women, he was obliged tg be continually on the guard. Moreover, during the season at which they came to exchange thair furs, he could only keep at®peace by showing himself always ready for hostilities.

The more southern inhabitants, as well in the features of the face as in the mode of their lives, seem rather to resemble the Yakoutes. The men, as with that tribe, are not much troubled with the appendage to the proper features of the face which grows with, such Tuxuriance upon the chins of the Russians; and I was informed by Russians who had seen some of the Kurilians of the islands, that the men of that tribe are equally deficient in this ornament of the human countenance. —

Such differences as appear in the customs and manners of the Yakoutes and the Kamtschadales probably ° arise from the mere accident of position. The Yakoutes inhabit generally a plain and grazing country, where, notwithstanding the extreme rigour of the climate, they are able to keep cattle; whereas, the Kamtschadaleg dwell in a mountainous country, and their means of subsistence are chiefly fish and the oily amphibious animals with which their coasts and rivers abound.

In regard fo the northern and southern inhabitants of Kamtschatka, the mere circumstance of their using two dissimilar animals for their beasts of burden, has doubtless tended to produce the difference apparent in

their characters—the Kouriaks and Ohlutors employing, as above mentioned, the reindeer; and the Kémtschas dales, dogs. Nor could they occupy or roam over tthe same territory, as the dog of ‘Kamtschatka destroys and devours the deer with the same voracity as the Wolf.

Many conjectures have been formed concerning the races to which the native inhabitants of the peninsula belong; but if what has just been said, be-considered in connection with many previous remarks concerning the tribes of the continent, it will scarcely fail to convince every one that the Kamtschadales, in gonmon with the Rouriats and Yakoutés, belong to the Mongolian famils, and the Kouriaks and ‘the Ohlutors to the same mce as the Tungouse; and that the three last-named tribes have a common origin with the aborigines of North America.

Therz is, however, yet enother, if not two mote, remarkable tribes inhabiting, and possessing independently the whole of that country which lies north-east of the peninsula, and is bounded on the north, the east, and the south-east by the Arctic Sea, Behring Straits, and the Sea of Kamtschatka, Not much is known concerniig them. The inhabitarts generally of continental Siberia believe them to be a branch of the family of the -Esquimohs; but I heard no reason given for this opinion. It seems most probable that they have. a common origin also with the tribes of tHe north-west coast of America. They have generally been termed by the Russians simply the Tchouktchi. In fact, not much more was known with certainty until lately, than that they are a brave and indecpendent people, who have resisted every attempt to subdue them, or to. pass through their territory; Some years since, the Russians sent 200 armed soldiers into their country, rather upon an exploring expedition than with any definite views of conquest. Not a man, however,

returned ; nor has any thing transpired that might lead to a solution of the mystery attending their loss. But as the TcRouktchi are known to be warlike, and skilful in - the use of the bow, there i@ little doubt that the Russians were destroyed to a man. Nevertheless, they occasionally visit the Russian posts to trade with the merchants, ‘where they chiefly exchange mammoths’ teeth and,skins for tobacco and vodka, tind this has led to the little knowledge+that has been acquired*concerning them. They appear to consist of two tribes, one of which issgbject to the other. The highest tribe the. Russians call the Sidiatchi Tchouktchi or Settled Tchouktchi, on account of theiy being stationary, and the other Olenny, or Reindeer, or Travelling Tchouktchi. The mode ®f life of a people confined to a climate so rigorous, with scarcely any commerce with strangers, must* doubtless be such ag would greatly interest us, could we depend upon what we might hear. Several of my friends had visited the mest fertile part of the penfasula in the mid-districts. They described it as comprising an extensive valley, lying for the most part between two ranges of hills, and watered by the River Kamtschatka. Here the soil is composed of fine mould, similar to that which we have seen prevailing in Siberia; and its natural productions are abundant, consisting of a]l the varieties of the fir and the birch, of adner growth than any to be found in the same latitude upon the Asiatic continent. It was the general opinion, that all this part of the country would produce ‘hemp, flax, and the principal culinary vege~ tables. Ships of 100 tons’ burden may advance 2U0 versts up the river which here fertilises the country, Raspberries, strawberries, whortleberries, currants, and cranberries, abound also in the same district. There is likewise much grass-in the lower lands; and many DD 3
.forest trees flourish on the drier soils, ‘such as larch, poplar, willow, cedar, and juniper.

The wild animals most abounding in the “peninsula are, bears, lynxes, sea and fiver otters, reindeer, foxes of different colours, wolves, and martens or Sables. The natives exchange annually about 30, 000 “of the skins with the Russian traders, for various articles of merchandise. Ducks, geese, and other bir ds,of passage, are plentiful in spring and autumn.

Of the fish with which the rivers abound, ines of several kinds is the most remarkable.» One sort, called krasnee (red). by the natives, is commonly taken from three to four feet in length ; and another called garbooscha (hump-backed) i is equally abundant. Herrings are as plentiful in spring and’ autumn, as upon the coasts of Europeand America, Smelts are likewise plentiful at the same season. There is’ also another fish called vachnia, about the size of a herring, and of excellent quality, as I am able to say and well rememLer from having received a present of a large basket full from Gospojah Machin at the moment of my departure, and which we found a true luxury on board the whaler. ;

There is little doubt that the peninsula is rich in mineral deposits, but it has been very imperfectly explored. The natives are said to know of districts which abound in the precious metals, kut which they judge it prudent to conceal, lest it should tend to increase the number of the Russians in their country, and by and by lead, as they seem to have a somewhat obscure presentiment, to their being forced to labour in the mines. That districts of the country abound in iron ore there can be no doubt. Capt.in Vassillief informed me, that perfect iron sand was found in the vicinity of Nijhni Kamtschatka, with which he was well acquainted. Coals are, probably, also abundant.

Captain Rudakoff informed me that they were found in great®quantities, and of good quality, in the vicinity of Tighti€k in the Sea of Ochotsk, to which he had made several voyages. Some tlft I saw at the governmenthouse, at Petropavlovski wére, however, hard and indifferent.

I was politely Goudueted over the hospital here by the commandant, in company with thé government medical superintendent. * It was an establislkment upon precisely the samg footing as d¢hat at Ochotsk. I must here mention, however, that the peculiar complaint prevailing in Siberia, of which the symptoms and effects have been particylarly noticed, does not exist upon this peninsula.

Petropavlovski possesses two humble monuments to the>memory of two of the earliest navigators wlio visited this bay, the unfgrtunate De Ja Perouse and Behring. I visited them in company with my friend Captain Rudakoff. They were both erected by the Russians. That to the memory of Behring-consists of a metal obelisk about eight feet in height. It was sent from St. Petersburgh, and has been placed: in the garden attached to the government-house, and is protected by arailing. That to the memory of La Perouse -is similar in design to the other, but is of wood and is higher. It stands upon an elevated part of the neck of land which has been mentioned as forming the proper harbour, and facing the bay, and is protected by iron railings. It was. erected by the Governor of Kamtschatka soon after the visit of Petit Tours. But, strange to say, there is no memorial of Cook.

Upon the 3rd of October (our 15th), the first snow fell that covered the ground, and upon the 4th, the dog-sledges; called nartees by the irthabitants, to the great joy of the Kamtschadales and also of their dogs, which filled the air with their howlings of exultation,
began to enliven the lonely little seat of government of the vast country which the peninsula compyrises.

The Kamtschatka dog has already been ntcntioned in the account of the latter ‘part of the land journey in Siberia, where he first came under my observation ; but as this remarkable animal is not there found in the perfection of his nature, it was considered better to postpone all'-hat it might be thought necessary to say concerning his character ard qualifications’ until our arrival in the peninsula, where he entirely supplie§ the place of the horse elsewhere, and where all his: useful qualities are better developed, better known, and mor¢, appreciated. "

, This remarkable and valuable animal must be considered as indigenous in this country, where’ he is found roving wild upon the hills, and subsisting in precisely the same manner as the wolf. In his nature, ‘both physically and in-respect to his temper and disposition, he seems about equally to resemble that tameless animal and the mastiff; yet not precisely in ahe manner that might be supposed to arise from the cross breed of the two species, but rather as possessing some of - the qualities of the one and of. the other, neither confounded nor modified, but distinctly marked, and perhaps in equal perfection to the same qualities possessed severally by those animals. He is about the ordinary size of the’ mastiff, and his colour is usually buff er silver grey, with the several darker or lighter shades of these colours as an invariable basis. The form of his body is like that of the mastiff;-but his head more nearly re-

.sembles that of the wolf. His ears stand up in the “same manner,,and are of the same form as those of the wolf. But it is in the eye, and the charicter.of the sense of which this feature is the organ, and in the habits which this engenders, and in his disposition, that the dog of Kamtschatka most distinctly resembles the

wolf. Like his fellow-rover, he sleeps more by day than by® night, and he sees better by the little light afforded’ by the stars or the moon than by the light of the sun; which has giverPrise to the same vulgar error concerning ‘his vision, which is not unknown among ourselves regarding the cat, that he can see in the dark.

If there, be any exception to the distinét manner in which the dog of Kamtschatka possesses the character and qualities of the two animals to which we have compared him, it is in segard to his voice, which is heard in loud cyies, and undistinguishable sounds, between the bark and the howl] of both those animals.

In respect, more particularly, to his disposition, and what may be termed his moral qualities, he may be pronounced to be very intelligent in all that regards thé labot in which he is engaged, very eager to work, and obedient, like the canine species generally, to one master alone, but without being susceptible of that kind of attachment which more or less in*all other species of the dog, enables us to sympathise with them, and even sometimes excites in us a degree of friendship which not every one of our own species is able to inspire us with. Thus, every pack or team of dogs must be always driven by the same hand and guided by the same voice, which the whip, and not caresses, has taught them tcaremember and obey.

The dog with these qualities becomes in this country a very serviceable animal. Whatever, indeed, our hoxses and bullocks perform for.us, if we except carry-_ ing us on their backs and ploughing our arable land, the dogs perform for the Kamtschadales, There is, however, littte employment for them in summer; at which season-they are allowed to range about and get their food, which they generally find in the rivers, in the best manner they can. Some pains are at all times required to keep them in good temper and at peace with their neighbours, both human and of tlieir own species. All who keep a team have near their houses, when the snow is on the ground, either stakes driven into the earth, or poles set up just in the same manner that they are placed to form the frame of a wigwam, to which the dogs are attached singly or in pairs. But it is necessary that, whenever they are paired, whether, indeed, at the stakes or in®harness, that those which are put together-should be nat only of the same family, but of iy same litter, or at least that they-should have been paired since they were puppies. The greater part ‘of them it is at no time safe to leave loose. The younger dogs are said to be the most dangerous i in this way. They will not only kill domestic fowls at all times (which cannot, therefore, be kept by the Kamtschadales), and dogs of the smaller species that*“may chance to be brought to the place, but they have been known to destroy children. While. they do not work, they are tolerably fed, and have usualiy an allowance of half a dried salmon, or a portion weighing about two pounds a day; but when they labour they are worse treated and more stinted than the Siberian horses, and are only given half the quantity of food they receive when at rest; yet they will under this treatment.perform journeys of three or four weeks’ duration with much less repose than the horse would sequire. Nay, they will even upon a journey of four or five days, work for fourteen or sixteen hours out of the twenty-four with~ out tasting any food whatsoever, and without appearing to suffer any diminution of strength ; and the universal opinion is, that the less food they receive on this side starvation when travelling, the better. *
There were probably about eight or ten of these packs or trains of dogs at Petrogavlovski at this time, numbering from seven to fifteen dogs in each, for the

number in a train is always uneven. The reason of this arrangement is, that the most intelligent dog of the pack is'selected as a leader, and runs alone, and is guided solely by the voice°of the driver, or hyourschik, as he is termed by the natives, without any use of reins, and the rest follow him. But on some occasions they Become wholly unmanageable, which renders it dangergus to travel with them. This, however, is chiefly in the country in which the deer abounds, where they are not often used, Such is their love for the flesh of thg. deer, that. they are said to smell that animal even at the distance of two versts; and whenever they get this incentive fo the chase, they start off, and perhapg leave their driver, and whomsoever he may be conducting, to perish in the snow. -

Upon this first day of sledging this season, tlie contmandant 7 politely sent me his nartee and his kyourschih with a train of fifteen dogs, to make a little excursion by way of trying this method of travelling. The nartee is a long, fight, little sledge, appearing at first sight as much too long as the Siberian ordinary sani is too short ; and its seat is not higher than fifteen or eighteen inches from the ground, and it very rar ely carries more than one person besides the driver. It is by no means a comfortablg vehicle, on account of its affording no shelter, and no means of reclining ; for which, indeed, ‘it could not be adapted without more inconvenience than advantage, on account of the constant upsets to which the traveller is exposed, owing to there being no beaten tracks*or roads, and -but a very little level ground in the country.

Having seated myself upon this frail little carriage, which had sonly a light frame back, and which luxury is not, indeed, a necessary part of the national sledge, the hyourschik placed himself in front, just as a lady sits her horse, with a stout stick in his

‘hands, about five feet in length, which was not, as a stranger might suppose, for beating or terrifying the dogs, but to keep the sledge from upsetting. This part of the duty of the driver, indeed, is in general a - most laborious occupation, as much owing to the perpetual obstructions which the sledge encounters, and _the unevenness of the ground, as to its‘ liability to upset, on accdunt of its own great length in proportion to its breadth. ’ ’

Among the better qualities.of the Kamtschatka “dog, has been mentioned his willingness and even eagerness to labour. But this partly, perhaps, arises from his being, at least at this season, too full of rest, and fram the less restraint which he finds from his,harness when at work, than from his chain when at the stake. The sight of one of these sledges in motion is, indeed, a sight so agreeable to the eyes of those at the stake, and the dogs in it are subjects of such envy, that wherever it appears itis the signal for a howl of exultation and hope, which spreads from pack to pack among all the dogs in the place, until the whole amphitheatre within which the town is. seated, resounds with the canine halloo. Thus, from this hour until I left Petropavlovski, the voice and peculiar howl of the Kamtschadale dog rang perpetually in our ears. M
Our little tour upon this occasion was by ‘the lake already mentioned at the back of the towr, and which I

. had before visited on foot; and, deducting the upsets, which were owing to the too great freshness of the dogs than to want of skill in the driver, or to either of the inconveniences above mentioned, the promenade was as agreeable as it was novel.

At day-break, the day after the first fal! of snow, we were all surpriseé: by.the sight of another ship in the bay, which was presently known so be Her Majesty’s discovery ship the Herald, Captain Kellet, which had

been in search of Sir John Franklin and his companions, and had‘ been before in this port at an earlier period of the seasdh. I lost no titine in going off to her, and I found Captain Kellet on board. The enterprising and gallant officer was surprised to meet a fellow-countryman at Kamtschatka, and politely communicated to me all he had experienced that was in any way remarkable during his long search beyond the Straits of Behring, and his conjectures concerning the ships and their crews, which we stidl look for in°vain.

Every on is foo well acquainted with all that has been done.and surmised concef¥ning our regretted countrymen, to render it necessary to make more than a short ‘reference here to the information I receivéd from the captain. He informed me that he had pursued his search until obstructed by the ice; after which, he had “deposited provisions wpon different parts of the desert coast of the American continent, and set up signal posts at conspicuous points, to attract and’ direct the advertturers to the spots where they might get relief, in case they should happily reach the open sea. And he had now entered this harbour a second time, in the faint hppe that the lost ships might have attained this place of refuge, as well as to leave the remainder of the supplics with which he was charged, in case they might hereafter make their appearance. Captain Kellet was at this time, hawever, of opinion that they had returned eastward; and he did not despair of hearing something of them upon lzs arrival upon the Western coast ‘of America, to which he was bound.

The weather he had expericnced durthg the whole of the summer in the seas he had been navigating, had been such as he had not expected, and the accounts he gave of it much sufprised myself as well as my companions of the voyage from continental Siberia. Upon leaving San Blas, on the western coast of Mexico, early in the past spring, he had prepared his ship for the storms which he expected to encounter in the higher latitudes ; but from that timé up to the hour of his arrival at this port, he had had no stronger winds than stiff breezes, to which he could carry his double-reefed topsails, with the top-gallant sails over them; while we had ex-~ perienced a series of gales in much lower. latitudes, which endured for nearly half the thirty-five days that we were at sea.

Before I left the Herald, Captain, Ke! iets finding my intended movements might prevent me-again seein, him, politely gave me at once a frank invitation to avcompany him on his return to the coast of America, but which I was induced to decline, partly on account of his early departure, which would have deprived me of my intended excursion.into the interior of the country, and partly that I wished to visit the group of islands to which the whaler was bound.

Tue part of the country which had been recommended to me for the excursion which I contemplated, was the district of Paratunka, through which a river of the same name flows, and empties itself into the Bay of Avasha. The route necessary to be taken was not obstructed by such natural obstacles as are at this season, in many parts of the peninsula, insurmountable, and it was through a country the most interesting to a stranger in the land, as well as a native, as the future hope of the Kamischadales of this vicinity, on account of its being the best watered of all the southern districts of their country. There were to be seen also in this direction some mineral springs and pools, which in’ themselves were described as cuxious and worth visiting for a few days.
On the morning after my visit to the Herald, Captain

Vassillief, who had volunteered to accompany me on the short expedition, sent word to inform me, that the shallop in which we were to commence our juurney by crossing the Bay of Avasha, was prepared; and at an early hour we set sail for the-opposite side of the bay.

The wind was light and unfavourable, when we issued from the snug little inner port of Petropavlovski, and our craft ‘was with difficulty worked into,the centre of the broad waters, where we were becalmed for several hours: Lut we had before our eyes the magnificent scenery above noticed, and we scarcely regretted oyr detention. Early in the afternoon a light breeze carried us to the entrance of a sheltered inlet, thorgh it failed us when. we wanted about two versts of the shore, which obliged us.to anchor.

We now landed, in a small canoe which the shallop carried ypon her deck, ona lonely beach, with three Kamtschadales whom we had brought for our guides, and a part of our effects, consisting chiefly of provisions. From this, we directed our steps on fout, towards a chain of small and narrow lakes, where some natives living in the vicinity had had especial notice sent tliem, by the commandant some days since to meet us that afternoon with a canoe.

Our path lay here through a forest cf birches and. limes, which though stunted in height, consisted of trunks and branches of large dimensicas; but it was chiefly remarkable, on account of the great age which the trees exhibited. It particularly attracted my attention; for though familiar with the virgin forest from an early age, the wood of similar character, on a narrow tcack in eastern Siberia, was the only instance of the kind I had before seen. Wherever else IJ have haa opportunities of making any observations, the trees have appeared as if they no sooner attained their full growth, than they rapidly gave place

to others that were rising around them, Here, however, nothing was rising, but all seemed aged, yet with but littl8 appearance 0 décay; and the captain informed me that this was the character of the greater part of the forests in the peninsula.

Though the distancé to the lakes did not exceed two versts, the way was so much interrupted by brambles and underwood, that we were as many hours in passing it. ‘Thus it wis full night before we reached the bounds of the ‘wood; and it would-have been infpossible for us ta proceed, hadinok tha snow which.was upon the ground.
eided the little light which a few dim: stars afforded.

‘When we issued frown among the trees, we found very little increase of light to direct our steps. We now, however, hailed with’shrill Indian voices, to ascertain whether the -canoe which we expected, was waiting; and we were soon answered by adiligent Kamtschadale, who had been in attendance during the whole day.

The little craft in which we “here embarked, wasmade of “a single ‘log of timber, and was very narrow, and not very long, and somewhat inconvenient for our party. As we pushed from the shore, there was scarcely light enough to distinguish.the tops of the trees which bordered the narrow lake. After passing through several guts an@similar lakes, which occupied us three hours, we landed and crossed a piece of cleared land laid out in pasture,°which brought us to a rough log house, where we found quarters for the rest of the night.

The good people here were one of several families of the Russian peasant class, which had been brought to the country by Admiral Ricord, when Governor of Kamtschatka, for the purpose of making a beginning in the good wor rk of mingling the Russian and Kamtschadale - blood, as an essential step towards civilising the native population of the peninsula. Marriages, indeed, had even frequently, previous to this time, taken place

between the two races. They had been, however, chiefly confined to Russian sailors, and occasionally theif officers at Petropavlovski, and now and then a pope; taking young Kamtschadale girls tor their wives, which had done nothing towards introducing industrious habits and spreading the arts of civilised life among the native population.

Our hosts for this night gave us a room apart from that occupied by ilicmmelyee: and we Jay down upon the accustomed’ forest substitute for beds, good fresh spruce boughs— often.much more welcome to the traveller upon his journey than swan’s down at home —~ and passed a very comfurtable night.
The next day we rose with the first dawn, took feu: end cakes which the good woman of the house had made from some flour we brought with us; after which, we renewed-our journey.

A short walk now brought us to the River Paratunka, where we found a more civilised Kamtschadale than I had yet seen, also waiting for us, liké the last, in consequence of a notice he had received from the commandant, with a canoe to aid our passage of the stream, and with a nartee and train of dogs to transport us to his abode at thé mineral pools.

We found the Paratunka here a rapid stream of about seventy or eighty yards in width, and bordered on both sides by an aged forest resembling that through which we had passed upon the preceding evening.

As soon as we had crossed the river, the dogs, eleven in number, which had been tied to separate trees, were attached in pairs to the sledge; and leaving our spare baggage to the Kamtschadales that had hitherto kept with us, to transport on their backs, we ‘eet off, under the conduct of our new guide, at full speed upon a path. which he had kept open over an even plain, with nothing to obstruct our way, and with the remains of
coarse grass lying mingled with the snow, and forming quite a wall of -two or three feet in height on both sides. °

As the distance to the Kamtschadale’s abéde did not exceegl, four versts, it was very soon accomplished. Upon our ayrival, the hostess met us at the door with a smiling face, that had been handsome, thongh the cheekbones might have appeared too high or prominent to those who had not become accustomed to the features of the Eastern races, froth'some one of which the Kamtschadales ufiquestionably-spring.’ Her figure was also such as in ‘any part of Europe would be esteen.ed lady-like; and she was dressed‘in a printed cotton gown, of Europegn manufacture of course, and not made unlike ‘those worn a few years since by our ladies in the-earhy part of the day.

It was our intention to°consider this our head quarters, from which we might make somé short excursions during our stay in this vicinity. As the house consisted of two apartments, one of these was appointed for our sole use; and as soon as we were established and alone, the captain gratified my curiosity by an account of our host and hostess, which I nvust here report.

As the Kamtschadales are indebted to Admiral Ricord for the introduction of the’ Russian peasants for the purpose of mingling the races, so also are they indebted to the same benefactor for the medns’ of making a first step towards whatever degree of civilisation they may hereafter prove capable of attaining. That enlightened and patriotic commander while in command here sent three Kamtschadale boys to Moscow to geceive a liberal education, with the intention of placing the instruction of the youths of the country in theirhands on their return. Gospodin Lazarief, our present host, was one of these. Unfortunately, however, in his case the admiral’s be- ; BER 2 oe nevolent intentions were not successful; for with the Jearning and the good manners which he imbibed in Europe, he unhappily contracted the crying vice of the Russians, the love of the vodka,-which is seen in its worst features wherever there is a moderate degree of education, as has often been shown in the examplés which we'have met with in other parts of the country. But he was now so completely lost to all selfgovernmeat, as to have been in mercy banished from Petropavlovski by the present.commandant, and placed in charge of these mireral pools. :

Our hostess, who was of the mixed race, had a ‘siste” in Europe, whose history is curious and interesting. ‘'o those who have not read Captain Cochyane’s jourral of his travels, it may not be known, that that gallant officer espoused a Kamtschadale young lady. the daughter of a pope of the country. The bride’ was extremely young; and the captain, on his return to England, whither she accompanied him, placed her at school, and then set off upon fresh travels. Alter three years he returned again to England, and found that his wife had become quite an English lady, possessed of all the ordinary accomplishmerts common in good society. Captain Cochrane, however, died soon after this, leaving his young widow all his property; and she afterwards married Captain, now Admiral, Anjou of the imperial navy;who is, I believe, at this time port admiral at Cronstadt. And here it is agreeable to record that, to the honour of this Jady, not a post, as her sister informed us, arrives (which is sometimes once and sometimes twice a year), without letters from her to some of her relations in this remote and inhospitable region of the globe. :
The springs of mineral waters are situated upon the western side of the narrow plain which we had passed, and at the very foot of the range of hills which form the

first step of the volcanic mountains which lie in this direction; and the house where we were lodged stands upon thé first rise of the lowest hill, about seventy or eighty yards from one of the several pools which are here formed by the mineral water.

We paid these curiosities an early visit after our arrival. They form a little chain of miniature lakes. The largest is nearly round, and about twenty-five yards in bréadth. Its depth in the centre is from four to five feet, depending upon the weather; but it gradually diminishes on all sides towards its banks. The temperature of the water at the surface while,we wore here varied from 28 to°32 degrees of heat; and the good people whom we were with, informed us, that 30 degrees was its average temperature at this season; Lut, that, during the summer months, it sometimes reached to 34; and thaty during the severest weather in winter, it fell o¢casionally as low as 25 degrees at the surface. ;

That the cold‘in winter has not more effect upon the temperature of the water, must be attributed to the constant supply of the fluid at a very -high degree of heat, which’ is oozing continually from numerous springs at the bottom of the pools, and to the free flow of the superabuiidance of the water, which is carried off by @ narrow stream to the river which we crossed upon the opposite side of the valley.

We lost no time after our arrival, in sani a trial of these natural baths; and as there was no accommodstion for unflressing at the water’s edge, nor other shelter than two little screens formed of dried grass to protect the bather against the stroke of “the wind on either side at the instant of his stepping out of the pool, we cast off our clothes before leaving the house, and put on our coloches, and wrapped our furs, which we brought for the occasion, around us, and after de-
scending to the principal pool, and hanging our furs upon the stakes.which supported the screens, marched in.

We found the water very buoyant, and th. bottom of the pool covered with a aght, loose, dark-coloured substance about, six inches in depth, which rose and thickened the water to the surface where | it was disturbed, but settled again in a few seconds. “ The smell, of this deposit*when taken in the hand was similar to that.of the substance left Within a gun‘after its discharge. 7. ;

As the waters of these pools have nct yet been. analysed, it is impossible to speak with certainty of their component parts; ‘ut, coupling the character of the deposit which is found in them with their sensible and immediate effects upon those who use them, which is a headache, with some people very slight and with others more decided, after the first two or three’ baths, it may perhaps be concluded, that they possess a large proportion "of sulphate of iron anda portion of carbonic acid gas. 7

The other three pools did not seem to differ from that in which we bathed, either in the temperature or quality ofthe water, or in any thing save their dimensions, which, as before observed, were sinaller.

The. season at which these baths shouid be taken, seems to be a point hot yet so much as discussed at Petropavlovski. Nor could I learn that they had the reputation of especial virtue in the cure of any particvlar class of diseases. Our civilised Kamtschadale, indeed, informed us, that the inhabitantsf the country from time- immemorial had used them whenever they were ih; but he knew nothing of their application for any particular complaint or class of complaints. He believed, however, that they cured every body who used them of every illness whatsoever with which they were afflicted. He had never heard of

any one having taken the waters internally. J drank about a pint from the freshest spring one morning before Breakfast, and about double that quantity the next morning ; but I was tot able to perceive any effects from these doses, and J did not think it prudent to take alarger quantity without being more certain concerning the mineral substances which the water contained, Our manner of.taking our baths, and the state of the weather af tht time, will give some idea of the little reygard paid to the methodsof their appiication.. On the day that we arrived, the ‘weather was fine, and we walked into the pools, as above mentioned, in the middle of the day. But upon the next day, when I awoke in the morning, I observed that it was snowiug in large flakes; but finding upon inquiry, after rising, thag. the captain was already taking his bath, I put on my schouba, and descended also to the pool for. the same purpose.. And here the scene was certainly droll. The snow was now falling so thick, that the opposite side of the pool was not visible. But to prevent the snow from settling upon the head it is the custom to wear a cap, usually of red baize, when ‘in the bath; and the captain was now standing in the very centre of the pool, with his head, which was alone visible, not a little magnified by the vapoury medium through which it was seen, with an inch or two of snow upon the top of his red cd@p. And this droll prospect was soon doubled, though there was no third party to laugh at our love of mineral bathing. We were sufliciently amused, however, in laughing at one another as we walked about the pool capped with red baize and snow and not always moving very steadily, as thie feet are subject to be so scalded by the oozing of the hot water from the earth at the bottom, that the bather must cither stand still, by which he will be too soon weary, or dance the polka step while immersed to his neck in the water.

The number of the baths that the captain took daily was quite an illustration of some remarks that have been before made upon the haste, and consequently imperfect manner, with which the Russians ‘are wont to do almost every thing they undertake. The gallant officer ‘began by taking four baths on the day after we ar- Tived ; and the second day he increased the number to six, which he'continued to take every day during our stay. Andso catching is every thing that is wrong, that - when the captain took six baths, I could, not avoid taking at least three..

Besides the natural. curiosity of the mineral pool’, we had the opportunity of seeing here a novelty in agricultural affairs. Among the benefits conferred upon Kamtschatka by Admiral Ricord, was the importation of potatoes for seed into the country. Such, however, has been the neglect of their cultivation, together with the rigour of the climate, that, as far as I ‘was able to learn, they are now only to be found in very small quantities among some of the native inhabitants in the watered valleys of the River Kamtschatka, and upon this spot, where they are preserved in a novel manner. They were put in the ground many years since; but this first step towards accomplishing the objects which the ‘admiral had in view, was, here at least, the last; for, whether owing to the ignorance of the planters or not, they were not dug up :n the autumn of the same year, and being found the next year both abundant and good, they were leftin the ground, where they have remained ever since, decaying and propagating continually, without being in any way affected by the seasons, dnd yielding always more than this family require. But in order to account for tltis fortunate circumstance, it must be mentioned, that although the snow covers the surface of the ground, which is frozen in winter, yet so great is the internal heat in this vol-

canic jicinity, that the earth is quite dry and never frozen below a few inches from the surface. Neither damp nov frost, therefore, can reach or destroy them. We had some taken up and cooked for us on our arrival, and eygry day afterwards during our stay. They were of a bluish colour, and in appearance and flavour, I found them resemble the sort we call kidney potatoes ; ‘but they were in form round.
We made ‘but two or three short excursions in our nartce along the basé of the lower hills of the mountain

“Ghee during our stay here: The chief intérest of our Crives was, the fine views we obtained of the near and dirtant mountains, which in every direction save that towards the sea, presented their snow-capped volcanic’ cones, sometimes in the evening amidst clouds and vapours, which the setting sun so magnificently gilded that they seemed as if they.were again emitting their destructive fires, and sometimes contrasting the chaste white of their summits with the deep azure of the autumnal sky. “"" :

There is perhaps no country in the world that is of more purely volcanic formation than Kamtschatka. The whole peninsula must be considered to be composed of but one vast range of volcanic mountains, and the débris which remains of the substances emitted during their eruption at different periods in the geological history of our planet. Many of them are still in a state of action; and earthquakes are perhaps more frequent here than in any other country. * The number of shoes felt at Petropavlovski averages eight annually. The shock mentioned in the account of our voyage across the Ochotsk Sea, was also felt here, and wa one of the severest remembered by the inhabitants. <All those who gave me an account of this earthquake, agreed in their descriptions of it; and the commandant infurmed me that it endured for no less than eight minutes. During the whole of this time, rumbl ng and loud noises were heard. beneath the ground, and the earth trembled with frightful violence and quick motion. Some of those who expericaced it, said they thought at one moment that the earth was sinking beneath thems and the sea about to rush in upon the land, and the next, ‘that they. were rising upon the crust of the crater of a voleano ili terrible eruption beneath the fround.
